advice: If you are not comfortable with disabled people and their accommodations, be transparent about it.  Don't destroy their careers. Be open to feedback about what things they are facing as obstacles, which you may not realize from your point of view.  Also, pay attention to women who are doing more technical work than men in the same roles but getting paid less, regardless of their level (602 vs 603) and promote them when they deserve it.
pros: Lots of options for roles, mobility, and education/training benefits - as long as you are healthy and conform to being normal. Benefits seem great, but I also pay roughly $700/month for basic just me; still, the in house benefits are pretty great. Free employee assistance program with mental health, free education benefits annually that never run out ($7500 a year for advanced degrees and some partnerships with institutions like Purdue and LSU, etc). Excellent PTO - 4 weeks, plus sick time, some personal days, and even volunteer days. Anything in tech you want to do, you really can - and there is internal training to move over if you started elsewhere, too. All open to you only if you are not disabled, as I discovered first hand. If you have a great manager - and there are so many really great ones - you will have the world.
cons: If you are disabled, you will face significant challenges - doors will be closed to you. You can contribute to many extra curriculars and work well above and beyond, but be invisible as a woman and as a person who is disabled. You will be foremost in your field and top in education and experience, train the dudes on your team how to do the job, and still watch them earn $30k-$40k more than you annually, all while telling the world how advanced in DEI we are. Very little work life balance while you try to chase a promotion for years and years, which you will not get if you are not a conforming person in every day - I hate to say this, but it is absolutely the case. Managers who treat you poorly have no risk in doing so - the company still celebrates them, which can be really difficult to stomach when you've seen them treat people terribly. Pay is below market for the level you provide. I was involved in hiring for a few years and that was a very common complaint and reason we lost great talent. If you do not have a great manager - and there are many who are not - you will never get promoted, you won't ever get a raise, and you can even kill your chances for mobility. The worst thing at chase is the roll of the dice you take with managers. Good ones are incredible, bad ones kill your career.

summary: Ton to learn, because so much is outdated
advice: Fight for your devs. So many people within JPMC seem to function purely on fear. Fear of deadlines not getting met, fear of what will happen if a deadline is moved. Fear of what happens if something isn't delivered the way it was promised. The whole hierarchy of management continuously presses harder and harder as each person fears they might "look bad." No one wants to say "no" or tell someone their workload is too heavy under any circumstances. Ultimately the buck stops with the devs, because we can't pass it on to anyone else. So when someone does the work to prevent devs needing to deal with all the pushback, it is an immense weight off of our shoulders and a way for us to focus more energy into actually doing dev work.
pros: There is a ton of opportunity to build skills into your resume from working here. There is a company wide push towards AWS and React which I have had issues acquiring skills for in my spare time to appeal to other career opportunities. JPMC being as big as they are also supplies a wealth of knowledge that I have not found in other workplaces. Granted it is quite unorganized, so you have to really search for it sometimes. But any kind of language/framework/tooling you can imagine you're likely to find some space to facilitate learning or demonstrate its use.
cons: Work From Home (Hybrid, 3 days in office/week): Jamie Dimon absolutely HATES the idea of WFH and it trickles down to every level of management. My team is split between people in DE, OH, NJ, NY and even India but we all HAVE to be in office for those zoom calls Office: The firm seems to be really focused on getting everyone back into the office while holding onto cost savings from COVID restrictions. Everyone has to "hot-desk" so there's no assigned seating. Full blown open office spaces galore, I've worked in call centers that didn't feel so loud/cramped. But don't worry, the upper management still get their cozy little offices. Work Culture: JPMC is the first FinTech company I have worked for, but holy mother of Tech Debt. There is such a spiderweb of dependencies between teams and no safeguard against backwards-incompatible changes that the majority of the work ends up being migrations because "team ABC has decommissioned their API, now we have to use this." There is the typical corporate culture combining oversimplified requirements and then being inflexible with deadlines. That much I sort of accept at this point. However, what JPMC seems to be particularly good at is allowing projects to barely reach a functioning state and marking it as "done." The team gets moved onto another project with the same expected capacity getting done each week but pretends there isn't another 1-3 months of support needed for the app that was just finished. What's worse is that 1-3 months of support is really a pile of "requirements" that were never brought up to begin with.

If you get a mediocre manager it can really sully your experience. 

Yearly reviews are VERY IMPORTANT! They can make or break your reputation at The Firm and it only takes one subpar review to damage your career for quite sometime. It is important that you keep track of your wins throughout the year (I was a young engineer and didn't do a great job with keeping track of my successes) so that when yearly review time comes you have a laundry list of your achievements. If not, you leave your destiny in the hands of your manager.

Also, there is a lack of diversity in the engineering space. When I left Feb 2022 there were 3 African Americans (not including me) in my LOB out of nearly 7 teams with two of them being hires as recent as the last 6 months. It hurt me to leave because I had been one of maybe two for quite sometime but hopefully there has been a renewed push on diversity.

The business does not listen to technology people. My team became more productive during the 2020 work from home. And the 2021 kerfuffle and lack of planning only caused stress among the tech staff - dates/times for return to office changed on a whim. 

What really gets me is how management DOES NOT CARE about you. Many people rightfully complained that it is difficult to schedule their lives around a constantly changing return to office schedule. And instead of doing anything, there was a mass email basicallh saying 'thanks for complaining, deal with the stress and stop bothering us'.

Cultural stuff - I was on a line of business call with our leaders and found out the hard way that they really do not care about mental health or the LGBTQ+ community. I brought up the fact that several mental health conditions would cause people to struggle with a rotating office schedule and a fixed one would be better. I was hoping for either the fixed schedule or a recommendation to use an internal mental health source - at least lip service. Instead I was told that everyone has to deal with their own problems and find your own help. Took until after I put in my 2 week notice and were hemorrhaging tech talent till they actually gave people mental health resources to help transition out of the pandemic.

Also, if you are a contractor you are at best a second class citizen.

The whole structure of how JPMC runs its trickle down management, pay structure, and how they went about return to office.

JPMC has two glaring red flags with management. 
First is that every development team is required to have a certain percent of contractors so if any budget needs to be cut the contractors are the fist to go. This allows JPMC to save face and say they are not firing anyone. 
Second red flag is how they do 'value adjustments'. Your manager can tell you to your face that you should be earning a salary 10k more than what you make, and JPMC will give you a bonus if you stick around until next February to 'compensate' for that lack of salary. They won't raise your salary to meet that level, just write a check and hope you don't notice how expositive this practice is. 

As for the return to office (RTO) - at first they gave us a 2 week notice to return to office in the middle of the 2020-2021 school year. Then, because management did not have a practical plan to keep social distancing and not everyone could be vaccinated at the time (NOT because it was a 2020-2021 school year where most parents needed to work from home because their kids were learning from home) they back pedaled and kept changing the return to office date and means. It was over two months of consistent changing of the RTO plan(s). 
I found out after I left that a friend and former co-worker self disclosed an immuno-compromise they have, and also this person is a new parent, and they were being pressured to resend their self disclosure and return to the office while COVID was spiking in our area. The reason for the pressure? It made their manager look bad.

summary: Disability Case Mgr "HR service delivery dept needs help"
advice:
1. Treat clinicians as consultants to review disability medical records to make a decision. The admin work (initial phone call to employee, eligibility, pay auth) should be completed by a non-clinician. 
2. Create a criteria set to be used by case mgrs to determine approval or denial to avoid the subjectivity within the Dept and law suits. 
3.,Hire licensed clinicians to review cases for credibility in the department. 
4. Research the Hartford group disability mgmt department operations. (The clinicians are consultants only) 
5. Allow some autonomy for CM reviewing disability claims and 
6. stop with the rigid based performance reviews. 
PLEASE implement work from home asap! There is no need for electronic records to be viewed in the office 100%. You're behind the times and missing out on increased employee satisfaction, increased productivity and less errors by not allowing remote work. The traffic is horrible there.

However, points are deducted for unimportant items when considering the goal/case resolution. There is no criteria available to use when deciding to approve/deny an employees disability claim. It becomes very subjective depending on which case mgr reviews the case. There are employees without a mental health background, degree or license reviewing mental health disability claims. summary: If you like growing as a developer, don't work here
pros:
- relatively good benefits (health, 401k and matching, pension)
- relatively stable workplace (don't feel like I could ever get fired lol)
- this isn't true for all teams, but my team has been very flexible in allowing me to work remotely full-time which has been great for me
- if you like finance, working for a bank, specifically as an eng in the IB, gets you as close to traders as you could get which can be interesting if you like that stuff
cons:
Working for a bank obviously has its cons but the biggest things that stand out to me:
- we don't retain good engineers (everyone leaves) and we also don't listen to the concerns of our engineers
- we don't have competitive pay compared to other tech companies
- lack of diversity in engineering (specifically among females and BIPOC)
- very hard to make it above VP level and we really don't promote women or BIPOC into leadership (levels are analyst, associate, VP, ED, MD, e-board)
- we don't adopt new technologies frequently so engineers skills remain stagnant
- tech stack is very internal (a lot of stuff was built in house so skills are not very transferable)
- teams are overstretched to the point where everyone experiences burnout (we don't backfill positions when people leave so team is still operating at previous level with less people)
- team has on-call rotation which progressively gets worse as people leave/we onboard newly built technology and our production support team effectively does nothing to help (so half of your job is site reliability which isn't for everyone)
- overall, seems like everyone hates their job which isn't the best work environment

summary: JPMorgan Chase: pays well if you have a strong stomach

pros: JPMorgan Chase is a "target-rich" environment for technologists -- there's always something to fix, or something to break and then fix again. The benefits are good, the pay is very good, the Columbus facilities are nice, and they have a lot of money to throw at shiny new toys. Some programmers and engineers have more stressful lives than others, but there is nothing like the horror stories one hears from game development shops. You can come across the occasional diamond in the rough or guru while working there, and it is a good place to network for future job prospects.
cons:
JPMorgan Chase is not a technology company. There is little respect for technical analysis or input. Management often overrules or ignores the actions of the technical staff, and there is almost never any effective recourse.

There is little room for advancement for someone not interested in management or finance. As a multinational bank, JPMorgan Chase must be one of the largest users of technology in the world -- yet as a rule, they give their janitors and their engineers roughly equal influence over the direction of IT.

Design by bullet point is a pervasive practice at JPMorgan Chase, since half of the people there are apparently functional illiterates. Death march projects are common. Often projects exist or proceed the way that they do solely to perpetuate various middle management fiefdoms.

advice:
The highest level management seem to be driving the company quite well, as reflected by profits and dividends.  However, they clearly are unaware of how the mid-level management functions, or how many levels of managers there really are.

Recognize and appropriately reward your employees.  Getting a bonus of $4000 at the end of the year is nice, but if you break that down into how many evening and weekend hours actually worked, it winds up being just a few dollars an hour.

Employee Satisfaction Surveys are completely invalid, as the user must enter their SID, and the reports go back to managers who only have 10 or fewer direct reports.  It's very easy to figure out who said what and the takers of the survey know that, so they lie.  Use an external company and don't require an SID.  That will give you a report of actual feedback.

Be aware that the "good ole boy network" is alive and well at JPMC.  There are people who only have the job they have because of it.  It's costing you money.

Any manager should have manager training and learn how to encourage their staff.  Managers should be rewarded based on the team output, and the team satisfaction.

advice:
* Stop Managing in the Moment *
-- Short term cuts to the bottom line in order to gain easy performance appraisal bullets invariably reveal inherently short-sighted, "path of least resistance" thinking after you have moved on.

* Do your ROI homework *
-- Make the case for investing in technologies that have an upfront cost (yes, there's a bill - deal with it) but end up paying for themselves many times over in the form of vastly increased productivity and streamlined processes.
-- Learn how to quantify lost hours spent compensating for a second-rate solution and *sell* the *right* solution to senior management.  This is a high risk move, but will pay out huge dividends when it succeeds.
-- Listen to your staff for clues on where to look for long-term investments - after all, these are the folks that will be supporting it on a daily basis, and can highlight current process strengths and deficiencies you may not be aware of.

* Lose the ranking system *
-- You don't need the current ranking system to reward exceptional performance, and you know it.

advice: Even though profits have been low, they are higher than most other banks.  And there are still profits, not losses.  Share with the little folks, please.
pros:
I've always held salaried positions, never paid for OT.  This is the first company where I haven't had to beg for comp time.  My boss actually *tells* us to take a day off when we've worked late.
When I was hired, I was also told that I was expected to change departments every few years, to avoid being pigeon-holed.  Most people in IT are familiar with that problem.  JPMorgan Chase wants their employees to learn as much about the business as is humanly possible.  It makes us valuable, not tired, stagnant, and unhireable (which is pretty painful if you've ever been laid off).  
I also don't expect to see any layoffs soon.  That's almost unheard of in the past decade.
cons:
Lots of bureaucracy, just like any large company.  Lots of forms to fill out, quarterly reviews.  It's hard to get new tools (like software) because it has to be approved at several levels, then tested.  On the other hand, while we don't have bleeding edge software, what we do have is pretty stable.
I was also led to believe that I would get a sizeable bonus at year end.  I was seriously disappointed.  The bonus was supposed to make up for the pathetic raise (which I did not have advance warning on).  Worst raise I've ever gotten.  And yes, I had a good performance review.

advice: Value existing employees over new employees.   Give them raises to remove the financial incentive to leave.  Allow them to make vertical internal moves to reduce attrition.  Get rid of the buddy-buddy review process so people aren't only giving bonuses to people they like.  Get rid of all the technological barriers and spend money on technology that will empower developers to work at their full potential.

summary: Very political company; you have to seek out your own success

pros: As a huge company, there is opportunity for moving around if you search it out yourself. cons: The culture is very much about cost cutting, to the detriment of investing intelligently in the business to foster growth. summary: JPMorgan Chase: Once your in, your nuts if you leave...

cons: It's a very large company, so there are many bureaucratic things you need to be able to deal with.

summary: A good place for new employment opportunity

pros: JPMorgan Chase is a very good company to work for.  They have a very good benefits program and for the most part they work hard to keep a good work-life balance.
cons: Unfortunately like any large company, they pay market value for new employees but for their loyal existing employees you are lucky if you are even keeping up with inflation.  it's very distressing to find the people just coming into the company with less experience and education than you are making more money than you. summary: Ups and Downs, Like any corporation
advice: Simplify management structure and hold management accountable for their relationships with employees.  Focus on providing opportunities to talent within the organization and optimizing their skills.  Annual review process needs massive update.  90% of the organization ends up in "meets" or "on track" and there are no opportunities for advancement or raises unless you happen to achieve the highest performance once a year.   Quarterly reviews would be nice, along with a more customizable review process.
pros: Structure, benefits, Pay on average.
cons: Management is disconnected from the average employee.  Too many levels of management dilutes the communication from top to bottom.  Employees have to basically riot for the smallest concessions.  Recruiting system is abysmal.  Poor forecasting results in massive layoffs and poor transparency about the future.  After two layoffs of almost the entire department, I realized that moving up in the organization would be impossible and it's time to look elsewhere for employment.

Pay is not very competitive and raises are difficult to get unless of course  you're a lifer.

All three managers I had the privilege to work with had been extremely helpful in communicating what they needed from me and helped me along during my stay there.  The work can be slow sometimes but you can almost expect to work 40 hours a week and go back to your family on a regularly basis.

At present all JPMC employees are perfect mercenaries and everyone in the firm knows it.

The "bottom 20%" are in fact just the ones that management simply does not like for one reason or another.  Thus, this practice (supposedly recommended directly by way of consultation by Jack Welch) is just a way to justify their subjective prejudices.
