advice: Stick with guidelines once socialized.  Stop relying so much on consultants.
pros: You can say you work at JPM Chase.  Benefits are good.  People are generally good, but sometimes not motivated.
cons: Red tape, beauracracy, change is slow, slow, slow.  Massive paperwork required and 10-15 signatures required to get a simple change put in production.  Extremely stifling for someone who is results-driven, especially having come from a high-caliber shop.  Working off a lap top as opposed to a workstation is another horrible experience.  Frequent re- orgs.  Management outlines one policy, and several months later said manager is no longer at jpm.  Typical response to an outage is: 1) freeze on changes for an arbitrary period of time.  2) have endless meetings (on a call, almost never in person) 3) reveal post-mortem for which the action item is to add another signature to any change.

summary: Where's the Forrest?  All these trees are in the way!
advice:
Fear stifles good ideas from being shared.
A genius working for JPMC would retire an associate.
Don't hire the disabled to do jobs their disabilities prevent them from succeeding at.
Fear has turned the organization into a bunch of "yes men".
Have an open door for things other than compliance issues.
Your people really only cares about their bonuses.
Being a senior manager doesn't mean your ideas are good by definition.
pros:
Great benefits.
To big to fail. 
Vision for change. 
Many good rank and file people. 
Numerous Opportunities. 
Every corporate culture is in there somewhere.
Once your established your financially set.
cons:
Inconsistent team management.
Profits transcend everything.
Pay and responsibilities don't align.
Death marches are a way of life.
Actual change is compliance driven.
Daily experience totally depends on who you work for.
Senior management clueless on how things actually work.
Priority is driven by what senior management is scrutinizing.
Ethics are preached but only really count if there is financial risk.
ADA is preached not practiced.

summary: It doesn't pay to be a high performer
advice: Reward your high performers for being high performers.  If you don't do this then they will leave and you have to hire new people that require training.  It blows my mind that the company and it's managers would rather spend money to train people instead of just taking that same money and paying their existing employees more.  People that feel taken care of will work harder than those that don't.
pros: Excellent work life balance in IT.
cons: Poor compensation increases.  Only way to get paid is to BEG or leave and come back a year later.  They pay people coming in off the street more than those who establish a career there.  Strange if you ask me.

advice: Stop treating employees like children. Give us more flexibility and trust. Less micromanagement. Better technology to compete with the fin-tech companies like Sofi and Ally.
pros:
-PTO
-Food days if you like food
-Snack cart
-Good benefits
cons: The flexibility is awful. You are given a lot of vacation time. However it can be hard to get the days you want, because they limit the vacancy to 20% which makes it very difficult around holidays to take time off. They tell you to enjoy time off with your family around the holidays though they don't really give you the flexibility to do so. You will probably work Black Friday and Christmas Eve every year unless you have seniority. There is no flexibility to work from home either. I always thought they'd come around with that since so many other banks already have but they haven't. Hours are strict, you will not able to make your own and will most likely get crappy hours if you're just starting. There is also no career mobility in Milwaukee as it only houses home equity unless you want to work in a branch or move out of state.

advice: Listen to your staff.  Offer assistance to the staff to allow them to grow and move up with company.  Respect your staff and what they have done for the company.
pros: Excellent paid time off and benefits.  Opportunities to work within the community helping others.
cons: Not a lot of promotional opportunities unless you are in tight with management.   Management was clueless on what teams were completing, often times being pulled in different directions by their superiors.  There was a lot of secretive discussions not shared with the teams pertaining to their job stability.  Minimal assistance provided to grow with the company, often times leaving you stagnant in a position or shuffling from lateral position to another - regardless of your past experience and what you have brought to the company.  Low salary for for positions that demand higher pay in the competitive market.

summary: big, bureaucratic, rampant cronyism, not a place for young, energetic, and ambitious
pros: Good benefits, salary, place to be if you are day-in day-out
cons: I observed rampant cronyism to the point when a people with only a high school diploma and no technology background were accepted into IT Executive Director positions, just because of "networking". The JPMC also goes out of its way to discriminate against straight white males, by using race, gender, sex orientation as criteria for promotion. The IT in particular is overrun by immigrants from India because Chase signed exclusive agreements with TCS and Cognizant (Indian IT companies) to provide all consultants, who are then converted into FTEs. As a result, it is common to see 80%  of the people on the floor are from India. Needless to say, it is just another form of discrimination.

summary: Great company especially when you put the work in!
advice: Don't be so hesitant and rigid when it comes to promotions, when someone deserves a promotion make it happen for the employee, don't weigh up time in role at a certain level, base promotions purely on promotion and effort put in - retention is key! People leave the company and then come back into the company to receive VP/ED level faster, I don't think this should be a thing, retain your employees and promote your employees when they should be!
pros: Great Benefits, great networking opportunities, diversity is rife
cons: Its very easy to get comfortable when benefits are good and salary is good but there are so many amazing opportunities so you have to learnt o balance your work life an attending events to ensure you are actively seeking new opportunities even when you love your job!

summary: Learning is good they have all kind of technology, financial growth is bad and there is not recognition.
advice: Give raises to your exceeds people and low pays to the new guys, they do the oposite and they always lose their Sr. Staff because of this.
pros: Always on top of technology day to day learning is awesome, for engineers is the place to be for 2 years and leave, chase will make you an expert on any field because they have all kind of problems.
cons: Management is weak, they dont fight for their people, they do the force ranking review that even if you are great you never get an exceeds because they have a budget (industry standard but is unfair) no raises, so be sure you cut the best deal before you get in, the new healthcare is realy bad you pay 3000 in deductible and 2500 coinsurance and month to month is expensive, very near to a private insurance.

advice: Greater attention needs to be paid to developing and promoting internal talent.  Processes need to be streamlined.  Do not require meetings on global corporate topics that have no impact on individual contributors
pros: The job was stable, you knew what was expected of you from day to day.  The work load was reasonable, and could usually be completed in a 40 hour week.   Once assigned a project, you were generally left to manage it on your own
cons: Worked on older technology, generally 2-3 generations behind.  Constantly bombarded by email about people and departments that you never interacted with.  Constant meetings that served little value.  Strict and often conflicting standards and policies imposed by various departments.  Very little chance for advancement as an individual contributor.  Training was not generally provided, and would sometimes need to research new technologies on own time

summary: A great place to gain experience and have a long and varied career
advice: Continue to treat your employees as valuable team members and realize that everyone can contribute, regardless of rank or length of service.  Recognize that the work environment is changing and allow for flexible options, locations, and activities to get the most from your employees.  Continue to treat everyone with respect and you will be more rewarded by your employees.
pros: Company provides a wide range of experiences in the financial industry, from personal banking to investment management, tax, asset allocations, etc.  The people are supportive and do not treat non-management like peons.  Company communicates well and discloses corporate information appropriately.
cons: Banking can have long hours, lots of travel which is great if you want it but can be difficult if family is of strong concern, financial industry has lots of ups and downs so be prepared to weather the storms

advice:
- Shift to a compensation model that rewards high performers in tech; Use record profits to grow salaries and bonuses for technologists, not just for bankers.
- Embrace the Work From Anywhere (WFA) model for tech, it's a proven model that works. In-office mandates are archaic.
- Prioritize removing barriers/silos between tech groups (product/security/ops).
- Improve the digital product development lifecycle internally to ensure end-users are more plugged in with product teams and the changes they roll out.
- Build a culture that puts a larger emphasis on change/transformation from the top-down, and cultivates stronger partnership between business and technology.
pros:
- Job security and benefits
- Smart, high-performing, and diverse teams
- Reputation and integrity
- Market leader; Technologically advanced relative to other big banks
- Opportunities for networking, professional development, and continuous learning
cons:
- Bureaucracy and red tape
- Tech group silos (product, security, ops)
- Lacks work flexibility and compensation for technologists
- Resistance to change/transformation

summary: Great Benefits, Poor middle Management - GTI
advice: They have to learn to become better mentors and understand that overloading is not the way to a quality product.
pros:
okay pay. 
great benefits.  
Work from home on occasion is not a problem with preapproval.  
4-weeks vacation to start. 
Pension, 401k with 100% match after a year; vest after three years.
State of the art Technologies
cons:
Work/life balance is poor due to the fact that they are understaffed, overloaded, and yet someone was just laid off.  So, the workload has only increased. I find myself working in the evening and weekends and yet still under water
Many managers do not speak much to their direct reports.  No Support is given by managers.  Its a sink or swim environment. 
Typically no raises, and bonuses don't necessarily increase so you may end up with the same total comp for years at a time

pros:
- Good Work Life Balance
- Allows for team mobility after a year of working
- Good benefits
- If you just want to get paid decently and just coast through life, this is a pretty good option.
cons:
- The development process is incredibly slow (as are most banks). It takes forever to make a change and get things out.
- They rely heavily on internal tooling and frameworks that are not transferrable to the outside world. So getting a job afterward is more difficult.
- Unless you're talking to a VP and up, a lot of people here aren't as competent with good developing practices.
- The amount of brown nosing that happens is really annoying
- Executives are always slow to adopt necessary tools and basically fish for praise when they implement a super simple idea that has already been around in the industry for years. They are also pretty detached from reality of everyday people.

advice: Listen better to your advisors, show the "care" factor.
pros: Many locations across the country, technologically well-equipped platform, good back office support, you can meet some good employees that can make your day better. Benefits are ok, although several years ago were much better.
cons: Base pay is somewhere between the lowest and avg in the industry, incentive plan continues to change for the worse (banking and brokerage), huge level of nepotism to older advisors (maybe 5% of all advisors on the platform) since their annual revenues are somewhat high, however, they have been with the company for 15+ years. You don't get a feeling that the management cares much, because you can't have real and honest conversations. If you are thinking about joining this firm, make sure you understand how politics work, fighting, literally fighting between the bank side and the brokerage side happens daily. Although it is one firm, it does feel like each department is on its own. Performance of their managed account is among the lowest in the industry, therefore there is a huge amount of outflows. Management tends to procrastinate any decision-making in a way of passing the responsibility to another executive, so not much gets done. Moral in the offices is at its lowest, many good bankers left to other banks and you are stuck with new bankers which expect you to train and often times have 0 financial services experience.

advice: Need to be able to make quick but smart decisions, somthing Ive seen a lack of in the past 6 months.
pros: Managers treat all employees with fairness and respect.  Everyone's opinion counts.  Feedback on how you are doing is given when asked.  Anytime I have asked to take off it has been given to me, even during times there are "blackouts".  As long as you know ahead of time, they are pretty reasonable with work from home/time off.  Career opportunites to move laterally and up are out there, but they wont just be given to you, you must ask and work at getting offers for mobility throughout the company.  Benefits are some of the better ones I've seen, generous vacation is given as soon as you start.
cons: Compenstation seems to be on the lower side compared to the average.

summary: If you're interested in finance technology, a good place to build a career
advice: Check in with your employees to make sure that they are not getting burnt out. That is a very common thing in JPMorgan but I will give them credit for trying to rectify that.
pros: When you get a good manager or a good team, you can really propel your career forward. Career is a big buzzword here at JPMorgan. They emphasize training, networking, and visibility to upper management. Plus mobility within the company is a very real thing
cons: With so many employees and so many various managers, there can be a decent chance you end up with one that does not suit you or is so caught up in their own career they don't feel like guiding yours. Sometimes dealing with legacy platforms can be a pain.

pros:
+ Supervisors were incredible, friendly, but still productive.
+ Flexible part-time hours
+ There weren't any unreasonable expectations set on anybody.
+ Very few surprises

The job was pretty much a cookie-cutter data entry position. They provided good accommodations for typists; good chairs, adjustable desks, standing desk options. Working with sensitive information requires a lot of precautions and regulations, and the supervisors did their best to mitigate them.
cons:
- No excitement/variance, though it's to be expected of a data entry position.
- Very strict breaks, lunch times. If you're not on break, you're glued to the keyboard.
- High security/lots of regulations. You pretty much can't take anything onto the floor except very specific music players. This just comes with the nature of the work, so I can't really blame the company/management.
- Keyboards were old and worn.

summary: I have never worked in a more discriminatory workplace as an American.
advice: To Senior Management: Please have in person, thorough training to your VP's, ED's on unconscious bias, inclusiveness and anti-discriminatory behavior when working for a US company. Inclusion and acceptance of people from different backgrounds and ethnicities should be taken VERY seriously as a US company representing American workplace values. I have never worked in such a discriminatory workplace as an American.
pros: Good name until you find your next job.
cons:
There is very little growth here because career development is a highly political task based on the following reasons:

You don't have to be a decent colleague, person or good technically. Culture and treatment and opportunity is determined by your manager's  race to your race. 

My team has production issues left and right, yet people who are writing bad code claiming they have 10 years of experience that are still getting the exposure and visibility to leadership because they speak the same foreign language as their manager.

advice: Communicate more often and be more blunt about expectations, deadlines, what you wish to see more of, etc. Provide individual criticism to help employees understand what they can do better and how they can move up.
pros:
- Lots of freedom, managers don't micromanage much
- The facilities are gorgeous and they have a Starbucks + 2 cafeterias inside + small snack shop
- The experience working here looks great on a resume
- Great benefits, bonuses are nice, referral bonuses can happen, there are a lot of ways to benefit from working here
- Many positions require late night calls because we work overseas. This can be exhausting and frustrating.
cons:
- Work is boring and generally unfulfilling
- I never feel like I matter here and cubicle work gets depressing
- It's a big company...if you like that kind of environment you'll love Chase, but it feels too big to me.

advice: Set up more locations
pros: The pay is great and everyone is pretty nice. The only down side so far is that the hours are really long but it goes by fast, you are always busy. They have a great system for when you put in overtime, you can order food easily and they pay for your cab ride home. Theres also a lot of discounts and benefits to being an employee.
cons: It can be hard to have a personal life at some points since work is so overwhelming but if you can manage your time and you like what you do then this is a great place to work. This might not be a downside to some people but I dont really like how frequent people have to travel, its alright if you are single but for a family it can get stressful.

summary: Too much bias in senior management.
advice: Give due credit to the actual employee who does the work instead of giving it to your "yes man".
pros: Good brand name to have on your resume. If you are targeting other big name companies, then it is a good name to have on your resume. I have heard back from companies like Google once I put their name on my resume.
cons: Biased management which will give credit for your work to their own "Yes Men". Horrible work/life balance missing something as basic as a library and charging you even for a simple water bottle. They will expect you to work beyond your 40 hours on weekends as well with no compensation or reward, however they will flag you on other days even if you are 10 minutes late.

summary: Like all of corp. America, nickel and diming. Highly rated managers have mastered the skill of avoiding collabaration
advice: As a too-big-to-fail institution, there is little incentive to do the right thing for customers. The lawyers and lobbyists are paid to keep you out trouble and they usually do. But this attitude poisons your long term prospects. If people can leave as customers or employees, they will.
pros: Salaries are on the rise. As long as you are entering the organization, they will compete. Individual departments can maintain team spirit. If you're working on a hot project, then you will be valued.
cons: Monstrous security bureaucracy (they kept promising fixes where on the way, maybe?). FUD is the main management tool. As in most corps, no loyalty given OR expected. Do what is best for you. Always!

pros:
Pay and benefits are okay relative to what’s expected of you.  Easy interview process. If you are just looking for somewhere to be, it’s easy to get hired here.

The company promotes progressive values and inclusiveness.

If you can stick it out for a year you can change positions internally. Assuming you want to stay.
cons:
Too much siloing and bureaucracy. People tend to be unwilling to go beyond their silo to help. It takes a while to get to know people because of office culture.

Unless someone really needed a job, I wouldn’t recommend It.

You’re forced to take poorly designed training courses that are well intentioned but ultimately a waste of time.  I’m sure there are good compliance reasons behind them though.

I don’t get the sense that many people are actually happy here.

summary: Education and backround mean nothing to Chase.
advice: Train your entry level managers to understand that they have talent above even their own in many site locations due to the current employment market. Doing so will dramatically reduce turnover and make chase an employer experienced bankers would like to work for. Your loosing your talented staff to you competition due to your hiring criteria for managnment level staff. IE: high school diploma and 1 year management experience...its a joke. No wonder Chase has so many legal issues.
pros: Large stable employer, Reasonable training
cons:
Chase promotes a culture of micro management where even some of your peers try to exert power over you.
Chase takes full advantage of the current economic situation by placing people in positions that are entry level even though they have masters degrees and 15 years exoperience.
Chase does not value its human capital at all.

advice: Too many acronyms, too many systems that don't talk to each other, and too much politics.
pros: Excellent benefits for employees in terms of Paid Time Off (4 weeks vacation, 9 Federal holidays, 3 Personal days, and 6 sick days), Maternity - Paternity leave ( Moms get 12 weeks paid maternity leave, Dads get 1 week at the time of birth).
cons: Too much politics inside the company. Internal job postings are plenty but you cannot even apply for them unless you inform your manager that you're looking. You getting or not getting the job completely depends on your current manager's feedback. Year end bonus and pay raises completely depends on your rating by your manager. The rating is finalized before you get to know. There is no discussion regarding the rating. Its more the management telling you the rating. If you're 'in the circle' then life's good.

advice: If it's not broken, then do not bother fixing it.
pros: You have a job.  Be thankful.  You have a great job.  Wash, rinse, and repeat and repeat some more.  You have a job.
cons: You leave dumber before you came into the company (brain drain).  PMC/Performance Management is a joke.  HR is a suicide prevention hotline.  A new fire drill to contend with every day.  Innovation is stifled.  People are not accountable for their actions and got away with being shluffs.  WM, CCB, and CIB were the worse people to work with.  When tempers flared, the CIO comes in on a chariot and calms the waters.  Extremely poor hiring practices.  Wrong people hired for jobs.  Company would put employees in a position so they would leave and not have to pay severance.  You are just a standard ID.  Run as fast as you can away from this place if you still work for it and don't look back.

advice: Develop the communication and the way the managers treat the employers. Follow standard like Scrum agile and don't try to follow manager standard because when you change to work with different manager every manager can has his own standard.
pros: I am not sure, maybe the salary and the value to have on your resume
cons: The manager is God, and everything depends from the manager you have. Doesn't matter if he doesn't follow any standard, everything has to be as he said, if he said I want you to finish this by tomorrow you have to finish, even if you try to explain there is not possible, he doesn't heard nothing. This was the first time I don't want to wake up to work, your quality life is gone. They way the manager talk you is not professional, if you say you expect to complete a user story in one or two day he interrupt you and laugh about the time you estimate and he said "I can do this in 5 minutes"

summary: JPMorgan is a great place to work, offers interesting, challenging work at competitive salaries
advice: JPMorgan should seriously consider revamping the performance review process, to make it less subjective and reliant on abilities of your own manager to present your case in an impactful way.
pros: From my experience, JPMorgan has many intelligent employees who are good to work with.  They also support mobility within the company.  A big bank like JPM has some of the biggest technology challenges, so therefore also interesting technology work.
cons: The huge size of the company can make people who aren't natural networkers not succeed as well as they might in a smaller place where their work is easier to recognize.  Also, the performance review and inter-ranking process is very tough as a manager, and can be unfair in some cases.

advice: In order to improve retention there should be more things done to show that the employees voices are being heard. Casual Fridays and other similar notions are weak attempts at creating a better office environment. There are no lounge areas and office space can be crowded since the company is in an expense cutting phase but I guess that can be expected with a finance company.
pros: JP Morgan roles offer exposure on the scale that few companies can match. They also offer at first glance attractive salary and vacation from entry-level through Officer level
cons: At the Delaware offices there was an extremely high turn over and little planning by management to help retention. Highly political office environment where you were expected to stay late even if your work was done, this differed depending on the team.

summary: WaMu WAS a great place to work.
advice: Senior Management should have used some common sense in the mortgage market.
pros: WaMu had a lot of great talent.  The company paid well for performance and did not give raises and bonuses to poor performers.  Achievements were publicly recognized, which is good, but too often those achievements were made possible by ignoring all policies and going full speed ahead.  The company should strive to recognize those that achieve great things while still following processes and policies.
cons:
The biggest downside is the company failure.  When WaMu was a going concern there was not enough accountability for poor performance.  Employees who did not perform well were never fired and were allowed to drift along.

Another downside was the lack of good training.  There were many online course offered but many things cannot be taught effectively in an online course.

summary: With the right opportunity, a great place to work!
advice: Make the tough decisions when evaluating staff for retention or promotion.  Often, the wrong person for the job is rewarded with the selection.
pros: In this economic environment, Jamie's fortress balance sheet can be extremely comforting.
cons:
The never ending mergers and acquisitions of other firms has resulted in a poorly defined and understood corporate culture.  If you are lucky, you will work with strong direct management  with a strategic vision to accomplish objectives.

In the current climate, mobility is an issue.  Although jobs are available, the numerous M&A's have resulted in decentralization of resouces.  If your willing to go to Columbus, Texas or the north-west, you may have an opportunity for mobility.  Forget it if  your tri-state based.

Carefully consider the compensation and benefits.  As with most companies, the overall package is becoming less attractive.

summary: The worst corporate culture I have ever experienced
advice: More than half of the management is redundant and serves only to protect itself and make life as difficult as possible for the employees - status calls, spreadsheets to track everything, dashboards, a giant waste of time.  This company could easily fire half of the people who are in management roles and have zero negative repercussions.
pros: Decent pay (but not best in class), and some degree of growth is possible if you play the political games and do whatever they ask you to do, no matter how stupid it is.
cons:
Routinely threatened to move to a "strategic" location (basically Ohio, Texas, Florida or NY/NJ).
No clue about letting people work from home, or other locations.
Micromanagement like crazy - managers demanding their employees get doctor appointments pre-approved before they make them.  
Constantly being told to do stupid and contradictory things.
Organization is completely broken due to processes and change controls, it can take months to do something as simple as setup a server in a datacenter or get access to login to a system.

advice: Stop the propaganda about promoting career-mobility if the senior managers wont let the employees go. People want to stay with the bank but not in the their current role
pros: unlimited overtime upto 6 months a year and good benefits
cons:
under-paid but you have the OT , peer group sucks - about 90% of the people complain but dont do anything about it. I was a part of a college group of 95 people and only 10% of the people are left after 4 years. People come and go all the time in this business specially with Chase. It depends if any money is the factor that drives you - this job isnt that bad but at the end of the day you will be soul-less. Management sucks - you always gotta be looking out for yourself. 
If you are 45+ and want a stable job till you retire: this place isnt that bad but if you are young and ambitious it will suck the soul out of you. Staying out of the corporate retail dept. is a good call.

advice: Stop sweating the small stuff and focus more on leadership and technical training. Let people master what they already  know how to do, before introducing  changes. Changes tend to reflect a "flavor of the month" culture, whereby go-getter managers sign up for initiatives (to make themselves look good) and then delegate the actual work to employees.
pros: Employees and managers were sincerely helpful and forgiving of mistakes. Best new hire training, continuous training opportunities available which prepare you for success at other companies as well as Chase.
cons: Every typo or non-impactful mistake is documented regardless of overall performance, however, managers see this as "coaching." Regardless, this hurts team morale and comes across as petty and ridiculous. Often asked to do extra, unnecessary (flavor of the month) work by management as a result of managers advancing their own career agendas.

summary: WaMu swollowed up whole by JP Morgan Chase.
advice: Senior Management needs to take a closer look at driving efficiencies in all areas and at all levels of the enterprise.
pros: One of the few remaining banks with probably the most promising financial outlook. If you have a job that made through all the consolidations and transitions with Bear Stearns and Washington Mutual, you should have a secure and maybe even prosperous future at least through this challenging economic crisis.
cons: Huge corporation. Inefficient in many processes. At Washington Mutual we had focused to drive down costs in technology for the last 4 years without sacrificing customer service or quality. While challenging, I do think significant progress had been made. This became particularly visible when aqcuired by JP Morgan Chase where some of the organizational structures and technical strategies reflected the problems and issues WaMu had dealt with years earlier.

summary: Great financial institution to work for
advice: Assess what are the new working methodologies, tools and techniques that can be employed so that not only the company, but employees also gets benefited.
pros: Excellent work life balance, as there the work was not stressful and we could finish day's work in 8 hours. The management was also flexible regarding working hours. While the atmosphere was laid back, we could work on newer technologies at our own initiatives and also take up and accomplish side projects as we wish. The salary and bonus structure was also satisfactory, so was vacation, health beneits
cons:
Sometimes I felt that I am not working on cutting edge technologies and not in sync with the latest working methodologies and working style. The policies, processes, tools were still old fashioned with sseniority being one of major criterion for promotion. 
Other than that, I really cant think of any negative points.

summary: JP Morgan Chase - Global Technology Management
advice: Realize that you can't keep cutting staff and still have a reasonable work life balance.
pros: Great Salary, Lots of responsibility, fast paced environment, leading edge technology
cons:
Long hours are expected. There were many weeks that I worked 60+ hours. It was needed to get the job done. 

They are constantly looking to cut cost and people is one way that they do that. Doing more with less it the common montra. 

I don't know if they still do, but they used to use a forced ranking system that demanded that 20% of the employees in a department were Exceptoinal, 70% were Acceptable and 10% were in need of improvement. This worked fine for a couple of years, but eventually good people were forced into a need improvement ranking because we had to meet the distribution curve.

pros: There are a lot of good people working there.  Overall, they try to promote you maintaining a good work/life balance.  I have been able on occasion to work from home but for the most part they like everyone in the office.
cons: The work pace can be heavy with a lot of expectations of overtime.  Although, that comes with our choosen field.  They don't have much of a culture of celebrating successes.  When, I first started here they seemed to try to promote an enviroment where people got to know people outside of just doing there job.  That has seemed to disolved.  More recently, they have been trying some new programs.  Perhaps, they have noticed this and are trying to change it.

summary: The people I worked with where great but the managers have no clue on how to manage people.
advice: Learn how to manage people!  Provide them feedback and goals so they can work to achieve them.  Meet with them regularly on their performance, and conduct weekly staff meetings.  Provide strategic vision to the team so they know where the ship is being steered!
pros: People are great to work with, helpful and friendly.  The pay is comparable, if not slightly better than industry standard.
cons: Management has no clue how to manage people.  Remote management never met with employees or held staff meetings.  The system's at Chase are legacy-based and ancient.  Company very slow and resistant to change management principles.  The political atmosphere outweighs people's work performance.

advice: Engage more with the teams and create an inclusive work environment. Promoting individuals only based on time in line of business rather than potential candidates with well-verse backgrounds adding value to the organization and LOB to enhance overall performance to achieve stated outlined goals. With Managers, some that require guidance and mentoring, have been in their positions too long feeling a sense of stagnation and the lack of experience or motivation to achieve maximum potential in their career and the ability to influence others.
pros: Excellent Benefits and current stability of employment
cons: No career mobility. The management team only looks at length of time employed in the department at Chase rather than a comprehensive review of experience in management, operational production, Career Achievements, and abililty to mentor and motivate our teams.

advice: Help out your team move to different roles, put out a good word for them, if they deserve it. Help them meet the right people not just advance in the department they are currently at.
pros: Great company with very generous PTO and 401K contributions. Culture is great, management is great. They keep you trained and up to date with what you need to succeed.
cons: Very difficult to move internally, even though they do promote career advancement. If you have the experience but not the right degree it will be very difficult to get considered for a different position yet alone get an interview. The positions that are available to you are more than likely lateral positions which provide you with a small to no raise in salary.

advice: Transparency for pay and everyone deserves inflation raises if nothing else for good performance.  I have seen them give people raises who didn’t even work but a couple months out of the year, managers don’t get to allocate raises, someone in HR does it.  There also not enough opportunities to work remotely or at least jobs that can be done from anywhere.  A company in Baltimore recently gave employees life changing bonuses, take notes and action Chase!
pros: Good culture where mild amount of pressure is present and if you are Managment you will get a very modest bonus.
cons: They pay to come in, but don’t expect a raise afterwards and if you get a promotion, don’t expect the raise till the next year in February if at all.

summary: Looks good on a resume, but....
advice: Learn to show more respect to your people, realize that the high turnover rates actually end up costing you more in the long run.
pros: Pay is pretty good. Job can be interesting when you actually get to do something technical instead of fighting bureaucracy all the time. And when you decide to look for a new job, JP MORgan Chase looks good on a resume.
cons:
Management has no regard for work/life balance and thinks it's fine to have you work 60-80 hour weeks on a regular basis. 

The level of bureaucracy and red tape to get even the smallest thing done is astounding. Most of your day will be taken up by endless, mind numbing meetings where you go over the same things over and over every week.

summary: Working as a Business Analyst at JPMorgan Chase
advice: Please try to be considerate toward the employees. They all work hard, and try to do their best. It would not hurt to let them know how good of a job they are doing. Provide some non-work activities to improve morale.
pros: Colleagues are friendly, and helpful. Lots of smart people that work very hard. Also, they are flexible about working from home, and taking time off.
cons: There is no real culture at JPMorgan. Everything is about meeting deadlines and getting the job  done. No much interaction outside of work. At the end of every year, the conversation tends to focus on the budget for next year, and whether there might be a reduction in headcount. Career mobility is hardly mentioned as an option.

summary: Unpleasant work experience with no structure and organization
advice: Employee appreciation, morale and loyalty is needed & should be strived and reached.   Professionalism within upper management needs to be better displayed at all times and use of profanity should never be used or acceptable in the work environment.
pros: Good 401k and retirement options
cons: Inadequate new hire training  which doesn't provide the employee with the appropriate tools to do the job; poor communication & inadequate guidelines, department policy & procedures were outdated and consistently being changed, which meant that the employee and thw work suffered; favoritism very prevalent;  need clearer and precise guidelines before the department can effectively meet business objectives & goals; and department head consistently exhibited unprofessional and inappropriate behavior in and outside of the office.

advice: You can be true to the client without being excessively restrictive to your employees. Learn to value them - and I don't mean with donuts and pizza and an annual favoritism contest.
pros: Pay is great, hours are okay, depending on what shift you get. If you are a permanent employee, the benefits are decent. During peak season, you have the opportunity to work overtime, and during low season you can take time off without pay if you'd like.
cons: In this small branch, there is little to no room for advancement. Management plays favorites big time, and if you're not on 1st shift, you don't hold a lot of sway. Rules for production are myriad and contradictory. They are very strict about electronics. If you are a temporary employee, during the low season you may be forced to take leave without pay.

advice: Don't offer networking events to employees if the networking doesn't work (and that is not just from me). We started with a group of 28 underwriters which now all are about gone due to not being able to move up or any other division at Chase.
pros: Great Work/Life Balance. Great Support by direct team leads and supervisors. Great training for the role you will do. Great place to start a career.
cons: Slow Movement upward. Hard to jump into other divisions of company. Consistent excuse of "we don't know you" although you meet the managers and others at corporate functions. No way to "prove yourself" for these other divisions - they believe you are only good at the job you currently do and do not believe you would be a good fit anywhere else. So, to move up, you must move out.

advice: Work life balance does matter. This is not how it “used to be”, priorities have changed for most people in the world and family is as important as a job, if not more.
pros: Teamwork and atmosphere depends on which group you are a part. Make sure you ask lots of questions regarding your leadership and their style of leading.
cons: Flexibility has been limited recently with chairman’s decision of everyone coming back to office. Many of us in technology are working in hybrid - 1/2 time WFH and 1/2 time office. Team collaboration is still limited due to COVID restrictions while in the physical office, we question the value of being in the office.

advice: Reward people for the level of their performance rather than giving them a salary that seems appealing coming through the door. Try to keep talent rather than just acquiring it.
pros: The best reason to work for JP Morgan Chase would be the actual wor enviroment. You'll find the people to be intelligent and welcoming. Manager's aare understanding when it comes to life events within the lives of their employees. They truly have a human side
cons: Compensation and Benefits are poor compared to other organizations. The company asks its employees for a higher level of production while not allowing them to see the reward. There are no incentives to outperform peer. It appears that the only way to see financial rewardsis to leave the company then return to the bargaining table.

summary: This is a great place for work / life balance
advice: Keep your eyes on the future. Don't be afraid to intelligently embrace the benefits that new technology offers.
pros: While JPMorgan Chase is a very big company, and managerial approaches differ, I have found that everywhere I have worked within the bank, the work / life balance has been very good. I have been able to take vacations, sick time, and other absentee days without being made to feel bad about it. Also, having the ability to work from home when necessary is a big plus as well. Although this would not apply to all positions in the bank.
cons: This is a very large company, and really good talent may be over looked for a while, and may take time to be recognized by upper management.

advice: Objectivity is sorely missing in the workplace. The current appraisal process is not entirely based on metrics, but on "FaceTime" and not what you know but who you know. Work/Life balance is preached as a concept, but not practiced. Management has made it clear that 100% is not enough.
pros: Benefits including vacations and the ability to work from home are great. Salaried workers receive 4 weeks vacation at the time of hire (pro-rated). The locations in downtown Chicago are near the trains and easily accessible to commuters.
cons: Appraisals are based on a curve, which makes it extremely competitive and does not foster teamwork. For example, if there are 20 employees on a team at the same grade level, 3 will exceed expectations, 14 will meet expectations, and 3 will not meet expectations. This is when politics, nepotism, and cut throat behavior comes into play. Yes nepotism is alive and well at JPMC! Additionally, overtime is expected and evaluated on your performance.

summary: Was a good place to work until they laid off everyone...
advice: To be more open to all levels of the orginization.
pros: The card service division was once providian which had its up and downs over the years.  Then Washington Mutual took over providian.  There were many good coworkers and a very freindly enviroment.  The management was very different department to department and the Washington Mutual core values did not seem to be followed / valued by different parts of management.   This was a good place to work until they laid off everyone after the FDIC forced the sell of Wamu to JP Morgan Chase.  Since then everyone spends there remianing time searching for a new job and going to interviews.  Good by Wamu and the crazy commercials.
cons: Not the best communication from management.  No heads-up to upcoming changes.

summary: A lot of bureaucracy with a corporate tech culture
pros:
If you like working at a large company in a very corporate environment, this may be the place for you. 

-Lots of opportunities to move around to different lines of business within the bank
-People in higher positions are very willing to talk to new employees just starting out
-People are generally friendly
cons:
If you are in tech and are looking for a culture with a more startup/relaxed feel, this is probably not the place for you

-There is no quality standardization to the development lifecycle process
-Quality of teams greatly varies, e.g. a lot of teams will have you doing mundane back office work, some managers aren't that great, ... it is very hit or miss
-General lack of openness to creativity given the nature of the business

summary: Poor middle management and no way around it
advice:
If you/your manager do not see eye to eye on items like work life balance, the availability of an agreed on solution is near 0.  Contact HR?  Yeah right, they'll contact manager 1st thing they get off the phone with you.  Contact skip-level manager?  Yeah right, put a "troublemaker" sign on your cube nameplate.  
Although I have seen a few occasions of mobility, the bottom-line is your manager sets your performance ratings, your potential new manager will see the ratings (and will have to decide to care what they are), your potential new manager can/will contact your current manager for feedback, and your old manager holds your release date - everytime I've seen this argued at executive director level (or above) with both HR sides involved.
Insight360 may hold the key with performance reviews (review manager->contributor and contributor->manager; and peer review).  However who is going to tell their boss they suck!  (Please read above on HR/management as a team).  Annual bonus raises need to shift to the real-time model to make the insight360 really work.
pros:
Great pay/benefits for IT work.  I appreciate the family programs and health rewards system.
Work with some of the best/smartest (some not so much, but alas its a big company; find the good ones and work with them)
cons:
Hard work and long hours is unrewarded, it is expected.  Often told "your standard workload done exceptionally is a meets, middle of the road performance".   Our team was small and had enough work for quadruple the size (which management is FINALLY putting into affect by off shoring).  So to accomplish the standard would require over 60+ hours a week for every individual.  No end in sight.  So I take on a huge project and work 80 hour weeks (3+ months); direct management barely responded with an email good job.
No work in team work, just pass the hard work and take credit for the "concept".  
Managers and HR are a team (as they should be), noone looks out for the individual contributor (you are alone).  No oversight/insight to a manager in the wrong role (my manager didn't know at a 10k ft level what swap or http vs. https (umm... we are a security first, devops team)), performing questionable (although not illegal) activities, especially with vendors.
Performance reviews are 1 way: down.  No way to effectively make a change, even if a written statement is proven inaccurate with other written documentation.  Email is the foundation of any written communication and only saved for 6 months.  Performance reviews are 6 months (a joke, only thing that matters is your rating, just a virtual signature effort) and 12 months.  Thereby everything is based on your written notes, any saved offline communications, OR what your management said happened.  Even if you have proven inaccuracies, there is no way to affect a change.

summary: Typical bureaucracy for a large company
advice: Less is More.  Streamline the process and you could produce the same amount of work with a much smaller workforce.
pros: I make above market wage.  Job is relatively easy.
cons: Every process and procedure is way more complicated than it needs to be.  I have been doing the same job for about 18 years for different mortgage companies.  I currently produce about 1/2 the work I used to due to the complicated structure and unreliable computer systems they have.  Upper management rules from above and does not allow lower level managers to make any decisions.  They purposely chose weak people (mostly women) as lower level managers because they will be compliant and do what they are told.

summary: This place kinda sucks for America’s largest bank
advice:
Start treating employees like adults and trust that the work will be completed. For the CCB team stop pressuring developers and ask every single person in CCB their opinion before you move offices on a whim or implement a new remote work schedule.

I’ll be leaving this company shortly.
pros: Projects are impactful and results matter
cons:
They don’t care about employees 

They lowball H1B and force us citizens to take the same salary, because It would cause pay gap.

They will move offices without asking employees on team how they feel about the move

They force you to come back to office even if you are more productive at home. They track when you are in office and hold it against you during year end review.

Managers put constant pressure on developers;

Developers need to manage so many non development tasks

I do not recommend CCB team.

advice: Management never told me how to be a software developer, so I'll not tell them how to be managers.
pros: I worked at JP Morgan for 11 years.  It's a huge, global bank so your own experience will vary depending on where you work, what you kind of work you do, and most importantly who you work with.  Working for a huge company has its benefits.  There's good insurance, decent facilities and resources (usually), and corporate perks like legal assistance, adoption assistance, etc.
cons: Giant corporations like JPMC have so much red tape and hoops to jump through that one sometimes suspects they are actively trying to discourage any work getting done. This can be frustrating and it does wear on a person over the years and saps his enthusiasm.

pros:
Bonus are good for employees
Salary is competitive
cons:
Transport
Health Insurance for parents not there
No proper trainings
No SOPs
Poor work culture
Not adaptive to change
Core applications are ancient
Zero work life balance

summary: Work hard, but make sure someone knows about it.
advice: Keep employees happy and work on developing realistic project deadlines.
pros: JPMorgan Chase has great benefits.  Salaried workers have twenty days of vacation.  Career opportunities are plentiful if you are willing to learn new things and fit into the role.  Great people to work with for the most part.  Managers believe in the idea of work smarter not harder which is great.  Communication is great, any concerns are handled by immediate manager, but having an open door policy is a great plus as well.  Very knowledgeable workers makes working here easier and helps when trying to pitch new technologies or solutions as people are willing to try new things.  Overall great company to work at.
cons: Politics do come into play just like in any other work.

advice: Put a greater focus on technology, work cooperatively instead of against each other.
pros:
- Safe job - even in re-orgs or when your team gets removed there is plenty of opportunity to move around within the company
- The cafeteria at the Dallas location was great
cons:
Not an ideal environment for the software engineering career...
- Very difficult to do your job due to: no admin access on computer, limited access to technologies and internet
- Developers are generally not passionate, the firm does not generally encourage using new technologies and tools or "hacking" new ideas
- Continuous learning was limited to very basic (and poor) internal training videos. Very few teams had funds to send developers to conferences, etc...
- Many employees (especially on prod support) had to work long hours, my team's work-life balance was fine. Normal hours.

advice: CEO mentions customers, employees & profits are given equal importance, try to keep that promise about employees.
pros: Good benefits, stability, decent pay. Company makes tons of profit. Good long term outlook.
cons: Very conservative towards change, new development mostly fueled by regulatory restrictions rather than need for improvement. New requirements handled in an ad-hoc manner without much plan or thought on the current workload, Agile means, keep changing the requirement until the day of release. New product development is rare, even that does not start on a clean sheet due to tight coupling with other systems. Mobility is said to be encouraged, however the selection/rejection is not very transparent. Poor work-life balance. All depends on whether you have a good manager and a great team with great projects.

summary: Good company, decent pay, good place to start a career
advice: Make staff feel like they are in control of their careers. This is partially the responsibility of the employee, of course, and subject to the conditions in the department, but I had some colleagues who had leadership potential that was not recognized, and this was an arbitrary circumstance more often than not.
pros: Rotational Program is very useful for starting career, but not sure if I would want to stay at this location long-term if looking to expand skillset. Utilize contacts in NY if at all possible to move into more challenging role.
cons: Pay is not particularly great relative to peers - since the company has such a strong name recognition and reputation, does not need to pay as much/more than peers in order to retain staff.

summary: All that glitters is not gold
advice: Be blunt, be transparant, give people enough information to make decisions in their own best interests before its too late.
pros: There is a certain prestige working for a recognizable global brand. This can work to your benefit in some circles. Good "3rd" company to work for (i.e. work at JPM, then leave, then perhaps return to JPM with a better sense of market value)
cons: Since everyone is clamoring to get in and work for a recognizable global brand, they're (aware or not) willing to forgo much more competitive compensation. Base pay is stingy; "meritocracy" is not what it seems, and you have no leverage as an individual to take anything other than whatever is given to you. Don't get too comfortable, 2-3 years tops and then leave to sell your self to a higher market-value bidder.

summary: Ok for about 2 years, then move on
advice: Move into the 21st century.
pros: Depends wildly on your team. I've found there is a strong focus on learning which is nice, as well as maintaining relationships. Decent work/life balance. Work can either be interesting or extremely aggravating.
cons: No real room for advancement unless you happen to be the lucky few to latch onto a senior executive. Salaries are below industry average and they will string you along if you ask for more without committing. Too many managers. The closer technical management gets to the front office the more childlike they behave - there is no unity in technologies across even very related parts of the firm because each manager treats their product like an individual product in an open market that must be preserved and advertised over other, similar systems; little cooperation.

summary: You start making too much money they will let you go!
advice: Don't get rid of people because of their salary - they have worked hard and long for your company to earn that salary. give raises based on merits not favorites, or sex.
pros: If you make more than your peers - they will give you less of a raise so they can give people who make less more.. Managers - give raises to favorites - not the hard working ones.
cons: I was with the company for 10 years in the IT department - I was making the most money because I was there the longest, so I got laid off, but then they hired 2 people who were making the equivalent to my salary.. so basically  they said lets get rid of her and we can hire  2 people

summary: Good People, good group, maybe less $$ than some competitors
advice: Too much politics, old corporate environment. Consider having younger people in senior position and foster a more creative environment.
pros: I was working full time in quantitative research in the NY headquarters. The group was very relaxed, incredibly smart and supporting people, inspiring boss. Work life balance was OK.
cons: We (quantitave researchers) were given no real responsibility of the algorithms and models we created. Our job was basically and internal consulting to the managements. All business decisions (involving our work) were done by senior managers who had no knowledge of the advance math and engineering we were using. If you are a talented quantitative person and want to do "real work" consider joining a quant hedge fund instead.

summary: Good teams exist - but need to be diligent about finding right culture fit
advice:
Team managers to be leaders; to be motivational, not demeaning; to be transformational, not transactional; to be respectful.
ACTUALLY be open to innovative ideas, strategy, re-engineering -- don't just throw these words around because they're "hip"
pros:
Located in/around NYC
Decent pay and "extracurricular" benefits (i.e. museum passes, botanical gardens, etc.)
Many people stay here for their entire careers, so that must mean that good teams exist
cons:
Managers, not leaders
Poor healthcare benefits - expensive and barely covers anything
Specific to my team:
-very poor team culture
-no team work to speak of
-disrespectful management
-yelling across the floor into the phone about good things, at times, but more often cursing that someone else on some other team isn't doing their job
-uncomfortable work environment because of the above

pros: Stable company, moving towards newer technologies will allow to learn new tools as Chase implements them in the company. Heavily works with AWS (Chase specific) and kubernetes. Moving internally is easy and if you don't like your team, Chase has one to fit your skillset or what you want to do. Chase also has a great entry level (college graduate) software engineering program (SEP), which will place you on a team that best fits your interests and skillset.
cons: Almost everything is "Chase specific", nearly 35-40% of what I learned while at this company cannot be carried over outside of Chase. Cyber regulations don't stop for applications that are external facing and even for internal facing applications it can be difficult and time consuming to comply with the restrictions.

pros:
- name recognition
- 401(k)
cons:
- Hybrid work environment requires you to be in the office certain days AND they monitor your badge swipes in and out. They also monitor when you log on from home.
- Wages are not competitive
- Very much a good old boys club; they talk a big story about diversity and inclusion, but promotions primarily go to certain groups
- Benefits used to be good, but they dumped their Cadillac plans and now you have to fight tooth and nail to get coverage from your health care insurer.
- Culture is rammed down your throats daily via emails and the intranet whether you agree with it or not - and if you voice any opinion, it is not received in the spirit of open discussion.

advice: Adhere to the policies and philosophies that Chase professesses to subscribe to. Some departments / management take to heart what employees learn in the compliance courses (eg, Fairness and treating employees with respect, etc) while others like to talk the talk but not walk the walk.
pros: Benefits are reasonably good compared to other big banks.
cons: It's a hit or a miss as far as whether or not you get a manager who will support you. I unfortunately didn't have that. It's nice getting the 4 weeks vacation that comes with working for a big bank but when you're working during all your vacations, it kind of defeats the idea behind vacations. Work load was way too much. Too much nepotism, clicks and back stabbing.

advice: Ensure managers chosen for interns actually care about the interns. Performance reviews are usually biased based upon how much the manager likes the intern as opposed to the quality of their work or workload.
pros: It is only a 10 week period but you stand to learn a good amount at a pretty decent salary as an intern. Most interns gain lots of positive support from managers as well as interesting work. No traffic in Columbus. JPMorgan has effectively come through the financial crisis and appears to be increasing steam.
cons: Manager satisfaction varies greatly by which manager you have. Some are extremely good, others are horrible and treat interns poorly. Columbus is an extremely boring city. HR very territorial so do not expect to move around.

summary: Overall, a good place to work at ...
advice: Create incentives for various areas of the company to work together.  The incentives given to various areas don't really allow for these areas to work for the best interest of the company.
pros: JPMorgan is a pretty good company to work for.  So far, I have encountered really nice and smart individuals within my department.  There is a lot of opportunity to try out different roles and grow your career.
cons: Like most large companies, JPMorgan has too many layers of management and there is a lot of disorganization in terms of getting some things done and avoiding the typical big company politics.  The salary and bonus numbers are not too great here as compared with other companies.

advice:
-streamline training and internally hire job-specific trainers, that way we can ensure they know what they're talking about.
-compensate employees that do more for the company (peer coaches get bas pay and often miss out on the chance to bonus, usually resulting in the new hires getting more pay than them)
pros:
-Very competitive benefits packages
-A lot of paid vacation time, even for new employees
-tuition reimbursement after working for the company for 1 year
cons:
-Management tends to tow the company line, specifically when it comes to policy that doesn't make sense 
-grading for quality standards vary from manager to manager
-training is not very good. peer coaching is excellent, but peer coaches are not adequately compensated so most stop assisting new hires after a week or so

advice: Be a bit more flexible on WFH and adjust salaries to meet market conditions
pros: Great company good perks and benefits. Challenging job but try and promote work life flexibility. Try and be social responsible promote diversity and fair hiring working practices. Seem clued into what is going on in world and environment on that front
cons: Since Covid significant attrition and salary’s have not adjusted to current market conditions (review as of 5/2022). Also been steadfast in making folks come back to work at minimum 50%. These two factors causing attrition

pros:
Great Company, nice working environment, employees are friendly and helpful.
Great compensation
Good name to put on your resume.
cons:
No room for career growth, yearly reviews are based on a quota or something like that so less than 3% of people will get Exceed performance rating and get promoted while the rest will range from meet to meet+. No matter how hard you work or what your accomplishments are you might get a mediocre performance review if you don't have he right connections and play politics.

I've seen a lot of people leaves JP after getting disappointed with the yearly performance review!! Their yearly salary raise is 2-3% and sometimes they don't even do it (Last year there was no salary raise for anybody in JP).

summary: Good job stability/security but red tape, old-school corporate culture, and questionable pay
pros:
- Good job stability; there's always work that needs to be done
- Very strong company (Industry leader)
- Get to work on projects that impact the global economy at both macro and micro level (e.g. retail and wholesale technologies)
cons:
- Stressful environment driven by deadlines instead of actual capacity, budgeting, resources, people
- They don't keep up with the market rate of salary growth or reward backend technologies with compensation (especially if you stay too long)
- Slow pace of change due to bureaucracy 
- The usual cons of banking corporations: you're just a number/resource, lot of red tape/policies that restrict personal and salary growth, old-school culture and mentality.

summary: Lot of potential but bad management
advice: Only by fixing the lines of communication can the team progress. Just having a leadership position and addressing the wider (200+) team as a family is not going to change how the business runs. In the long run, stuff will collapse miserably as the foundations are shaky.
pros:
* Good tech stack (depends from team to team)
* Interesting work with private cloud
* Opportunities to learn AWS and work on it
cons:
* Too much politics at the management level in the Corporate Technology line of business directly impacting product direction and day-to-day work
* Broken lines of communication leading to duplicate products being developed, eventually leading to the collapse of some products and thus teams losing jobs 
* Poor compensation (realized much after quitting)

advice: Rework the insurance plan!
pros: The company is very pro growth opportunity.  Mobility is big and is seen as a plus.   It's very multi-cultural and tolerant of differences.  It celebrates it in fact.  Literally.  I love the fact that I work at a company as diverse as this.  And not only that, but I work with people located all around the world.
cons:
Some managers need to work on giving feedback throughout the year instead of just during review time.

The health insurance is not great.  Maybe all companies are suffering due to Obama Care.  But my family deductible is $3k which is obscene.  If you don't get sick, it's great.

summary: Heavy Red Tape, not much common sense
advice: Allow feedback to influence planning, do not be deadset on an idea from the start and never change it.
pros:
- very little pressure short or long term
- Randstad offers certification training reimbursement/incentive
- some remote work available during COVID
cons:
- you will be bored 95% of the time, there is almost no work to do and when there is large projects they hire out
- Except when they don't, and then you're doing heavy physical labor you're not supposed to be doing.
- There is no specialized industry knowledge to be gained in this role (aside for excel opportunities)
- Feedback not asked for or considered by management during planning, and the final plans never make much sense.

advice: Relax HR rules around promotion, enable internal candidates to get the salary and title of new positions on start date.
pros: Great working environment, ample opportunities for growth, one of the most respectable companies to work at, access to senior management, great pay, meritocracy.
cons: Internal moves are lateral even if you are moving to a higher level, you get more responsibility, maybe more hours, but same pay same title (Officer, AVP, Assoc. VP, ED) until you are recommended for a promotion. HR policies make promoting people an uphill battle. External candidates get the Title and Salary of the position posted (unlike internal candidates, but internal candidates have preferred status, followed by JPMC Alumns)

summary: Great Company - If You Get a Good Manager
advice:
Management who only sees the numbers in the reports should really put in the actual work and you would see why numbers and productivity over quality become quite stressful
Managers (all levels) should be required to Take Mgmt 101 (and others) courses. Especially with COVID, communication changes and there will always be demand for improvement on all ends.
pros:
Great Pay
Time Off
Benefits
Values
Company Employee Appreciation Days can be fun
cons:
Raise Rates
Sometimes Numbers seem like the only thing that matter that can really deplete morale
Some Managers are either too busy or come across as condescending and will not try to help you succeed (this is rare from my experience, but I had the experience)

advice: do not ignore your junior employees, because for the most part they do the real work, everybody else bs their way through work. Be appreciative of peoples effort, and only offer constructive criticism.
pros: the salaries are competitive if you bargain right, it is a huge firm so you are assured of career stability if that is what you are looking for. They give back to society a lot and there is a lot of room for growth and challenging opportunities.
cons: There is less career mobility though the company makes a not of noise about it. there is hardly work life balance, another thing they make a lot of noise about, and the culture is a throat-cutting, backstabbing one.

summary: Hard work, not the best pay, big name, lots to learn and keep you busy
advice: Be more flexible - know the value of your employees and understand the amount of investment that goes into learning how these incredibly complicated systems work.  If you find a talented, knowledgeable employee KEEP HIM/HER.

pros:
Name brand for the resume.

cons:
Poor gender diversity — Low women's representation within management makes it difficult for women to advance.

summary: A good place to work with smart people.

advice: Listen closely to the rumblings in the ground or on the street. When people have concerns, please do listen to them. Not everything is about cost savings, the employees there love what they are doing and serving the customers. Be transparent to them about everything.
pros: Lots (and I do mean LOTS) of things to learn and at first glance, the company is indeed big. You can easily spot various and several areas for improvement and if given the opportunity, you are allowed to tweak them in order to adapt to the signs of the times. Also, you can get to be selected, if not volunteered, to be the champion of your respective domain if you are a performer (lots of them there).  Pay is good; benefits are so-so. Lots of supportive folks who will help you along the way. A lot of managers take care of their own and stick to their guns and principles. Some will even go the extra mile to fight for you and your accomplishments and value to the team, if not to the business.
cons: Ever heard of office politics (a lot of people keep score especially if you put them on the spot and make them seem to lose face; once had a manager who even questioned the feedback received and why such was given. Ever heard of free speech?)? When put on the spot, some people go up the chain (aka their boss) to fight for them, if not clean up their mess). Red tape (would you believe calling up the help desk just to raise a legitimate issue ticket will take you several minutes even for an urgent one when the business is already getting calls from customers)? Bureaucracy (classic case of too-many-cooks-will-spoil-the-broth)? Throw in stagnation (two words: dead end), favoritism (I've worked with a team from different locations and guess which one always gets the early worm despite their tardiness and poor performance), finger pointing (lots of this so HEADS UP and this is the norm by the way), throwing under the bus (also, another one of those "part of the norm" things), ego and power tripping (yep, the moment you meet people who suddenly become leads or managers? oh boy, you're in for a long day), etc. Quality of work? Just a buzz word and the "in thing" is statistics and metrics. Don't get me wrong, but if you managed to latch on to a group with good managers (dwindling number, sad to say and as the saying goes, how come the good ones always get to leave) then you're in good hands. Otherwise, good luck. Things change fast so be on your feet ALL OF THE TIME. One must have a ton of patience, perseverance, guts, and a very thick skin if you want to work for a long time in this company.  Business partners? Good luck as well! Depending on the group and location, some folks tend to be territorial of what they do specifically. Like most companies, everything is a touch move, has to have confirmation, etc. Depending on function/location again, some tend to sleep-walk on the job (you know, going through the motions like a bot, a program), job abandonment despite the fact that they're taking looooong breaks even when it is past the 15 minute or 1-hr mark. You'd be surprised when you get to meet people who are oh-so unqualified for the position (I hate to say this, but again, LOTS of them). Oh, did I mention people also like to cry wolf? or like to press the panic button as if the "world is always on fire?" Your past accomplishments and experience? Throw them out the window and you won't get recognized for having those under your belt. You have to beg the "gods" if you want to take a leave or ask for considerations, etc. and a lot of managers there prefer to impress upper management instead of taking care of their people.  Great discrepancy of work among locations (contrary to the equality value they "try" to espouse). Not being a sour grape, but after a few months on the job, you'll get to see the "real" deal and what you signed up for.

summary: Continues to make anti-competitive decisions and won't listen to employee feedback
advice: Start learning from other tech companies. I understand that JPMorgan is a bank and other banks have similar salaries and work-from-office requirements. I believe Bank of America has already pushed for their employees to return as well. The problem is that we also claim to be a tech company, which means we are also competing for talent with other tech companies. It is no wonder why you can't hire and retain tech talent when they are receiving other offers for 6-figure salaries and permanent work-from-home. You need to start looking at other tech companies as competition too. You also need to start listening to the feedback you are collecting.
pros: Their benefits are pretty good. There is also a lot of recognition for working at a firm as large and well known as JPMorgan. If you are someone who likes working for someone well known and likes the recognition that comes with, then that is a plus.
cons: The salary is not as good compared to other tech companies JPMorgan has to compete with. They also insist on "Return-to-the-Office" (RTTO). While we are hybrid right now, their ultimate goal as stated many times is to return 100% to office, which is the exact opposite of most other tech companies. They are also continuing to loose top talent and now there are many positions open across the firm that can't be filled, mostly due to the salary and RTTO decisions. Management recognizes this exodus of talent as a major problem and have hosted sessions which they called "feedback circles" in order to figure out why this is happening. Other employees have mentioned salary and RTTO countless times during these feedback sessions and it continues to go unaddressed. I also want to point out that salary does not improve that much with a promotion. I have colleagues who have left because they were promoted but didn't get the bump that they really wanted.

summary: Stable for the banking industry, great people, about average for pay and benefits
advice: If you want to remain competitive, get with the times as far as flexible work arrangements.   We live in the age of technology and are a global company, so recognize that employees can be productive from home computers.
pros:
Certain benefits are great by comparison.  4 weeks paid vacation, 2 personal days and 6 sick days are standard for salaried employees.  The company also provides a small pension in addition to 401k matching.   Performance bonuses are just that...based on performance.  Onsite backup daycare is provided at no cost for 10 days a year, which is a great fallback for emergencies.  Maternity leave is paid for 12 weeks.  

Mobility within the organization is encouraged.   The employee is expected to be in charge of his/her own career path, and (most) managers embrace assisting employees get where they want to go.    There is a wealth of career development training, networking and mentoring available.  (Although finding the hours is sometimes a challenge!)  

The environment is casual, people are generally happy and friendly.

The company name is great on a resume.
cons:
This feedback is specific to Information Technology areas. The company is huge and there is a TON of bureaucracy, so if you want to be on the cutting edge of fast moving change, this is not the place for you.  

Pay is average.  Once you are in the door, it is difficult to get a substantial increase.  Internal moves to other roles do not translate to pay increases, even if then new role has more responsibility.  

Health Insurance is below average.  The company offers only two plans to US-based employees, and both have very high deductibles before they pay for anything other than a primary care vist.  ($3000 or $5000 for family plans.)  The deductibles are offset by a company-provided medical reimbursement account; which can be anywhere from about $500-$1200.  The insurance benefits are probably fine as long as you aren't prone to sports injuries or have young children.

Although the company touts flexible work options, they are not widely supported by management.   JP Morgan Chase lags behind its competitors in embracing telecommuting as a way to keep employees happy and productive.

advice: Managment should listen to and ACTION the concerns of employees if they want to retain top talent.
