cons: Management tends to ignore or not action employee concerns.  Management has a tendancy to favor people like them (which is not a good thing when they are difficult, disrespectful, and manipulative).  Morale tends to be low in most groups; everyone that I speak with does not like working here for various reasons.

summary: Good overall culture, stability and good benefits, but inconsistent leadership and a few pockets of malignant idiocy.
advice:
Be more prepared, know what you are doing, don't be afraid to take a healthy risk, and spend less time covering your butt and more time serving your customers.  Too many managing sycophant busy-bodies that act like they are busy and confident but lack critical thinking and independent thinking.

And when you tell people the direction to go is the direction things are already heading, you can't say you have vision.

Thanks for keeping things stable, despite the issues a big company has.

Keep up the firm-wide enterprise architecture initiatives.  Could have happened sooner, but better late than never.

Manage internal information better, make it searchable, accessible.
pros:
Overall Software Development and Technology within JPMC is improving company-wide, after years of not having a firm-wide vision.  It's still like living out a Dilbert cartoon, though.

If you are in a good organization, you can really make a huge difference have a lot of fun.  These pockets of greatness make the company that customers like.

The facilities are great.

A huge push to raise customer satisfaction, which may fix some other issues internally. 

If you truly have a good idea, there are multiple ways to get it to management and if you stick with it, they may not only hear you out, but put you in charge of implementing it.

Many great people, and often a way to get around impediments.
cons:
It's like a mine-field until you know a lot of good people.  It's all-too easy to step into a fear-driven dis-functional group or organization and bad leaders take many years to get pushed out.

Transparency and honesty isn't part of the culture like it used to be.

Management principles are old-fashioned, some practices well-proven as ineffective, but still in use.

After about 10 years, negative experiences occurred more often than positive.

Inconsistent pay and culture between lines of business.

Information is hard to find, even very basic things.  There are times when I found more information regarding a project I was on from the public internet than the internal network.

advice:

While knowing how to speak and present yourself is important, back-office developers need a strong technical background to do their jobs efficiently.

Also, including little perks for lower level employees will likely keep up employee loyalty more.

Other than this, JPMC is a GREAT environment.  Don't get me wrong, Management, DOES support change and ideas.  It just needs to be presented at the correct time of year.  ;-)

pros: (NOTE: I last worked here in 2009, but I could not select that in the dropdown.) Since the company was large and well-resourced, we rarely had budgeting issues on projects. summary: A smart organization, but one not without some significant inertia
advice: JPMorgan constantly emphasizes the importance of a nimble organization, and it continues to struggle with becoming one.  The bank works hard and fast on a particular project, without any real reconsideration of the approach.  If a manager recognizes a deficiency, and that deficiency is significant, the effort is abandoned and replaced with something else.  It is noteworthy that JPMorgan does even that, and doesn't just plod further into a poor decision; however, the bank should work to rebalance the projects as they progress, consistently re-tailoring them to the problem.
pros: As with most large banks, JPMorgan is very technology focused.  The company makes a concerted effort to consistently improve their existing technology solutions, and exhibits a healthy respect for the need for constant improvement.  As such, there are always many interesting problems to be solved, and JPMorgan definitely supports employees that are working towards those goals.  Additionally, broad common goals are obvious to everyone in the organization, and as a result there is generally good communication across divisions of the firm.
cons:
JPMorgan, like other banks, has a very rigid hierarchy, so its not uncommon to see vast - and unplanned - changes at low levels as the result of fundamental changes further up the ladder (hiring or firing at senior levels).  This is an effective way of bringing about change, but often times the resultant changes are poorly thought out or unnecessary.
  Within the technology side of the bank, everyone is more or less on the same page about roles, responsibilities, goals and requirements.  However, outside of the technology groups it becomes apparent that the rest of the bank views all technology costs as simple necessary expenses, and not capital outlays that could generate real revenue.  As a result, there is a significant that employees in technology groups are less respected than their business-side counterparts.

summary: Much more than just a prestigious name

Managers tend to get so busy with work that the new analysts and associates that join feel world's apart from their manager.  Usually, the analyst and associates do not want to disturb or waste the manager's time for career discussions, but this is extremely important since the manager has first hand experience with what it takes to rise the ranks.  Managers should make an effort to at least offer some assistance to the new employees.
pros: J.P.Morgan Chase has been recruiting top talent from all around the country. While the benefits and corporate perks are being cut down by our CEO, the money saved is going towards higher employee compensation and increased company stability.

Most of your conversations with colleagues will be work related and you will rarely see a group of people chatting by the watercooler.  As with any company that recruits from the best schools around the world, you will find it a major challenge to rise the ranks faster than your peers, as the requirements for each promotion are structured such that you should have a certain number of years of experience in the previous position.

summary: A mega-sized company with a lot of resources and well-meaning intentions

For individual contributors, managers of all levels and the company as a whole. "They" or "someone" will not get it done one day; because "they" and "someone" are us; each and every one of us.

- CEO does not trust his people enough to let them work from home despite of the ongoing pandemic, firm's requirements for employees to get vaccinated and boosted, firm's statements of commitments to be responsible global citizen and dedicate huge money amounts to social causes such as climate change but not take stock of all the carbon footprint incurred from requiring employees to commute to office hubs

summary: Decent Company; Just not for Software Engineers

pros:
I worked in the Seattle remote office and will be comparing it to other companies here, since even non-tech businesses here function as tech companies.

The base + bonus combo is pretty competitive for Seattle.

Work-life balance is pretty good.

It’s in a decent location downtown.

Most coworkers aren’t jerks despite being a huge company; generally a nice workforce.
cons:
So many meetings. Why does every meeting need 18 men in a room shouting at each other?

Diversity is good but remember JPMC is a global company so there will be culture clash. You know how somebody from Jersey and someone from California will probably have some miscommunication even though they’re both American? Well this will be amplified 10-fold when you’re at a global company. You will probably have a lot of remote meetings at random times with people across the globe. Moreover, there doesn’t seem to be a huge push for diversity and the majority of tech is the same majorities you seem to see at tech companies, and if you’re American of any race you’ll probably be in the minority. And remember, non-Americans haven’t confronted issues about race/ethnicity or as long as other countries, so prepare to hear some random tone-deaf remarks from immigrant coworkers (nothing mean per se, just tone-deaf).

The Seattle branch is facing the same issue that most non-Amazon companies face: every employee tends to be ex-Amazon and thus the new company becomes little Amazon. Recruiters love to reach out to Amazonians because they don’t know how the sausage is made, but those that are on the inside know they bring a certain Type-A culture and letting themselves be overworked. Moreover, recruiters assume Amazon experience == AWS experience, but really the non-Amazonians I’ve worked with had more hands-on AWS knowledge. 

It is still a top-down culture so there will be times when some random higher-up you’ve never met in person and is probably across the globe mandates an initiative with an arbitrary deadline.

Health/dental are overpriced. No benefits like orca card yet. Like a month of PTO depending on level.

Moreover, the dev environment is so locked down due to “security reasons”, which is fair. However, it means you’ll be using dated technology and if JPMC really cared about development experience, they’d spend some of that $9b quarterly profit to hire more security folk to help the developers get a modern experience to develop more business value. Instead, you’re between a rock and a hard place of getting arbitrary deadlines with so much red tape and so many meetings. Hard pass especially in Seattle where there are so many more fast-paced environments.

I’m all about company for a couple of years at least but it was extremely difficult to stay longer than a year at a company with so many meetings, so much red tape, so little development, and so bad for the resume, especially in Seattle where complacency is killer. Unless you’re hired for a very specific team and a very specific project that’ll perfectly align with your career goals, i would say don’t bother.

summary: JPMorgan Chase Mostly Cons and a few Pros
pros: JPMorgan Chase offers great benefits. The health insurance and life insurance benefits are very good and the out of pocket expenses are very reasonable compared to other companies. They have a legal benefit that is very inexpensive and well worth it. It's nice to be able to have free checking and savings accounts for the whole family. I like the fact that the company is very ethnically diverse. The company always makes it a point to make sure that it's on the forefront of all the latest technology only for customer facing applications and systems.
cons:
*The company has grown too large and is out of control with too much red tape and bureaucracy. 
--It takes too long to get anything approved and there are too many manager approval levels involved. 
*Senior managers are involved with approving menial expenses instead of spending time on more important issues and concerns. 
*The company is top heavy with far too many directors, managing directors and executives, and there are far too few employees to actually take care of business and do real work. 
*JPMC does at least 3 rounds of layoffs each year, and each time they layoff more mid level and entry level employees that do the work.
--Consequently, those employees that are left to do the work end up doing the job of 3 - 4 people. 
*Also, it's very important to note, that when they do the 3 rounds of layoffs each year, they target workers that are 55 years and older. 
--So while JPMC is constantly bragging to the media and to their employees that they champion diversity and inclusion and that they don't practice discrimination of any kind, they are clearly and openly discriminating against workers that are 55 years or older. 
*Global Technology Infrastructure is the worst line of business to work for because the company treats GTI as an expense. 
--If you're going to work for JPMC, it's best to work for one of the other lines of business such as Chase Investment Bank, Asset Wealth Management, Commercial Bank or Mortgage Banking. 
*JPMC makes internal applications and systems for employees their lowest priority, and it makes it very difficult to get work done. 
--In addition, JPMC has gotten rid of most of the help desks where employees could talk to someone to get help.
--Unfortunately, if you are having issues with an application or tool that you need to get your work done, you will be relegated to opening a ticket through a clumsy automated system and it could be several days before anyone addresses your issue.

summary: Not a company for tech employees
advice:
Modernize job grades and titles
Match 401k in paychecks
pros:
Free on-site medical clinic is nice
Columbus McCoy center is awesome with plenty of food options.
cons:
Job grades need modernized; there are 2 levels of associate and then you become a VP. Trying to get promoted to VP is nearly impossible because it’s not about merit but how many executive directors you know. If you come from tech with levels like engineer 1-5 and principal engineer and the ability to easily get promoted then steer clear. 
Bonuses are under par from most other tech companies, my other employers had targets like 10-15% but at Chase they give you no idea; my bonuses were 7% and 9%. They only care about making bankers and brokers happy not the people keeping the systems working. 
Raises are very poor after 1 year I was not given a raise and told my 7% bonus was high which is why I started looking for new jobs, the next year I only got 2%.
401k matching is horrible, they do not match every pay check and will deposit the funds January the following year if you are still employed. 

No one takes responsibility for their products, if you have an issue with a system good luck trying to get support and it fixed. I had open tickets for bugs for 8 months that were never resolved. Most documentation is nonexistent or outdated.
I understand having to deal with risks and audits but the people managing risk are incompetent. They will say you need to fix this but tell you no information on how to or where to find resources. The whole SDLC risk team have the worst archaic system for getting an application from dev to prod, you have to paste screenshots in excel documents and post it to sharepoint. Every tollgate basically asks the same questions and you just end up copying and pasting from one worksheet to another.
I was told our team would hire new employees to help alleviate the team workload and over a year later they finally opened a couple contractor roles not even FTE as promised. By that time I was burnt out and already planning on leaving. 

Health benefits were great before changing MRA requirements, before you did some activities every quarter to get funds but last year they switched to making you wear a step counter and walk 7,500 steps 20 days a month. I don’t like wearing watches or things so I just decided to forfeit about $500.

summary: Great place for experience, but need to jump ship to make the real money.
advice: You should not promote a place that encourages you to find another job within another company, rather than just fairly compensate your employee.  Chase is very stingy with salary and negotiation, they should actually calculate geographical averages rather than utilize the completely senseless means of calculating this number now.
pros: Bountiful amount of vacation, sick, personal and holiday time.  You almost get too many days off if there is such a thing. Chase also utilizes the latest technology which maximizes efficiency in the office.
cons: While Chase does have many notable upsides, their shortcomings unfortunately take the spotlight. Their toxic politics and unfair business practice make it a stressful place to work.  They would rather you quit and get more money from another company, and then match you a year later if you came back, rather than just give you a good raise that you deserve.  That is sad.  I started with the firm almost 8 years ago and I took home more money on my 1st day than what I make now.  They took wind that as an hourly employee, I made too much money in overtime.  I was then 'promoted' to a salary position which was pretty much my base salary, minus all of the OT.  I made 16k in OT one year, so imagine the significant pay cut I endured.  I then 'promoted' several other times as a lateral move and received no additional compensation other than a yearly 1% merit increase.  I finally did receive 1 raise as a result of a promotion, but out of 5 promotions they still fell very short of what's fair.   My work kept piling up, and then was approached about training to be a code programmer and taking on the job.  This is a very complex job and Chase paid quite a bit of money to train me and also promised a raise.  I did the job for over a year and had to apply within the company for another position just to actually get a raise and job title change.  The new job offer was not very good and I do not recommend working here if you do not already make a lot of money.

I joined despite the warnings from friends noting that this place is a "shift" environment. I didn't know what that meant and ultimately felt it wouldn't be a big deal. I just thought it would be like any typical dba job. What they don't tell you is that this place tracks your entire activity. You have virtually no privacy. The standards are very high here and this place is highly competitive. You  are measured through a lot of dimensions such as number of tickets closed, how you closed them, what you create, how others rate you, how your manager rates you, and you have to seek feedback to essentially justify your existence. I felt my manager never had an idea what the team was doing. It didn't help that he wasn't even in the same office. There was always a disconnect. 

The workload was just highly stressful and sometimes over bearing. What I hated the most was I felt the work was very unfulfilling. You are very limited in the scope of work you do here compared to other places. A lot of people come here with a broad set of skills and essentially lose them because they don't get to use them. As you can imagine, the environment is very locked down and things, even internally, take forever to get done because there's so many approvals needed. The on call rotation here is just awful. What they don't tell you is that being on call here is basically you working a full 8 hour shift the entire weekend. You're logged in remotely and the whole activity tracking still applies because the desktop environment is completely virtual. The team is burnt out and usually leave for other internal teams as soon they are eligible. Depending on the amount of coverage, expect to lose several of your weekends.

cons: Being a huge company, some of the mgmt decisions don't seem to make sense from a local perspective.  The company does make an attempt at being transparent, but its efforts could be improved.

advice: Get ur head outta u know where and stop acting like your above everyone. Management walked with their nose in the air and GM NEVER talked to anyone.
pros: Great pay, great bonus. There was always opportunity to work OT. Raises yearly and the environment was always fun.
cons: Constant change. Department gone. Constantly hiding things from reps until the end. Even when we saw the news of Chase getting sued, they denied it. Then they started writing people up for talking about it.

summary: Product Control Analyst At JP Morgan Chase
advice: A larger headcount and more robust staff with varied experience would greatly reduce the level of stress and load when individuals decide to leave.
pros: Analytical skill and data usage in excel is learned on job in addition to communications between Front Office, Middle Office, and Ops teams. Many professional fundamentals can be learned here in addition to some P&L centered experience in and financial product knowledge
cons: Work is particularly grindy. Hours are long. Often times this role is hindered by system limitations and lack of communication from other teams.

advice: Work/life balance is the worst it has ever been. Recently, the management have tried to require 8-10 overtime hours a week to keep up. This is extremely unacceptable, especially if you have family or any kind of life outside of work. Employ more people, don't overwork the current loyal employees you have. Additionally, the lack of diversity is appalling. If you're not into the buddy buddy system, or white, your opportunity for growth significantly diminishes.
pros:
Competitive compensation 
Great Benefits
cons:
Poor work/life balance 
Lack of diversity 
Underqualified management

summary: OK place to start your career
advice: Adopt agile!!!
pros: With such a large company you don't have to worry much about job security and there are many opportunities for career advancement. There is also a good amount of work-life balance, at least in the IT line of business. As far as perks, there are a number of benefits that you can choose to take advantage of.
cons: Boring at times. There is way too much bureaucracy. The compensation could be better considering that this is a rather large financial institution but it is not too far off industry average for this area.

summary: Lots of opportunities but little reward
advice: More opportunity for advancement and some measure of career progression through job titles
pros: Interesting, complex projects with opportunity to learn new things
cons: Virtually no opportunity for advancement, hr is all about lateral moves.  In addition, bonuses are continually disappointing, no matter how well one does the excuse for stagnant payouts is always because the overall business did not meet all of it's goals.  The firm could pay us more but chooses not to.  And parking at the Columbus office stinks!

advice: Incredible work on fostering an inclusive, friendly, and productive culture.
pros: There are many amazing people I have the opportunity to work with here.
cons: Because of the size of the company as well as its diverse roster of heavily regulated businesses, the overall pace of technological advance (both remediation and innovation) is quite slow. But it's a very stable, dependable career option. Something I would value and trade for fast paced excitement if I were 20 years older and well established in my career.

advice: -Be willing to listen to associates' concerns and needs for a better workplace environment
pros:
-Great people to work with
-Work is challenging and productive
-Plenty of room and growth for mobility and career advancement within the
 company
-Great pay and full benefits included working with the company
cons:
-Cultures and values (very mixed, unclear at times)
-For a financial institution, unnecessary rules and regulations to follow (red tape)
-Management OK- could some improvements when assessing associates, but at the 
  same time listening to their concerns and needs

summary: Easy pace work, nice coworkers, and good pay (for columbus city)
advice: maybe no
pros: First good money, you can have a confortable life with your salary in columbus city; second, the working environment is very nice; third, the boss is not pushing, so you may get lot of leasure time; fourth, the business is located in columbus, a very safe and beautiful city.
cons: When you get the offer, you seldom have the chance to choose from the positions, they are assigned to you; the life is so confortable that you may not be aggressive any more.

summary: A big company with a big heart
advice: Look closer at allowing employees to telecommute when possible. The hours are much more flexible and the productivity much higher than those in the office.
pros: The people "behind the scenes" at Chase are some of the best trained and loyal people you will ever come across in a global company. The management has a standing "open door" policy and interacts with their personnel daily.
cons: Some of the HR policies are out-dated, and need to be reviewed.

summary: Good work life balance and solid compensation
advice: Allow full time remote for workers that want it and have shown they can still be productive. As a software developer full time remote works fine.
pros: Able to pay better than most companies and depending on your team you should have a good work life balance where 40 hour weeks are typical.
cons: Large parts of their tech stacks use custom internal frameworks that leverage open source stuff. It can be difficult to trouble shoot anything that is created internally

advice: Maybe if you listen to junior staff, operation would run more something.
pros: Good benefits, great pay and career growth opprutunities.
cons: JPMC is exactly like the stereotypical big bank.  It is demanding, cold, and is lorded over by the good ole boys.  While I enjoyed my position greatly, I was always on edge as more than once colleagues were lambasted during conference calls (once with 50 plus people on it) or through under a bus for a mistake they may or may not have made.

advice: Pay for performance, not because annual bonus/salary is the same as in the past. Staff departments as work loads permit.
pros: Flexible schedule (depending on your department and manager), okay benefits, good 401K plan, and free banking products. Overall pros will depend on the department and manager.
cons: Pay ok, but not up to par with other national banks. Bonus and promotions are very political. Workforce was cut in the downturn and now most departments believe they can perform at that same staffing level. More work with less staff.

pros: I was in the IT LOB for the entire time I worked for the company.  There's good opportunity for career growth if you are politically savvy.  The pay, benefits, and work-life balance are decent.
cons: There is still a lot of reorganization going on.  If you're happy with the company, do what you can to stay.  It's a challenge to get back in the door once you leave.  Also, the parking can be a challenge depending on your location

summary: Competitive and A lot to learn
pros: There are a lot to learn here. But it is all up to you. No one will really push you to do the work. You need to it yourself. You learn not only tech stack but also how to be a leader.
cons: Very competitive atmosphere and sometimes it feels that people are only for themselves there to get experience and leave. I would say cut throat atmosphere, every point counts and make sure you do your work, otherwise you will be written out

summary: Good place to work in Argentina. Must take career on your hands
pros: Good people and teams. People is willing to help and not overcompetitive. Mobility opportunities are open, within BA Hub and to other countries, but you need to move to seize them.
cons: Bureaucracy is crazy high. From promotions to improving anything, way too many steps in the middle of doing anything. Appart from that, you are just a number and if you don't move on your own, you will be a number tipying numbers only.

summary: Easy if you have right credentials
advice: there was no leadership, otherwise the WaMu would not end up being destroyed. Hopefully it will be a good example for other companies.
pros: My qualifications closely matched the job description, so the interview was easy. Though people who hired me moved to different jobs in the next 6 months, the job has proven very interesting and exectly matched the description
cons: There is no WaMu any more. JP Morgan Chase did not want to use the WaMu talent, so we all were let go.

summary: no wonder it went under - senior mgmt was overly impressed with themselves
advice: doesn't really matter at this point - company drove itself in to the ground and threw out the employees like garbage
pros: large, easy to hide and do nothing - paid large salaries to senior techs and managers - no formal performance review process
cons: no advancement - incredible lack of technical innovation - large company so management loved to assume a "bully" attitude toward employees, partners, vendors - complete strategy, architecture and management by "PowerPoint". never saw formal documentation

summary: It has been a great overall experience - good people and good focus on customers.
advice: Keep up the good work!
pros: Great benefits, world-wide organization, they have focused on technology and they have good support, I have the tools I need to do my job, it's a solid company - leader in field, well respected CEO.
cons: It's well organized and they have processes in place - some people don't like structure. A lot of people try to come back after they find out the grass is not always greener.

advice: Invest more time in growing your people, make the pay scale more even and fair, hire leadership that is more than just big talk and fancy degrees, work on your company culture
pros: 401k and stock benefits are ok.
cons: Managment is a joke to say the least, no development or career progression will ever happen, lots of big promises and talk never any action, honestly this cons list is never ending.... Just go into this company knowing "this is just a job not a career"

summary: Communication can be too much but financially the pay is good.
advice: Staff that can work from home should. I bet they'd be more productive in 6 hours at home than 8 in the office.
pros: Pay was good. They payed for most of my college undergrad at DePaul thanks to employee education reimbursement they offer.
cons:
Staff elimination to other countries or "relocating" jobs to lower cost areas. (Chicago jobs moved to Columbus as an example)

So many team/project meeting in a week push you to have to work extra hours due to loss of productivity.

advice: Find a better system than have quarterly Audit deadlines.
pros: Great work-life balance, super friendly team, even the stakeholders are really nice because they understand the value and purpose of internal audits
cons: I live in Philly and am tired of commuting to Wilmington, DE. Wish there was a Philly office with internal audit. Otherwise, it's great work and great company. The new quarterly deadlines are pointless and just cause a bunch of stress for no reason (solely so we can have good "metrics")

pros: Some good people working on the team, friendly colleagues.
cons:
The managers in this team are terrible. Low technical competence, they don't involve in the team; they feel superior to his subordinates.
The managers give orders and don't lead by example; they also blame their subordinates if the projects don't succeed. 
The managers never share any technical know-how (maybe for lack of hands-on experience).
Also, some colleagues described the ambient in the team as "toxic."
Summing-up, not the place if you want to learn and develop your career further.

advice: Stop the bias and start acting like a global corporation.
pros: You work with the latest technologies and work with highly capable human beings.
cons: Extremely strong East Coast bias.  Even when faced with metrics that prove midwest employees outperformed those from NY & NJ, credit rarely fell upon the midwest teams.  High level managerial positions were not given to Midwestern candidates.  The company valued outside talent with fewer years of experience over its own employees. In IT, weekend only releases made for extremely long hours.

advice: Continue to be collaborative with Managers and their project leads.  Be open to suggestions which drive success.  Be agile in approach and methodology.
pros: JPMorganChase has many large project initiatives which challande the most seasoned Project Managers.  Programs involve both complex business and high Technology in an ever changing environment driven by federal regulations.
cons: Program Resource requirements can easily be underestimated which places extra demands on the project teams.  This can lead to a very stressful situation when deadlines are mandated.

advice: Place more emphasis on obtaining feedback from direct reports and solid 360 performance reviews of the IT Leadership and Management Team - Specifically ED and first band MD's.
pros: Very large Organization with the opportunity for mobility with Excellent benefits package.
cons: After 10 years I found the IT organization lacking sound leadership.  Within the various IT groups I worked within, you work long hours and very hard, most times this is unnecessary and mostly due to misguided leaders in key positions providing poor direction.

advice: Quit giving jobs to foreign contractors and quit taking such huge bonuses for yourselves
pros: Good vacation plan and decent healthcare
cons: More and more IT jobs are being outsourced to both offshore and onshore Indian contractors.  TCS has taken over.  There have been layoffs which will likely continue as the jobs are given to Indian contractors. There is no opportunity for advancement and no new employees coming in, only more contractors.  Employee morale is very bad in some groups.  Raise and bonus were insulting and determined by a Director  2 levels up the org chart who I have never even met.  Everybody gets "meets expectations" on their annual reviews which are a joke.

summary: Large company where you can grow in many areas
advice: Improve in communication
pros: Allows you to grow in your career and certain position allow you to work virtually. Always a wide range of professional opportunities.
cons: Certain job are available in certain locations that you are limited to grow unless you relocate.  Progression to next grade ranking is sequential, so if you qualify for a position you can only move up to the next grade level. Must be in that position for a year before moving again

advice: Please revise your policy . It's 2017 !!!!
pros:
Great company!!
Great CEO
Talented folks!
Work life balance is moderate
cons:
Management style: very bad in promoting internally. Long queue to get promoted...
Wrong outdated policy:
If they want to hire an employee, they can't , because they have policies of not to promote anyone from outside, on the other hand, they can't pay the person enough unless they promote the person. Catch 22 situation.
How they would attract, hire or rehire talent???

advice: Get your ducks in a row for remote workers, offer better support and training and the process to obtain lending authority should not take months.
pros: Salary and benefits are excellent,. The people have been pleasant so far.
cons: Very corporate and lacks common sense underwriting. Antiquated loan system that is very difficult to learn. Not prepared for remote workers and lack of communication and instruction. Training was not efficient and process of getting lending authority takes months. It's nearly impossible to get systems help with computer issues.

advice: Provide the pay that matches the job field – and provide regular ideas of next raise timeline along with bonuses. It gives us a little glimmer of hope.
pros: The shift towards becoming a technology company is great.  Depending on the team, you can have great coworkers! Management seems to be open to change.
cons: Processes boggling down on development time. The culture here needs some work, though I see that there is a shift happening.  Hard to move up in ranking positions.

summary: Great working enviornment and improving, but...
pros: Great working environment for project management teams, increasing push throughout all of the company to promote diversity and inclusion, stable executive leadership, name recognition. Work life balance great since WFH due to the pandemic.
cons: Pay rate for experienced workers is falling well behind the industry standard which is causing a massive exodus, promotion criteria more confusing than before and not nearly as transparent as it is portrayed to be. Strong push to return to office due to real estate pricing reasons rather than productivity reasons.

pros: Lots of opportunities to learn and develop yourself in other areas within the same industry. Many networking opportunities and company events. Great employer, great people working there, and great opportunities.
cons: In the beginning there is not much to do. We were left to learn and take time settling in (may be a pro, but I wanted to hit the ground running). There is no pay increase for the first 2 years and many benefits do not kick in until after the first year.

advice: Take the time to evaluate skills from aquiring company - many would be beneficial to your vision
pros:
Good management usage of aquiring company resources
Communication was good at the working team levle - informed of plans, challenges and roadblocks
Working cross multiple locations and time zones is a strength
cons:
Senior management not as effective in leveraging resources and treat people sometimes as number - not focused on the people/relationships and very bottom line / profit first oriented

Some areas were not as effective in leveraging skills and knowledge of aquiring company

advice: The bank is well run, as has been proven throughout the financial crisis. Systems could be improved to facilitate better deals and risk management in derivs.
pros: Great bank, smart people, presumably even better after financial crisis. Infrastructure is good and the work is interesting / challenging. Comp is ok.
cons: Hours can be long and work / life balance may not be as good as in other banks (pretty much average I suppose). Comp could be better at HFs or a few other banks.

summary: Great benefits and great people but be prepared for a lot of bureaucracy
advice:
Invest in technology, foster greater communication and cooperation between LOB's. Embrace 
firm wide solutions for common problems instead of allowing each LOB to have their own versions of common solutions (CRM etc.)
pros: Great benefits, 401K Match, Pension Plan, One of the most stable banks
cons:
Bureaucracy, Sometimes slow to react to changing market conditions. A lot of regulations and audit work. 

Technology can be very advanced in some areas like mobile technologies but very outdated in others (punch cards and mainframes)

advice: Stop with all the reorgs.  As the review title suggests, all it amounts to is rearranging the deck chairs on the titanic.
pros: Some good people to work with.  Mobility to move within the larger company if willing to relocate.
cons:
- constant reorgs, every week comes 3 emails about some new structure
- very process oriented to the detriment of getting things done.  would be acceptable if the process meant something but it generally means nothing more than checking a box blindly and holds no real value
- very penny-wise pound-foolish

advice: Please get folks with a solid (or any) technical experience a little further up the chain. Critical technical decisions are being made by people who clearly have little experience working with platforms or skill sets required for the systems they are in charge of.
pros:
They enable you with the tools you need
Growth opportunity is decent
Large scale platform exposure
Interest in new technology
cons:
Non-Technical managers in technical lead roles
Large gaps between IT and Business
PMO core can be  weak
Difficult to challenge status quo

advice: I don't know. I understand the need for quality control but they pile on so much work and demand so many files per day that people are being rushed and making mistakes.
pros: Management is ok. They understand the issues facing not only the underwriters but they are grossly understaffed
cons: You work at Chase? If so LQR if not LQR  -  They audit a lot of files and when you make a mistake it's they treat it like a major major issue and it the whole moral there is horrible

summary: Great company overall however, your experience there may vary greatly depending on your department.
pros: Great exposure!! Because the bank is so large, there is a lot of opportunity to have experience in different areas. You can move around LOB relatively easily.
cons: If you are hired into a smaller department your growth opportunities are often limited. There are many small departments within the bank that, because of their size, there are very few opportunities to move from lower level staff to an officer.  Smaller departments typically offer promotions once a position opens up.

summary: Performance driven yet relaxed atmosphere...they will take care of you
advice: Focus on training lower level managers better.
pros: Good compensation, good training and realistic expectations of their employees. Upper management is very open to feedback and will work with you if you prove yourself to be a competent worker. Very progressive environment with lots of opportunities for networking.
cons: Lower level managers are not always the cream of the crop. Hours and repetitive work can be taxing. May not be the ideal long term career choice for every one.

summary: great company with no engineering culture
pros: Great work life balance. friendly and nice people to work with. Benefits are decent. pay is below average. Company culture is amazing. People really care and work hard regardless of pay and title.
cons: bureaucracy everywhere. extreme corporate culture. the complete opposite of startup culture. Best in finance but technology is not the core function and they make sure engineers feel that way. No autonomy poor product and decision making. Engineers don't run engineering teams. The only way to move up is management.

summary: My experience at Chase was great love the challenge.
advice: The management was great I think Chase had the best of the best as their Management team they all had the same general goal.
pros: Diversity, Overall great company to work for benefits are great. Coworker was  also great just and overall environment you did not mind to to. Great chance for advancement.
cons: My only downside to working for Chase was when the company relocated to Lewisville, Tx and my commute went from 10 minutes to 1 hour plus. Then came the layoff.

advice: Ask for feedback from staff while they are employed as far as improvements that can be made from the top.
pros:
The culture; I found it to be professional and respectful

Zero tolerance for gossip and other such behaviors that can wreck havoc on office morale over time

Trained managers in management positions;  not random individuals who lack required managerial skills 

An environment that encourages new ideas, creative insight, trying new approach, and welcomes fresh ideas

Flexible work schedules
cons: Felt distant from upper management

advice:
-pay people more if they move to a job that deserves it
- it should be easier to get a VP title within the company, dont hire so many external candidates as VP who arnt qualified
pros:
-great rep on the street
-great mobility program, take your career where you want to
-decent work/life balance.
-work from home on occasion
cons:
- easy to move to another job within the company, but pay doesnt change
-bonus for IT employees in IB fairly low (~8% of base) for associates

summary: I learned how to take criticism, and how to be a better team player.
advice: Workers needed to be supported! There were many times I felt frustrated!!! There was to many employees gossiping about each other's!!
pros: We worked in groups, I was comfortable asking for help. Training was excellent, I gain knowledge in each area I worked in.
cons: I worked on 3rd shift, I was exhausted, never learn how to balance work and life. The lead and supervision did not pay enough attention to what was going on the production floor!!

summary: Low Pay, Old School, Restrictive Growth
pros:
+ Company name on your resume.
+ Co-workers are generally intelligent and pleasant.
cons:
+ Low-salary
+ Working from home can be risky for companies. I get that. But, if I'm in an approved group for access to various platforms, I shouldn't have to spend most of my days wondering "what will frustrate me today?"
+ Management is okay. But, there's definitely a lack of respect for your time and if you think a meeting might end on time...well, you're in for a surprise. Meetings, meetings, meetings.

summary: After 5 yrs working for the investment bank I left to restart my career, they weren't going to teach me a new tech skill
pros: Investment Bank Technology pays well, and if you play the political games bonuses could be outstanding.
cons:
Working for the technology arm of an investment bank breeds a kind of competitive behavior in tech people that is counter productive.  We we not on the same team, each person was looking out for number one.
Training was sometimes hard to get despite being required

advice: Jamie Dimon is a excellent leader however he should review hiring and retention policies.  Senior IT management needs to realize that current employees are over-worked as they are not hiring at the levels to replace those that leave for better opportunities.
pros: A large diverse company with plenty of avenues/career paths to take
cons: Shortsighted on the benefits of a widespread workforce.  Focuses on having to have the majority of technical positions located in Ohio.  Have given up talented people if they won't relocate there.

advice: Understand that 50% of your employees do not have the same political ideology as the company. You can espouse all the DE&I you want, you care only of diversity of skin color,  not thought. There are several BRGs all of which assemble a ven diagram of alienation to one particular group of people...straight white men.
pros: Benefits (if hourly), Worklife-balance (if exempt), 4w vacation upfront(if exempt or >5years if not). Career Growth until you hit Assoc.
cons: Pay and salary increases are laughable. Everything is identity politics and woke corporatism.

advice: The only advice I would have is to keep up the great work. I think management was doing great.
pros: Great benefits such as backup child care 401k medical dental vision , vacation, recognition.
cons: I worked for Chase at one time and it was great, however I have tried going back but keep getting denied although I'm greatly qualified for the positions I have applied for.  I would love to come back to Chase anytime, I think it is a great company to work for.

summary: Working with other systems in the bank.
advice: Well since there is no managment left and JP Morgan chase has taken over I guess there isn't much left to give advice about.
pros: Great support to get the job done. Direct managers were awesome always felt like they were looking out for me and my team. Helped me grow personally.
cons: Slow moving train, the bank was notorious for dragging it's feet on the latest technologies. Probably a just all the regulatory rules we had to go through to migrate.

summary: Very well managed financially, but poor culture
advice: Improve the culture, make it more inclusive, and a true meritocracy, and stop promoting dead wood.
pros: Very respected firm, one of the strongest, and literally too big to fail.  Pay is good, and firm seems to be making money even when almost everyone else is struggling or losing money.
cons: Poor culture with a toxic environment, and a lot of politics.  Many teams do not like to listen to and take input from newcomers, or from other teams

summary: Great company to gain experience in high volume environments
advice: When experiencing layoffs, offer intensive training programs for the affected employees to fill open positions within the company.
pros: Competitive compensation. Oppurtunities for career mobility. Relocation assistance. Talent reassignment(assistance with job placement after being laid off).  Reputable company. Great company to gain experience in high volume environments.
cons: Mortgage department experiencing major layoffs across the country. Not many entry level positions with competitive compensation. Issues with at least a lateral move when attempting to take another job within the company.

advice:
Provide more recognition to technology contributions.
Provide realistic career path for technology staff
pros:
Structured work environment - generally from 9 to 5
Some extent of flexibility and work life balance - Work from home is allowed in many departments. However it may not be allowed by some departments
Training programs are available, mostly online
Good training programs for one who is aspiring to be manager
cons:
Low salary increase and few promotion opportunities
Process oriented and bureaucratic
Lot of inter-department politics
Less recognition for technical work
Ask to take mandatory redundant training programs for legal compliance

advice: Be honest about what an employee in that position can expect in the future.
pros: The company will provided a lot of training before you start the position. The people in the program tend to be very close, and in fact interact outside of work. Great way to start a career,
cons: The company had made a lot of promises about moving up in the company, all of which would be facilitated by the firm. However, the "opportunities" were subsequently narrowly defined, and this forced many to leave the firm.

pros:
-Part of a program that sends its graduates through a training program in NYC and other regional offices for a month
-Benefits: Dental, Health, Vision, Group Legal Plan and etc.
-Free admission to certain museums
-Base salary with over time pay
cons:
- 2-year guarantee program
- Certification is only available in certain regions of the company
- Management heavy
- There is much to be desired for its online internal training program. For $100 (managerial approval) you can get access to (Business or Tech) books through Books 24x7.

advice: My advice would be to have a more uniform treatment of employees across all lines of business, regardless of it's effect on the bottom line as support services are necessary to keep the engine moving.
pros: As with all large corporations, the ability to move laterally within the company is a great advantage.
cons: As my LOB was not a revenue generator, we constantly felt the money crunch to our cost center. As internal consultants to other LOB's, you got to see the amount of politics, and bureaucracy  at play.

summary: Great place for established Employees, Bad place for young talent
pros: 4 weeks vacation, 2 personal days, 6 six days.  2 weeks Paternity leave.
cons: Forced ranking system, frequent yearly employee staff reductions.  Most ranking decisions are determined by short term accomplishments achieved in the first half of the year, rather than end of year.  Raises and bonuses are decided by employee ranking, and are subjective.  Company outsources with short term contractors as replacement for laid off full-time employees.  Company does not pay young college/masters graduates competitively compared to peers.

summary: Wouldn't work here given other choices
advice: Get rid of the "looking busy" culture.
pros: Company culture is generally lenient about taking time off, lunch break, etc. Pay is about market rate.
cons: During slow times you might have nothing to do, and during fast times you can have too much work. You might have to go on call during weekends or in the middle of the night. The tech is really slow and clunky, and developers seem to break a lot of stuff when they make new features.

pros: You can meet a lot of smart people in the Quantitative Research team, who graduated from MIT, Oxbridge, Ivy Leagues, IIT, and etc. Culture is similar to the IT company with a lot of focus on self-guided research.
cons: Salary increase is limited and moreover, you will get used to corporate life after 3 years of work. It's not as dynamic as start ups or small companies. If you are super ambitious, this is not your place.

summary: Senior Associate for Quality Assurance Group
pros: JP Morgan is a great company to work for. It has a comfortable yet professional environment to offer. Offers great flexibility to individuals who have families. They continue to provide training and keep employees up to date with new policies and procedures.
cons: Many people say the pay is not the best. Realistically speaking we cant have it all. It's either the compensation or a comfortable environment.

pros: Got off early on Fridays due to volume of work
cons:
Management very obviously played favorites - the favorites would be given easier tasks, or would never be asked to file/scan paperwork 
Poor benefits with no chance of being hired on - there were many employees who had been there years without being hired on full time
Wouldn't be allowed to bring your phone or even an mp3 player while working, employees were restricted to a cd player and 2 cds

summary: Long career, significant culture change with each merger.
advice: Build unity among your team. People still work in silos. To stay ahead in the industry invest in your people holistically. Diversity of thought keeps you honest.
pros: You own your career.  A social butterfly will be very well liked. It's truly all about building your network. Knowing the right people opens the doors.
cons: Diversity of thought is not welcomed  by those who have big egos in high positions which is detrimental to the organization.

advice: I think J.P. Morgan is a terrific place to be.  The benefits and pride that the company has is a large contributor to employees' level of satisfaction.  Keep it up!
pros: Terriifc benefits, people are proud to work there, good work ethics.  Salary is competitive and the work environment is very positive.
cons: J.P. Morgan is a high pressure environment.  There are times when everyone is just desperately shooting for the numbers.  Can be exhausting.

advice: If you move someone up to be a supervisor or lead, make sure they have good work ethics and have the personality to respect the people they will be "supervising".
pros: There is a lot of chance to learn to software and also chances to be creative in software development.
cons: Some employees that have been there for a lot of years tend to be lazy and get away with not doing very much. This brings down the morale.

pros: A good amount of money to spend, when you can get your hands on it.
cons: So bureaucratic it's not even funny. It runs more like a sweat shop. It's all about execution and no time for strategy or planning. The hiring practices are so inconsistent and the quality of hires is low. It's all about volume. The place is riddled with under performers but it's so big that it's easy to fly under the radar, and they do.

summary: Company is too large to summarize; Depends largely on which team you are in
advice: Hire more senior management that is actually competent and doesn't just talk tough

summary: Terrible technology stack, terrible leadership and a tragically awful work-life balance
advice:
Fix the work life balance.  Turnover was so high because you treated your developers so poorly.  The great ones all left and you were left with the ones who couldn't find something better.  

You have to break the cycle or you will never be an employer of choice, just an employer of last resort.
pros: Compensation was good.  I had four weeks of vacation and then a few personal days and a week of sick time on top of that starting right away from day one.  Base pay was average for the local banks, but a bit above average for the area.  I did not stay long enough to receive a bonus.
cons:
Terrible technology stack, terrible leadership, and a tragically awful work-life balance.  You will carry a pager, work weekends, late nights and early mornings.  My team was also Agile, but in name only.  The focus was project based timelines rather than product based change management. 

I was on a team of 12 (way too large for Scrum or Agile) and we had 3 teams and one of the Scrum teams was closer to 20.  Yet with nearly 50 employees, we only had 8 full timers.  As a full time employee, when the project slips because it can't adapt to change, all the pressure will fall on the handful of full time employees and you will be ground down with long hours and weekend shifts supporting a project built by contractors.  

JP Morgan is a fine place to work if you can get into a small, noncritical project.  But if you get pulled into any new development, you will be stretched way beyond industry norms working with the cheapest contracting labor.  While the pay was good, my wife got pregnant and with such an awful work life balance I had to leave.  If you have young kids that you want to spend time with, do NOT come here.

Culturally, senior leadership felt very strongly that it was best to be second and to follow the industry leaders because it was much cheaper than taking risks and inventing something novel outright.  Senior leadership had several townhalls/meetings expounding upon this ideal.  The problem with this approach was after somebody succeeded with a specific project JP Morgan would have to run twice as fast as the original inventor in order to launch fast enough to garner any significant market share.  As such, any new development projects were already way behind schedule and had overtly unrealistic expectations causing pretty widespread burnout among full time employees.  

As a final aside, this shop is 95% Indian males within the Wilmington development groups.  JP Morgan has a much, MUCH higher proportion of Indians than the surrounding employers.  It was not a problem, but the complete lack of diversity was a bit surprising for a fortune 500 company.

summary: Working in the Real Estate & Facilities Department was a disappointing experience
advice: People and Real Estate are some of your greatest assets. I would expect one of the largest banks in the world to be a more well oiled machine. The person who was our leader was not leading. He would point fingers and intimidate. The moral was low. End users would abuse or try to abuse me and other Project Managers. I understood their frustration, but it should not be tolerated.
pros: Nice office space, great location in NYC. There were some really nice, knowledgeable people that I worked with. Salary and benefits were good.
cons:
1.) The position I was being hired for was nothing like what was described during my interview. The size of the projects were smaller and dollar value was well below what I was told prior to being hired. It felt like I took five steps back career-wise. 
2.) I sat down on numerous occasions with my immediate supervisor, to discuss the "gap" between his understanding and my understanding of the position I was hired for. I was appalled by his attitude. When I pressed him on certain points, he later confessed that I was not the first person to have these issues. He had heard it before.... I also found the person (thru LinkedIn) who held this position prior to me, and she quit because of the same issues. Nothing was going to change. 
3.) Many of my immediate co-workers were miserable. They hated their job and hated the work. Some were former Bear-Stern Facilities people and felt grateful to have a job. This made for a very low moral work environment.
4.) There were several employees that I had to work with that were lazy, lied and withheld important information that was needed to keep the projects moving forward. I would ask for the information in-person, during meetings and as an email as a follow up. Once I would copy our supervisor, along with his boss, these employees would somehow "remember" the information and provide it. 
5.) I found many of the people I worked with were uneducated and lacked the basic understanding of construction, furniture or how to plan a facilities move. They worked their way up in the company but did not have a clue because they were not trained. Conversations had to be dumbed down constantly. Often I stopped to explain whatever it was that my co-worker didn't understand, and I would wonder what else they needed to know so I was not surprised at any point in the process.  
6.) There were a few people I worked with that were "loud talkers". There were small conference rooms available for conference calls or calls that could be made on speaker phone. Why these few felt it was okay to hear their entire conversation, I will never understand. 
7.) Somehow the end users felt it was okay to complain and send nasty emails to me directly, about how it was not acceptable that their new workstation was smaller than their old workstation because they worked at the company for x number of years / or that their job title required a larger workstation. I felt like a punching bag.... I would remind these people that the cubicle size was determined by the higher ups and not me. 
8.) The IT people were impossible to deal with. They could not commit to a date to move equipment... even something as small as a fax machine. So it became impossible to schedule the movers and the furniture people until the IT people could provide a time and date. IT somehow did not have to work with others. 
9.) The vendors were all very nice and very patient. It was hard to not provide them what they needed in a timely manner. It was even harder each week to hear my immediate supervisor to remind us all in the weekly meeting, that "we hand out the lollipops, so they (the vendors) can wait." 
10.) We had a department that took care of all of the artwork thru-out all of the office spaces. I sent out many emails to this department giving them the location of the artwork, the day and time period that this artwork needed to be moved. I also provided them with two names of contacts for people who worked on the floor in question. I copied everyone on these emails so everyone had the same information. On the day the artwork was to be moved, the art movers went to the wrong floor and started taking artwork down off the office walls in occupied areas. I was in meetings in another state, no where near this office space and was bombarded by phone calls / texts / emails. Anyone who would have taken a half a second to look at the information that was provided would have seen that the art movers were on the wrong floor. But instead... they called my boss. They told him that I made a HUGE mistake. He calls me up ranting and raving. And when I forward to him the emails he has been copied on, he does not apologize for his behavior. 

In conclusion: I was at this job for three miserable months. If the economy would have been better, I would have quit after two weeks. I was not a good fit for this position and the department was not a good fit for me. I am sure there are some great departments to work in, but I did not find any.

summary: Worst job I've ever had, by far and I've had many
advice: Burn the rotten structure to the ground and start over
pros: Um... they used some cool technologies I guess
cons:
I would rather work at McDonald's that come back here. Every minute of every day I was worried I would be fired. I saw countless people quit or get fired. Early on people were fired left and right, but when people quit like crazy they found they wouldn't have anyone left to manage at this rate.

The organization I joined was an automation testing organization, testing their various apps and website. Despite over a month of background checks, and that they knew I was coming, I (a Software Engineer!!) never got a laptop ordered. Several weeks in, I finally got one when a coworker was fired. I waited 3-4 weeks for my badge to let me in, until then I would beg several people via text to let me in. I didn't even have a consistent place to sit for several weeks, again until the forementioned employee was fired.

I was hired as a contract employee, and long before I had received my laptop or had any of the necessary software installed, management was already demanding to know why I hadn't completed all the tasks assigned to me.

There is nonexistent planning. Requirements gathering, estimating, etc nonexistent. They are always asking you to complete impossible tasks in a matter of a week or even a few hours, tasks that should be given months or even years to complete. If you don't manage the impossible over and over again, they ask you to work weekends pro bono, making implied threats to your employment status. It is always YOUR fault and not theirs that the impossible wasn't done. Their is nonexistent coordination between the project managers, scrum masters, managers, etc. They all operate independently. The people in charge of the madness only interact with you in the form of threats, yelling, and making demands.

They run things by fear, brow beating, yelling, and intimidation. As people were dropping like flies they finally started to get an inkling that maybe the way they run things needs a tweak, but things were still an unmitigated disaster.

It's a huge company and I don't pretend to know whether the rest of the company is run like this, but the organization I worked in was worse than can possibly be imagined.

That said, my immediate manager Sergey Tuchinsky was a swell guy and several of my coworkers were great people. Everyone above him were some of the worst people I've ever encountered.

summary: Would be *perfect* if not for a hypocrisy of values around flexible work
advice:
Trust(!) employees to come into collaborate when collaboration is occurring in office, otherwise imposing a rule for no reason feels like school. 
Or open more branch community offices in underserved areas if the rule is going to be enforced in this way? 
There are no branch community offices outside the SE of England which seems absurd and London-centric. It's disappointing as it feels like Lloyds are one of few major employers to place major focus elsewhere in the country, but then don't consider the plethora of issues people outside London face, like diabolical public transport.

My advice would be to establish a culture of 'anchor days' - of no specific frequency but team lead driven for when it feels necessary. In-person anchor days could be earmarked for collaboration, learning and team bonding - and then otherwise leave office attendance to the discretion of the employee? The employees not attending on anchor days would much more visible and detrimental to the business than someone who doesn't attend an arbitrary 40% of time but is present for all in person and online collaboration.
pros: Fantastic pay scales, great working hours, vast range of opportunities and progression, very interesting work, great office facilities, lots of importance placed learning and personal development.
cons:
Arbitrary 40% in office rule that feels against the Lloyds value of Trust. I'm very happy to, and do come into office to collaborate if my teammates are there and collaboration is earmarked for that day. But otherwise to sit at a desk on my own in a noisy environment, still take meetings on Teams and pay lots!!!! of money on extortionate and unreliable trains and adding 3/4+ hours of redundant travel to my day feels pointless, frustrating for me and my family who rely on me, and against all logic. 

Very difficult for employees who live in regional towns or rural areas. 
Given Lloyds' focus on environmental sustainability and regional development it seems hypocritical to make life arbitrarily less green and much more difficult for people trying to live and thrive outside of major cities. Driving people towards large cities through enforcing presence like this only exacerbates issues like cost of living/homelessness.

If the majority of large employers were to allow greater employee choice of working location with no detriment to the business (see advice), this could have more of an impact socially and environmentally than lots of the work that occurs within Lloyds to combat these issues.

summary: Great if you are interested to grow in banking, security, architecture, and mangement. Good support, pay & benefits..
advice:
Hire more (direct permanent) employees, less outsourcing and partner companies. Approach more technically brilliant people and hire them. Form a few small core teams (like startups) with strict high standards only comprised of permanents. Ones that you could trust in terms of delivering & good decisions, then give them more freedom, more responsibility and grow them.  A few "islands of technical culture" nuclear trustable core teams, that they can hire too. Keep track of and review the long-term performance of the software of those people -- who left for different teams.  Provide visa sponsorship to access brilliant employees. There is already a vetting process. To avoid unknown untraceable background of international (for vetting) just make it necessary to have worled/lived a few years in the country (ask for UK work experience).  It will be necessary to find people who can choose good people, but those need to be from the new hires.
I can provide more details about this particular plan and the way that I call "incubated autonomous nuclei of excellence".
In general, upgrade the legacy to newer versions, even if at a high cost. On the other hand, the issue of trust of managers to the technical ability of engineers. This is the root of the use of partner companies. Hire more brilliant people and let them work together to form nuclei of brilliance. Leave room for creativity, by pursuing multiple streams of something, and then choose the best approach. You will end up spending much less money on things in the long term.
pros:
Recommended if you want to get experience in large professional teams with advanced processes. What you will engineer, will be used in real life, will have a large impact, and what you do will be used potentially by millions of people. Many teams, Good Agile, Disciplined, Good & skilled scrum master, automated tests, CI/CD. Good management: supportive, and respectful (if they are from LBG itself, not partner companies). 
Exposure to large corporate management style and organisation. 
Technically, If you are interested in Banking or Security, or both, it can be great. Opportunities are given for you to grow (managerial). Encourage you to take courses in cloud technology. Multi-Cloud exposure. DevOps skills are valued a lot. Highly paced, delivery. Paid well, continuous salary increase. Computer Security, Web, Cloud. You feel supported by diversity, job security, benefits, & health support. Respectful behaviour by LBG employees. Compensations and benefits are good. From time to time you will find out that your salary has increased for random reasons. Actively initiation to improve test coverage, test automation, BDD, etc. If you like software management, if you want to become an architect. If you want to learn agile or become scrum master, etc, it is recommended. Willing to bring new technologies, such as the newest cloud platforms. Things change, and technologies will arrive. You see less or no ego (at least on the surface). Management is ready to solve any issues and support you at various levels (including health). In a way, management is self-aware and honest, but politically correct. Since the pandemic, it stayed fully remote. I realised maternity benefits were great. During the 2-3 years, there was a lot of advancement in technical abilities and learned lessons. A true transformation (but naturally slowed down by the vast size of the organisation and the complexity of decision processes with multiple people ).
cons:
The official process of things can be complex and you may have a limited scope. Of course, high-security sensitivity may slow things down (but you are paid for that). Of course legacy code. Sometimes it feels like it is vast, like a country, which is interesting (especially from the point of view of management and organisation), but you have visibility about a small part. There is a legacy of outsourcing mindset in the past. But there is awareness about them. The new decisions are better and I felt the transformation in various aspects. 
Sometimes legacy & brand lock-in, but you are paid high for such inefficiencies that are typical of large corporates.

advice:
Woled for Lloyds for over 12 years and left due to mental health reasons. I had finally had enough of the toxic culture and environment that is Lloyds Bank. There is a consistent high turnaround of staff, especially within the customer service departments which should be an instant red flag to anyone thinking of applying to work with Lloyds. Managers there are typically ones who have been in the job for decades and have no desire to progress and are just awaiting their retirement or people who have been pre selected before interviews have even begun because their 'face fits'. About 70% of the Managers within customer service (especially fraud) are absolutely useless. No common sense and couldn't lead a horse to water if they tried never mind a team of 14/15 people. They claim all applications for management roles within customer service is sent to a fair and transparency team but that's not the case. Like I said, they know who they want before they've done any form of application intake or interview. If you're off ill, they will hound you to call them every day or every week even with a sickline and will quiz you as to why you're off, what medication your taking, what dose, what symptoms you have, when will you be back, are you really ill? Etc etc. Before I left, management sent out an email requesting people who were reporting an absence due to illness, to call in via teams video chat. Who wants to do that when you're ill? Needless to say, this was reported to the Union, but its things like this that management will try and get away with. 
I moved away from customer service to Business Management and Needless to say the grass wasn't greener. Left after a few months and there was nothing in way of a leavers interview, no call from anyone in management to thank me for over 12 years service, not even a goodbye card. Nothing. They pretend to care, but they don't. You are and always will be, just a number to them.

This is how the senior leaders have lived this value over the last year:

1. Announced a mandated return to office, for 40% of your time, without providing any evidence for the benefits they claimed. This includes people who were hired remotely, the other side of the country from the team they work with, who now have to travel into their local office, with no one they know, because of "collaboration".
2. At the same time, announced removing consolidated working arrangements that had been in place to support those caring for sick family members, newborn babies, etc. They replaced this with a policy putting a limit on the length of these agreements. There are now people having to ration their holiday allowance to use to take time off to care for family members.
3. In response to the above two announcements, thousands of people spoke out against it in the comments on the article, but employee's concerns were brushed off as people "struggling with change".
4. A follow-up announcement included all senior leaders piling into the comments section voicing their support for the changes, while replying in very passive aggressive ways to people who didn't, asking those people to have a "chat to understand why they feel this way". This led to people not feeling comfortable sharing their opinion.
5. Subsequent announcements had comments turned off, preventing people voicing their opinion.
6. A survey was released promising to 'listen to colleagues' on this subject, which included loaded questions forcing you to pick between 'I care about the company' and 'I don't see the value in the changes'.
7. Contract changes, removing any right to redundancy packages if you reject a role they arbitrarily think you're suitable for, even if it's nothing to do with your skillset and requires a complete change in your career aspirations.
8. Changes to restrict internal applications. Managers are notified automatically if you apply for another role and you can only apply to one role at a time. This will heavily dissuade some colleagues from applying and enables managers to prevent you moving roles if it's not in their interest.
9. Pay increases have been significantly below inflation. This is constantly eroding employees buying-power, during a cost of living crisis, while selling it as a positive thing we should be grateful for and the bank also announcing a 57% increase to pre-tax profits.
10. Locking in a two year pay deal, passing the risk of a significantly volatile economic environment onto employees.
11. Disingenuously using PR and spin that a political would be proud of on all internal announcements. Including one off payments into year on year salary comparisons. Using forecasts from the BOE in their announcements to staff around pay to make the offer look competitive, but then just a few days later releasing their own forecasts via a company report that were higher. 
12. Re-worked some offices to be open plan unproductive hell-holes. Conveniently, senior leaders have their own private and quiet offices, where they don't have to deal with the sensory insanity around them while still trying to focus on work.

Due to all of the above employee morale is at an all time low. Charlie Nunn in a recent all-colleagues call brushed this off as a 'minority' of people feeling that way, but I haven't met a single colleague who isn't feeling deflated and under appreciated because of everything that's happened. 

In a single year the senior leadership team has destroyed the morale, trust and goodwill of a workforce that's taken years to build.
