summary: Once Great, now not so much so
advice: Do not espouse yourselves as a corporation that values meritocracy when in the end, it all comes down to tax-breaks and off loading your best workers for faceless off-shored "resources".
pros: Been with Citi for over a decade. In that time I've seen my skill set expanded, my responsibilities grow and have met colleagues that have since become friends.
cons: 9 months after being hired, pension was done away with. 3 years in, took a 5% pay cut. 5 years started seeing mass lay offs in the Northeast. Eventually talent and institutional wisdom was lost.

advice: Offer better and affordable benefits such as Medical and Dental. Offer more PTO. Bank of America offers 30 days after 1 year of employment and co coats for all primary provider with a PPO plan.
pros: Management is actively engaged on making sure you have the right work life balance and the resources your need to succeed. Ability to work on from home 2 days a week in a Hybrid schedule.
cons: Only 18 PTO days and not very good benefits. Dental insurance is expensive. Medical insurance has really high deductible and no copay options.

advice: Give credit when it's deserved. Also, I think that all employess should be held to the same job responsibilities since the position pays the same for all employees.
pros: I liked it because It was challenging and I definitely learned a lot. There are many different roles/positions at Citi.
cons: Citi has a glass ceiling affect. You feel stuck sometimes. When you are good at something, they expect you to do it all. And when the people that aren't so good, the weight is taken off their shoulders and placed on the other persons; who is then overloaded.

summary: Good company to work, but not fun after some years
advice: I worked there by 9 years and they are not able to keep good people increasing some money to convince people to continue. You must do what you say: meritocracy is something that I saw so few times when people had any carreer's advancement; there are some nepotism practices when managers are assigned.
pros: Very stable, confident and there are some good benefits.
cons: You will not get any important salary increase. The technology improvement is very slow and you will not have chance to change so often what you do.

pros: Advantage of working in a large investment bank is that you get a lot of feedback for your design, because your application handles hundreds of thousands of orders in an hour before exchange close with each of the order being different from others. A single failure out of all these is highlighted. So you get a lot of feedback about every bad design decision made by you.
cons: Enterprise politics is the worst part of the job. Another problem is low productivity because of spending time in mundane manual tasks to take care of compliance and bureaucracy in the system.

summary: Good place to work if you're willing to move around internally to get higher increment but can run into difficult boss
advice: Keep up the good work in leading the bank in the right direction, adopt security process that makes sense & doesn't sacrifice efficiency, keep diversity in workplace
pros: Internal mobility is supported, lots of learning opportunities, mature bank with processes already in place, lots of nice people to work with, able to quickly recover from global financial crisis in 2008
cons: Can run into difficult or incompetent managers, a bit excessive in my view when it comes to internal security control

summary: Big Picture in a Small Screen
advice: ADVICE TO THE HR - USE THE POWER VESTED TO YOU, don't just show the glimpse and store it back in the locker.
pros:

advice: Invest in people! I find it pathetic that American tax payers helped bail this bank out and as soon as they are released from the consent order they go and offshore jobs to India. pros: The benefits within CitiGroup are very good. Insurance coverage is really nice and low cost to employee. I really enjoyed the people I worked with.
cons: The salary in comparison to other mortgage businesses is low. Senior leadership does not show an interest in employees or seem to care about issues. This company has been offshoring massive amounts of jobs to India since being released from the occ consent order.

advice: Should pay employees according to a true end of year review not just a minimal pay justification to spend the allotted amount of pay increases per year.. pros: Great Learning environment with good  policies and procedures

advice: Give your employees room to breathe.
pros: Friendly people. Global corporation. Good exposure to different technologies. Automated access requests make for quick work with new hires.
cons: Heavy workload with long and stressful work hours with no extra compensation. Too many layers of management and politics. Constant disagreements between Global teams. NO dedicated project managers so little to no coordination between support teams during major upgrades or initiatives. Senior management have unrealistic expectations, constantly changing their mind, and are too metrics focused resulting in many unnecessary time consuming tasks which adds to already long hours. No work life balance if you work in support.

summary: A lot of benefits and cons
advice:
Listen to your employees. We really work hard for the company to help it thrive but new ideas or suggestions are completely ignored or dismissed. I know Citi is a large company but when we are treated as a number we don't do our best work. 
I want to love working at Citi and make a career here but the micro managing is insanely frustrating.
pros: Citi has great health benefits. They are always having fun events where they give out free stuff and prizes. The team I work with is great. Great work/life balance. They do a lot of community volunteer  work and they will even pay you to do it. There is a lot of room to move up in the company.
cons: Layoffs are constant so job security is a worry. My last job at Citi they laid me off with about 300 people and are still laying people off. They have a 'voice of the employee' program which is suppose to be for employees to share ideas and concerns but during meetings management doesn't actually follow through with any of it. Micro managing is also an issue, it is all about the numbers and not about the person. They always talk about how it is all about the customer experience and then create new policies that only hinders the customer service. I am really good at my job and get some of the highest scores but there is no benefit to this. No bonuses, commission or overtime. It is all about who you know working at this company. The technology at the company is not only incredibly outdated but it also doesn't work a good portion of the time. It is common for me to spend at least an hour on the phone with IT every other day.

summary: It is a great company to work for but be sure you know what you are getting in to
advice: To SVPs, stop being afraid of your manager and find your voice. Notice if you have a manager that has never hired anyone that ends up staying as their employee. It could be the problem is not the employees but the manager. Be aware that the culture there is to be afraid of management and to never speak to them. That really should be a red flag to you. Fear and intimidation is no way to manage. Ensure that your management team is not managing by withholding information or playing favorites. Having to re-hire and re-train staff costs the company a fortune in the end.
pros: Great benefits, the company is very open and diverse, they offer "Angel Days" an extra day off a year if you donate an hours pay each pay period. They offer a free day off to allow you to volunteer in a charity. The facility I was in had a world class cafe with chef prepared offerings and a gym for $12 a month on site.
cons: The old saying that your job is only as good as your boss is true. If you don't have a good working relationship with your manager and there is no growth opportunity or transfer opportunity where you work in the company, you are doomed. That was my experience. The entire floor is set up in tiny half walled cubicles. Everyone and I mean everyone (VPs included) were in them. It did not matter how much quiet or concentration your job required or what the stakes were if you made a mistake - you were in a bull pen environment . No one respected your space or need for quiet in that environment. The managers all had conference calls at their desks, meetings at their desks. Parties in other departments on the floor. Citi was also very bad about having "clicks" and the management tended to be hobbled by senior management to the point that they had no real decision making authority. What resulted was a "Stepford" like unit. There was just no escape and no one to tell or who would listen.

advice: Please be more gratuitous to your employees. I feel like another cog in the machine, and underappreciated. I wouldn't mind working late if I felt like I mattered.
pros: The benefits and 401K yearly match is nice. There's a lot of different committees to get involved, always something to do here. The work is new and challenging every day.
cons: The hours vary from working a typical 9-5 day, to having to put in extra hours for projects. Since my team is short staffed I'm putting in a lot of hours, feels never ending.

summary: Big, but not lumbering. Ordered, but not rigid
advice: Like any company, you must always value the input and experience of those who work were the "rubber meets the road"...there are times where there is a gap between very high level corporate directives and how they should actually be implemented. With Citi being so big, this is not surprising, but if there was some kind of system to communicate down and ensure feedback was passed back up, that may make things better.
pros:
There are many diverse projects and technologies, which is understandable given the size of the organization. You can be involved in as many technologies as time and interest permit. Even with the turmoil in the financial sector, Citi appears to be fairly stable internally and there is always enough work to keep you busy and engaged. The organizational structure in the Technology side takes a little bit of work to understand, but does make sense.
As a contractor, Citi is not in the least stingy in the hours they'll let you work. I have also heard that their alternate work location program allows people to not have to work our of a Citi office, I even know people who work remotely full-time.
cons: There's a lot of work, and I mean a lot. This is ok for contractors, but it has to be hard for employees as they usually don't get comp time or overtime for working more than regular hours. The sheer size of  the technology groups can make doing anything seem very slow and like your always getting bogged down in a bureaucracy that  doesn't always make sense. Also, as Citi likes to buy other companies, we are always working on integrating acquisitions, so if you expect either things to stay the same or to be able to do things quickly, you're going to have manage your frustration.

summary: hard work is not encouraged, politics is

pros: good start up salary, good name to be associated with, if you are active -- a lot of people to learn from, huge international presence
cons: Politics is everything ( at least on the Ops side), unless you are client facing  - poor bonuses and raises, management encourages brown noising, prefers to hide ugly things under the carpet, promotes based on the favoritism

advice: Do away with the ranking system so that people can work together as a team and trust each other. Be more honest with employees about their performance and their future.
pros: Coworkers very nice and most of them are hard working.
cons: Takes too long to get anything done due to all the red tape.  IT department very slow to react to changes due to inefficient processes.  Morale very low because of performance management system that ranks all employees, forcing teammates to compete with each other for recognition, raises, and bonuses. Benefits/profit sharing poor compared to other companies.

summary: very few Indians and lots and lots of chiefs
advice: I am not sure who the manager of the hour is to give advice. Who is in charge today?  No one seems to know!!!  Some managers come from another department to try and tell you what to do, when they have no concept of the position or the duties.
pros: Health benefits are above most. Live well at Citi is an excellent program.  Child care on premises. Employee cafeteria has a lot of choices for lunch, although quite expensive.
cons: Lack of direction.  Extreme favoritism. Everyone is jockeying for "postion".  Management talks down and degrading to employees. Pay is not the best on the street.  Left this company for very greener pastures including salary! Turnover is rampant.

summary: Depends on what you are after
pros: I was at the Blue Ash, OH location.  There is a wonderful group of people at this.  Everyone was very friendly (genuinely friendly!)  I felt welcome from the first minute.  The company also sponsored a lot of activities at the site - annual employee appreciation cookout in the summer, holiday lunch in December, lots of little 'feel good' activities that seem to have disappeared from a lot of companies.  I had a strong sense that the upper management at the site was involved and engaged with the employees and felt that they were approachable if you wanted to talk.
cons: It is a global company with a lot of folks from outside the US working at the site.  As such, there was  a lot of push to attend meetings and calls from 8am in the morning until late at night.  Also a lot of sense that it was expected for you to be in the office during the core hours in addition to participating in those off hours calls.  On top of that, they had what I will call a typical big company sense of being dysfunctional -- i.e. there were always a ton of meetings and very rarely would decisions get made.  Also there was a lot of sense of folks trying to protect their territory even if that meant fighting for a solution/implementation that did not make sense.   I almost don't want to word this as a con as I think some of it has to do with banking regulations and such but for me it was a con in that I frequently felt that I did not have proper access to the things (data and systems) that I needed in order to do my job.  Again, this may be common in financial institutions so it may not be fair to word this as a con, but in the grande scheme it makes for a big headache for an employee who is used to getting things done.

advice: Although the company does a good job of collecting data from employee surveys and round table discussions, not enough is done to implement change for career growth and merit increases.
pros: Working from home is a bonus. The medical benefits are some of the best.  Great Peers/Team Environment Good.
cons: Opportunities for internal career advancement is very subjective.  The company believes in a diverse work environment so advancing from within is challenging as the company would rather hire from the outside versus taking into consideration all the skills/knowledge an internal employee can bring to the table.

advice: Listen and promote any talent. Pay your employees a fair wage and give them tools to do their job.
pros: Great place to work for 40 years and retire. If you like slacking and politics, this is the place for you!!!
cons:
If you are a developer or somewhat technical, stay away. It's impossible to get development done.  They just buy vendor products and hire people to keep them running. Mostly contractors. 

We had to rewrite an application we spent 2 years building in a different tech stack because our new manager "didn't like the language" it was dotnet core and he wanted it into python cause he read stuff about it.

They don't give you the tools, software, hardware, anything. 

Everything is a fight. 

Real CI/CD is non-existent.

advice: Cut the bureaucracy and promote employees from within by opening up the internal mobility process with more transparency.
pros: Flexible work arrangements.  Generous leave and benefits.  Good training ground to learn the business and then move on to greener pastures.
cons: Bonus and base salaries are the lowest amongst the top 5 global bank. Need to navigate bureaucracy and lack of opportunities to advance your career.  Internal mobility is a misnomer if you cannot find someone to recommend you to the hiring manager which is impossible as you don't know who the hiring manager is.

advice: Overall a good company filled with high achievers and good leadership.
pros:
Citi sets very high standards for hiring which is reflected in the quality of people you work with which is exceptional. Colleagues in my immediate group were wonderful which made coming to work each day very enjoyable. They were also a helpful and collaborative group.

The organization touts that it is dedicated to promoting from within and they honor and execute on this. Once you prove yourself you should find ample opportunities to move up, around, or get involved in outside projects to learn new skills. Training is always available and ongoing. There were also a lot of great leaders in the organization to learn from. However, like any large organization it can be highly political and tough to navigate effectively at times but doable. 

The Brandon complex has most things you will need during the day. This includes a dining facility with multiple restaurants and food choices. A banking or ATM machine. An onsite doctor's office was really convenient and a tremendous time saver. There was also an onsite gym with lockers and shower facilities as nice as any top-rated gym in the area. The benefits were also really quite good.

Most of the building/complex was organized or structured as a hoteling setup (call center-like). The space is very attractive. You work in large groups at long tables very close to one another. You are given a small locker to keep your personal items in and can't keep personal items in your workspace. The table chairs and workspace were ergonomic and nice. Finding a quiet place to concentrate was a challenge at times.
cons:
Not a con for everyone. It just did not work for me. 

People work close together and noise levels were significant in my area. I had an auditory processing condition making it difficult to hear people on the phone due to the background noise. I purchased special headphones but they didn't help a great deal. I was not comfortable seeking an accommodation for this.

If privacy or being able to have a personal space is important to you this is could be a negative and worth consideration. Hoteling is not for everyone. At the time working home for Tampa employees was not an option.

Navigating the organization can be challenging and political. Getting things done quickly can be challenging. This includes getting access to resources needed for your job. Speaking up can be tricky and fraught with peril. Be very mindful of who you direct request/s to...and how you make that request. Optics are important.

I worked for Citi during a time of significant departmental change. I really enjoyed the people I worked with outside of the environment.

A company that definitely tries to incorporate diversity and inclusion into it's recruiting culture but still has a way to go in terms of creating an environment that feels like differences are at home.

summary: It was good until it wasn’t.
pros: Lots of Flexibility when it came to work life balance. The group I supported was a wonderful group who had great ideas.
cons: Direct manager was great. Senior management, not so much. Always looking to save a buck. The team wanted to be innovative but they were always held back because they never got the funding they needed to make changes. When all the offshoring started it never stopped. Too many long tenure people (15, 20+ years) were let go to save money and move jobs to low cost countries.

advice: Benefit cost increases often out-pace merit increases resulting in compensation going back-wards year-over year.
pros: Good company overall with many really good people working there.
cons: It is often said that the "C" in Citi stands for Change.  To enjoy working at Citi you need to embrace the constant change.  This is not only a result of the changing market conditions but also managements continuously changing priorities.  It can be frustrating at times to work full-throttle on a project to have it set-aside to begin work full-throttle on a new one, until it happens again.

summary: Big money center banks are all pretty much the same
advice:
If there is an open position please find someone within the US to fill it. What does the US government get by way of taxes if the job is offshored?

For a moment, forget about the taxes the US government would get. In what way does a job created in India benefit Citi in the US? If you employ someone in the US, there is a chance, however small it may be, that the person would come back to you for a mortgage loan or a home equity loan or a credit card or a checking / saving account. In a worse case scenario where the US employee does not offer you any business, there is 100% chance that the money earned in the US would at least circulate within the US and help American economy. The job created in India has near zero chance of helping US economy. And remember, when the American consumer rolls, the US banks tend to improve their earnings as well.

One might argue that the employee hired in India generates similar business opportunities as the employee hired in the US. Well, if you have the statistics, please make the numbers public along with the business volume in USD terms.

This problem is not seen just at Citi. This is common place occurrence where short sighted American corporations are shooting themselves in the foot. Wake up !!!
pros:
The company has a global footprint and hence offers plenty of room for career mobility within the company. The company offers comparable 401K and other benefits though there as been some level of reduction in health benefits recently. 

They do believe in meritocracy but occasionally, one does see old boy networks playing their part. This is arguably true for most big money center employers, so one could give them a pass on this one. In short, if one maintains high level of efficiency at work and keep up good relations up the chain, getting a promotion would not be difficult.

Work wise, they do offer a reasonable balance between personal and professional life.
cons: Ease of mobility does not necessarily translate into higher wages. They have been outsourcing a lot of their back office/technology work. This tends to bring down not just the morale but also the compensation levels of the work force in the US. In addition, they have also embarked on re-locating a lot of positions to low cost states such as Texas and Florida. While this may bring in some savings to the employer, it may not always be the right option for people with school going children and working spouses to relocate for example - from New York to TX. So watch out what you are getting into.

summary: It's an ok company. You may have a chance to move up if you know someone.
advice: Take the time to value your existing employees and review the time/effort they put in. I worked at a branch in NY. I was rated satisfactory or better, did all the training to move into the ABM role, went to different branches to help when needed, used workforce to make schedules, reviewed accounts, reviewed teller transactions, cash counts, filled in other roles like customer service when it was a position, went on company interviews/workshops which had all positive results, had a substantial knowledge of internal systems, and even had increased authority in my head teller role. However, when I went to apply internally for ABM positions in which I had completed all the required training, I only received one call back... Ever. And during that interview, the Area Operations Director, had a quite an issue with the distance I lived from the branch I was applying, which she made apparent through our interview. After that, the rest of my applications were never even considered. And I even went on a mock interview in LIC after that. During 2012-2103 I literally applied for every single Assistant Branch Manager position in NY and NJ. I sent out over 20 submissions and did not even receive a response to one. Meanwhile, the company hires inexperienced external candidates and also left various spots unfilled. Ultimately I needed to leave the company because I clearly did not have a chance to advance and a tellers salary was just not substantial enough for my situation anymore. I even wrote in depth about this in my last VOE. In the end, you lost a good employee.You wasted thousands of dollars paying me, sending me to extra training, sending me to career advancement workshops for a new role, for nothing. I would have gone to just about any branch, would have gladly worked overtime, weekends, etc. all for a the chance to have an intensely stressful job, with long hours, and little recognition.
pros: Work-life balance is ok. Not a bad place if your branch staff is competent. Good chance for advancement if you are related to someone.
cons: Concerned about service and operations but doing away with more operations and service positions. Slim chance of moving up unless you know someone. In addition to family, will advance anyone that has amazing sales stats even if you are incompetent. Raises kind of suck

summary: Good opportunity to enter in Financial industry and good scope for growth available here.
advice: Please outline the basis of giving bonus or increment to employess since it does not go inline with perfomance ratings given.
pros: Good scope of growth available in this company. Managers are very much supportive in terms of work and also personal life when it comes to take time off when you need it to support your family.
cons: You get good performance ratings but at times it does not result in good increment or bonus. It hurts when you work hard and don't get rewarded monetarily.

summary: If you wanna be stuck in a job with high expectations and no $ , then work here!
advice:
Promote hard working performers.
Get rid of the Manager's with hidden agendas.
Ask for 360 degree feedback from works on their managers, you will be enlightened!
Get training $ to the employees, or you are going to lose some really good IT people like you did ME!
pros:
Telecommute - Many received mandatory 3 days a week work from home due to downsizing of real estate in key states, New York, New Jersey, etc.  Ability to work from home was a benefit to me.
Holiday/Vacation Time off - Received 17 days vacation on hire in, and 12 holidays.  It is probably typical, but was more than I had before.
cons:
Training - They have no money in budget for training.  They will expect you to be CISSP, but getting it approved goes all the way to the top, and then they won't pay for travel.  Any other training you need to stay current on IT will never be approved, and if you had to travel to the class or conference, it will NEVER be approved.  They have high expectations on your IT skill level, but do not send you to any training that's critical for you to stay current!  CAREER SUICIDE!
PAY - Worked there over 5 years, my pay went up 1% or less each year even with great performance reviews.  Citi = no money.
FAVORITISM - People are promoted based on Senior Managers needing head count under them so they look important and don't lose their jobs.  People are promoted not based on experience/skills but on hidden agendas.  Bonuses, training, pay increases come from who you know, not what you know.
LAYOFFS - Merry Christmas, Citi likes to do mass layoffs at the end of the year to avoid bonus payouts in January.  They have reduced their size by over 100,000 employees in the last 1-2 years.  This is not a career company.
VACATION DAYS DO NOT CARRY OVER - You can't carry over more than 5 days, and you'll have to use them by March 31st.
TECHNOLOGY - All the banks they acquired during the getting fat/rich days, created a lot of older technology to be supported.  The recent sell offs the last few years has gotten rid of some of it, but the current technology wasn't able to be maintained and invested in.  Many systems are running 4-5 years behind current releases.

advice: Retain talented employees with benefits compensations according to their work.
pros:
In my case, my job responsibilities consist basically in attending calls and discussing topics with people around the globe, so I improved my english and soft skills a lot.
Really talented people work for the company.
cons:
Company processes are very complicated, makes it hard to get things done. 
In terms of technologies used and best practices a bank is not in the cutting edge... So be prepared some long and sometimes boring calls.
Salaries are tied to union agreements meaning there are no raises. Getting a promotion takes 2 years minimum.

advice: Keep up the good work and I am  proud of being working in Citi.  There are lot of technology solutions are implemented in Silo in various regions and should be integrated for cost optimization and to leverage across the region to improve both top line and bottom line growth.
pros: Nice team and part of very big team. Leadership is good at Sr. management level. Good brand name. Variety of technology to work with.
cons: Team is distributed across many places including various offshore places. Communication is difficult but team is good, so one can pull thru.

pros: Overall, great company to work for.  Interesting projects to work on, and the opportunity to work with global teams.
cons: Each time there was a change in upper management, the top priorities would change.  Although, it does make sense to assess potential changes, and definitely cancel certain projects, it does not make sense to kill a project when it is ready to implement and the investment has been made,  just due to the fact a new leader doesn't feel the value in the project.

advice:
When you promote staff to managerial positions please ensure that they get managerial training and her constantly being assessed on their continued ability to lead people.

In some teams,  a situation where a senior staff member simply appoints his crony and clans man/woman to a position of leadership without throwing the position open for team members to vie for, creates leadership by godfatherism, which is the opposite of meritocracy.
pros: Citi is a great company.  They have a strong brand. You can grow your career at Citi.
cons: Some managers lack professionalism and run their teams like an extension of their father's farms.

summary: Great company to start your career

cons:

summary: Overall a great place to work
pros:

- Lots of opportunities to work from home or full remote
- Career progression opportunities are plenty
- A lot of quality training for professional certifications available through udemy.
- 6% 401k match
- 22 days of vacations for VP level and above
cons:
- Work life balance has  not been great the last couple years.
- Company is very large and can be very bureaucratic.
- 401k match lump sum at the end of the first quarter following the performance year in which it is earned.

summary: Great Professional experiences with a world renowned company
pros: The opportunities are vast and wide at Citi.  On a daily basis, one has the privilege of working with people sitting right next to them, and around the globe.  In my experience, I have gotten the opportunity to help set up new call centers, call recording technologies, and manage software development projects for one of Citi's largest strategic programs.
cons: It is difficult at times to see how the scope of your individual assignment plays out in the larger picture of what Citi is doing as a whole.

summary: A great place to experience and gain in depth knowledge about global banking.
advice: Immediate manager have no control or say on the employees performance review.  Corporate message and actual culture is not in sync. Management does not seek and/or value employees feedback

summary: My experience at Citibank was great.

cons: Because pay was less than average for the position I spent a lot of times working overtime and trying to bonus.

Additionally, it gets noisy in the HIVE.  It's a great concept, but it's not being executed well in my opinion.

advice: Ensure that employees are growing in their career. Refine processes more and focus on consolidation of units. Have a clean-up week each year for people at each level to think about how to make things better rather than get stuck into a rut.
pros: Smart people who are always pushing the boundry to deliver more. People work together in cross-functional teams and collaborate well.
cons: Being a corporate setting, it is easy to become complacent after a while. The company needs to push people to be active about their career and make sure everyone is also advancing personally.

pros:

-Company culture seems decent (though all companies are somewhat cult-like with many their leadership principles and so forth). Citi actually donates to many foundations so they do put their money where their mouth is 

-Healthcare (aetna) is decent 

-
cons:
-Slow moving, things take forever to get done here. In order to push something to production for example there's a long arduous process to get approval and so forth. advice:

pros:
1) The base pay is OK-good and the health benefits and pension contributions are good-excellent. BUPA is the health provider and they were excellent. 

2) There are some fantastic colleagues who are really talented engineers. 

3) The offices are generally very pleasant. 

4) Some of the engineering work is really interesting and can be exciting.

5) If you get a good/supportive manager, you can boost your career growth in a shorter time span.
cons:
1) Is there ever a month that goes by in which Deutsche Bank isn't in the news for money laundering? It's demoralising working for an organisation that has a nefarious history and continues to be involved in dodgy activities. With the hundreds of millions spent on KYC processes at DB, it's incredible that such crimes continued to still occur very frequently. 

2) The resource planning that I witnessed was at times absolutely absurd. It got to the point where some teams were incredibly stretched working on key deliverables with tight deadlines and with a small team. And yet, DB hired external consultants on several ocassions who would be paid extortinate sums of money to come up with 'digital transformation' ideas that would be executed by DB engineers. So, the company is paying at least twice. That inconsistent approach to resourcing seemed to happen frequently. 

3) Some colleagues, especially around the VP level, are medicore and there's a layer of fat who enjoy good benefits which they realistically wouldn't get elsewhere who just stay and do just above the minimum while some really talented juniors get less benefits and tougher objectives. So, it's not really ultra meritocratic although if you really, really want it, you'll tend to get it. Also, at below VP level, no bonuses are paid. 

4) Also, the obsession from the senior management and board to get all employees, at least in Germany, COVID vaccinated and describing it as a 'moral obligation' in internal memos was creepy and a gross overreach. How about let employees decide for themselves what is best for their bodies or is that concept too hard for a German company to understand?

5) I experienced some super crazy politics that meant that collective objectives weren't met. At a VP+ level, things can become a bit machiavellian in that what's in the interests for the company aren't necessarily in the interests for your own personal career growth but that's an elephant in the room that everyone ignores. 

An example may be that a certain legacy system wasn't migrated to a new system because it has some critical functionality and the team supporting the application were fired very quickly in the past for some unknown reasons. By migrating the system and saving the company money, you wouldn't be able to have X budget to keep maintaining that sytem and having a bigger team. So, you would lose headcount and budget by doing what's a positive thing for the company. So objectives need to be better aligned. Also, teams would compete with each other for 'territory' as that would bring in more budget so things get quite odd when officially, you're in the same boat but unofficially, you're conspiring how to 'one up' them all the time. 

6) DB engineering tends to build things with the best of intentions and then some new top dog will come in and make wholesale changes, like firing an entire team that supports/maintains some applications, that make the past 2 years of hard work totally pointless and redundant. Technology and ways of doing things do indeed change but the lack of a consistent approach / consistent goal over different eras of Managing Directors results in a bit of a headless chicken effect.

7) It is getting much better but diversity at the top level is still lop-sided. There are measures being taken to address this but there's a long way to go.

summary: A company which is too large to be effectively managed but has a great brand
advice: As mentioned above, Senior management need to get the resourcing balance right - they spend too much money covering their backs by spending money on audit whilst they need to spend money on core functions such as technology.  Secondly attrition is a major concern - even in the current market environment (August 2008), collegues are leaving voluntarily.  Thirdly, there are far too many contractors and consultants employed at the bank.  These should be reduced as it is often the case that key contractors are kept as they "know too much" about critical systems.  Finally, Senior Management should seek to "westernise" the company.  The bank is still too bureaucratic and Germanic for the 21st century.
pros: The Deutsche Bank brand is brilliant - it is widely respected to DB's clients and because of this, it is also highly respected in the job markets.  The name on your CV, particularly if you can mention investment banking related experience, is worth a great deal.  In my opinion, the best reason to work for DB is it's global brand name.  Compared to other investment banks, its salary is competitive.  Another great reason to work for Deutsche Bank in the London office is the work life balance.  Unlike other investment banks, it understands that you have a life outside work!  For example, the social networks such as the family network are very active.
cons: Although Deutsche Bank boasts of a "one bank" culture, this is far from the truth.  The 1 bank brand is strong and it is worth recognising that there are roughly 80,000 employees at the firm; many of those work in the retail arm.  Although the retail business keeps things going in a downturn, it makes the firm far too large to manage.  Senior management is far too Germanic in their approach and fill your day with unproductive administration.  For example, technology and business audits are continually carried out but due to cost constraints, resourcing is so tight that there is no time to address these.  Some areas of the bank thrive but others consistently fail.

summary: Don't expect to be rewarded if you work in Technology.
advice: Pay people who work in Technology at least the market rate and provide them with performance related bonuses. If you pay peanuts, you get monkeys.
pros:
Technology in Deutsche Bank is way behind pretty much every one of its competitors. Thus, if you join technology you can be a part bringing it up to speed with the competition, and gain lots of responsibility in the process.

Hours are 9-5.
cons:
Compensation is exceptionally poor for people who work in technology. Bonuses are entirely politics based. It doesn't matter how hard you work. You might come up with a trading algorithm or technology enhancement that enables the trading desk to increase PnL by 50% to £1m, but don't expect that to be reflected in your bonus. You're still getting a fixed 20% so my best advice is to go home at 5 and not make the extra effort.

The business side still has absolute control over the budget, changing it widely from +/- 10% EACH quarter. It's impossible to plan any kind of stable headcount.

Management is poor. If you come up with a great idea in DB make sure you keep it to yourself, because EVERYONE will steal it and give you no credit whatsoever.

There are lots of opportunities in DB, but no one is going to help you take them. You've got to play political games all the time.

The graduate scheme is pretty awful. HR have made the assumption that if you're a graduate you know nothing about either banking or technology. I learnt nothing in the time I had training. You also get lumbered with two "Change Management" projects, which are essentially a load busy work and a waste of time. You teams management won't give you support in doing this so you're going to end up working weekends on it.

advice:
1) There should be one manager, not six. 
2) The manager should be leading and directing, not saying yes to everyone then denying responsibility for their decisions. 
3) A general rule is that one person should not suffer the consequences of another persons mistake, therefore stop low-mid level managers costing people their careers for errors that the managers make.
4) There is a recognised push to deal with the dishonesty and lack of integrity but the managers are not fulfilling this and employees are left with consequences. Example, a manager could make a mistake and blame it on an employee, the employee is then fired. This is simply not acceptable and you absolutely should not allow it to happen in this day and age.
pros:
They pay very well as a salary instead of a bonus.
Their pension contributions are very high, you don't need to contribute yourself.
Work life balance can be ok in some teams.
cons:
1) Horrendous incompetence. It is really apparent from the first day. There are an awful lot of people there who make a lot of mistakes or who just can't do their job. It is great that DB want to keep people, but it really is these long-timers that are holding DB back.

2) Many, many people who all think their job is to micromanage you. This is particularly bad in tech. There are VPs who have no idea what a work item is or what it does or what is needed but have spent years in a job where their role was to find someone else to do the work. As a result, these people will grind projects to a halt.

3) With so many VPs in some teams compared to AVPs, there is a problem similar to the NHS "too posh to wash" problem. If there is six VPs and one AVP, none of them will do any work since they don't want to seem downgraded to AVP. it is absolute nonsense.

4) One day you're told to do one thing, the next you are berated for not knowing someone else decided you should be doing something else. Yes, silly culture.

5) Very old and poor quality software in a lot of teams. This is well known, and often a problem with old systems, but at DB it is horrendously bad and a consequence of the incompetence they are also known for. Their systems make no sense, neither does their code. Their low quality VPs that have been there a very long time and have not kept with the latest technology cause this.

6) An astonishing amount of VP level employees. In some teams there will be just one AVP and six or more VPs. Absolute nonsense. A lot of these VPs will have been around for a very long time and not very good at their job. Their knowledge is out of date and they hold newcomers back from introducing new technology or ideas. This is a problem a lot of companies have, but as usual DB simply doesn't respond.

7) There is air of dishonesty in this company which can be seen by the actions of managers and some VPs, and is a reason for the endless negative media reports surrounding them. They do seem to lack integrity and make decisions with complete disregard for the consequences of those affected. This is simply not how companies operate nowadays. Instead mangers should be accountable, decision makers should be accountable - instead their incompetence affects people directly and causes them to lose their job in some cases. This simply shouldn't be tolerated anymore, other companies sorted out problems like this years ago but DB is just not responding.

summary: Great reputation and brand, let down by very poor management - frustrating at so many levels.
advice:
Stop promoting your friends, stop all the horse trading that goes on when deciding promotions. Promote only on merit.

Have a flatter structure. Hire better managers. Don't be afraid to sack people who are not performing. Offer training to those you want to keep so that they can actually do the job at hand.

Reward those that do well, and focus on keeping them at the bank. The attrition figures for the high performers are attrocious for a leading bank.
pros: Excellent benefits, friendly workforce, opportunity to work with a variety of people on many different projects, largely due to their outsourcing strategy. Met some really likeable people here.
cons:
Very very very poor management.  They're trying to reorganise the technology division but are just making it worse. Too much management, too many layers. In fact, it often seems that the place is full of managers. Everybody is trying to become AVP, or VP, or Director, or Managing Director, most of the time without merit. People are promoted for the wrong reasons - for length of service and friendships rather than deliverables - definitely NOT a meritocracy.  People are more focussed on promotion and building their own mini-empire rather than delivering well.

They also outsource a lot, and accept work done at a sub-standard level. Most of the management do not understand technology and do not have a handle on quality of work and timelines.  They waste a lot of money on this. Most of the technology staff are sub-standard external consultants. This leads to poor results.

People are also free to choose whatever technology they want to get the job done. There are very few standards.  The people at the top of the technology division need to ask themselves what they are doing and why such basics standards are not in place.

They need qualified people brought in to change things. People with guts to get rid of the mis-firing management, and greater focus to bring in talented developers who will hold the knowledge long after a project has been delivered.

I cannot stress enough how frustrating it is to see layer after layer of middle management.  I do not understand why all the MDs, Directors and VPs are needed, and moreso, what they actually do.   Don't get me wrong, there are some very bright people here at all levels, but they are diluted by really poor employees.

They struggle to keep their best staff for many reasons, and tend to hang on to the people who are performing poorly.  They should look into why this is if they really want to change technology at the bank.

summary: Appalling place to work if you're in technology
advice:
This advice is to senior management - GET RID OF ALL THE LEVELS OF VPs! You're looking to cut costs, there's 90k per person right there!
Invest in IT if you want to be a leading/cutting edge company. The company I now work for has a healthy budget, no unneccessary managers, values a meritorious culture, and is the world leader in its industry. There's food for thought!
pros: some decent honest people, great place to work if you like to backstab, play the game and use a lot of jargon in your day-to-day life
cons:
Where to begin - please note this is based on working in IT Infrastructure (London office) and so may not be typical of the company as a whole, only my experience of it in this area:

- a culture of long hours where they aren't required! Sure we all have times when we have to stay late, or even want to stay to finish off that project or meet that deadline. But here people consciously stay at their desks and chat, go on facebook, make personal calls etc, until 8-9pm, then make a show of sighing and leaving, and come in the next morning (often around 10am due to their 'late night') and tell everyone how they never left until 9pm. And they actually gain promotion on the basis of this!! 

- constantly driving down costs and reducing teams who do all the work, resulting in teams of 1 or 2 running entire regions, all the while keeping multiple layers of management. As an example, you can have 2 people reporting to a VP, reporting to another VP, reporting to a D, reporting to another D, reporting to an MD, reporting to another MD before you advance to any real level in the company. The amount of money being saved is completely negated by a completely unnecessary hierarchy

- completely sexist - no women advance in this area unless they 'look good'. Those who don't have to work hard but never advance

- advancement based on friendships and contacts rather than achievement and potential

- no clear focus of where they are headed - the same projects and improvements cycle every few years justifying projects and looking to change and improve standards with no real intention to do so

- offices falling apart and drive towards 'clear desk policy' whereby all staff work on a stark white open desk with no privacy walls, and have to put all desk and personal items in a locker (no pedastals allowed under desks) result in offices with all the charm and personality of a hospital

- the lowest morale of any company I have worked in (over 20 years City/finance experience)

- the new CEOs came on board with the amazing idea of reducing Infrastructure by 60%. I know they're not sexy like the traders, but they keep the rest of you running! Don't forget that! 

- more of an opinion this one, but every single person I encounter where the subject of DB comes up has some sort of bad story - "I know someone who worked there who had a nervous breakdown", "aren't they a terrible company to work for", "I've heard they're bad". Now as I say, this is opinion, but I've never had this for any other place I've worked, and as mentioned above I have 20+ yrs of corporations

And this is all that immediately comes to mind. I'm sure if I had a think I could find a lot more!

summary: Staff Augmentation!  Come here to be bored.
advice: Keep hiring senior people from outside the company so you can cement your positions without the threat of more competent existing employees being the obvious choice to replace you.  In other words- keep not promoting the employees who know both banking and software.  Keep working people on weekends and late hours for the non-existent bonus or recognition award so they quit and  you get the chance to build an organization of drones.
pros: There's a free fitness center.  There's a cafe.  You get lots of vacation.  In some teams, you can do absolutely nothing, work 5 hours a day and go home.   If you are a mediocre developer, if you can get onto a team on the second floor, you might have a long career there.  Bonuses used to be good.  Salaries are good.  Insurance is good.  If you can put up with it working here, you'll have a good chance to be poached by a different company.
cons:
The office in Cary is filled with incompetent senior managers.  The least competent is at the top, followed by the management team.  Why?  Because they're cast-offs, or imports from elsewhere.  The ones in banking don't understand software development, and the ones in software are the people fired from middle management of other companies.  

This is honestly a dead-end if you want a career.  They talk about "expert path" for technical people which doesn't exist, at least not in Cary.  You will have no autonomy as all the decisions are made in London and NY.  Your senior manager is put in place by those same teams nervous about hiring outside of the hubs, so his job is just to work you until you quit and not to make any noise such as picking good software or practices.  Your failure provides them cover to not transfer jobs from their location.  They have never promoted anyone in Cary to a senior position- the last three directors weren't even from other Deutsche Bank locations; they went outside the company instead of promote one of the more than 100 existing managers or senior developers.  There is a serious flight of talent- other companies are easily able to poach people who are competent, able to work under pressure, and worth every penny of their salary.  Speaking of which, you used to get a bonus for all the downsides mentioned above.  No more.   It depends on the performance of the company  to get a maximum of 4%.  Take a look at the stock and you'll see how unlikely that is.    Diversity is overdone- protected groups can't be fired, and no one cares to take the time to hire good talent, they just want to have bodies to fill their hiring quotas.  The center head stood up in front of the employees at a town hall and said he's going to hire 50% women. What happened to equal opportunity hiring?   Oh and the fitness center and cafe mentioned as "pro" are just 'meh', but I had to say something nice to fill in that box.  Which is what you'll do for several hours a week- mandatory training classes for financial stuff which you'll never use as a developer but bureaucracy rules.  The HR team is horrible- they live in a little private area, through a card-key door, so you can't interact with them.  If you ask them a question, they'll reply with "call the hotline'.  Everyone desk is a 'trading desk', meaning they've crammed people into huge open areas with the same double-monitor and phone on the side of the desks with employees 5-wide and back to back.  Even call centers have more room.  They've got 800+ people in one building that other residents of the office park have closer to 300 in theirs.  If you need time to concentrate on working out a difficult debugging or clever software solution: give up.  The noise level doesn't allow it (*See working late or weekends comment).  This sardine-like setup also has an unfortunate characteristic of if someone skips a shower, everyone knows it.

Deutsche Bank's corporate culture, at least in the New York region, was to be cowboys - we were encouraged to do whatever possible to get the job done as soon as possible. Later, after the Bankers' Trust/Alex Brown acquisition there was too much process. Only now are we starting to get a good balance.

advice:
Improve the hiring process and hire the right people for the right positions.
Create a mechanism to allow feedback from direct reports on people managers' performance.
pros:
Nice office, although I personally have never found the time to use the play rooms.
Various training programs, although these are available only after 6 months of employment.
Work for home option - 4 days a month.
Free & good coffee and tea.
cons:
Low technical knowledge level in most of the teams.
Organizational chaos - roles and responsibilities are not always clear. Often ended up doing lower level tasks than what was described in the role description.
A lot of waste in the so-called “agile” projects.
No mechanism to share feedback on your direct line manager’s performance.
Long working hours, including weekend, in some projects.

advice: perhaps triaining for managers so that they actually can properly guide the careers of motivated employees as opposed to selecting only "high potential" candidates towards increased responsibilities and growth.
pros: Flexibility in your work situation and remote access is great.  Many colleagues work from home at least one day per week-this is great for working parents.  There are many great programs relating to cultural diversity that promote and enhance a very inclusive environment for staff.
cons: DB has the potential to be an exceptional environment for real growth and development, however there is way to go before that becomes a reality.  Current management changes, ongoing upheaval and outsourcing makes this difficult. This puts undue stress on staff who are looking for guidance and direction.

advice: Do think about how you are going to achieve what you are trying to achieve.  The new people culture that you are bringing in isn't going to take you there.
pros: The money is/was good.  The bank is now trying hard to be a technology company, but not sure how successful it would be.
cons:
The bank had never been a technology company, and had heavily relied on its outsource partners.  However, in the recent months it is trying hard to be a technology company and trying to bring in expertise and intellectual property.  But in doing so, the culture within the bank has taken a back seat.  It is not the same place anymore.
Work life balance is taking a back seat.

advice: More work from home flexibility would be nice.
pros: Awesome benefits! Great pay! The Cary location is really investing in creating a community. There are employee engagement groups that work hard to make this a great place to work! I am working in cutting edge technologies and the company seems to want to invest in their employees and in employee retention. The office space is very nice including an onsite cafe and gym.
cons: There is less flexibility than in most tech companies I have worked for. At the Cary location, you can work from home on occasion, when necessary, but most people are in the office most days. It is a bank. As should be expected, there are security and process requirements that can impede your job efficiency.

summary: Great place with a few flaws
advice: Seriously...take a look at the middle management.  We are moving away from focusing on the job and getting more into nasty politics.  Vision in the right direction, but the middle management has too many incompetent managers.  Other than that...thanks for making DB's technology group such a great place to work.
pros:
--Great Pay
--Good vision by senior management
--Global presence
--Incredible place to start your career through their graduate program
--People with diverse backgrounds
--Business understands the value of technology
--Mobility encouraged and promoted
--Spends money for social causes
--Great benefits
--More vacation time than you can spend
cons:
--Senior management comes up with brilliant ideas, but picks morons to implement them
--Middle management (VP/Director) level is full of nasty politics
--Complete lack of diversity in upper management (mostly male and white)

summary: Stuffy work environment but with global possibilities
advice:
- Hire younger energetic people with good ideas
- Give people enough for them to be vested in actual improvements but not long enough for them to be regarded as indispensable or rulers of their kingdoms
- Document processes more effectively and be more transparent on performance metrics with all reports. Especially in cases where performance cannot be simply measured but must be gauged by VOC, etc
pros:
- Stable work environment
- Global outreach for personal development and career options
- Interesting people to work with
cons:
- Stifling work environment sometimes : pseudo innovation rewarded rather than actual improvements
- Lethargic on technology changes
- In India, DB has a very nepotistic and "arse-licky" culture, especially in the back offices

summary: High Tech Labor Salvery.. too much bureaucracy.. too much panic all the time (Assistant VP)
advice: Have some "American Spirit" , this is America not London or India!
pros:
It's situated in calm and peaceful Cary, NC
Bonus ( If you are are good in internal bureaucracy and manage to get it!)
cons:
In over 15 years of my IT career I have never seen such bad work atmosphere with so much panic and work pressure from chain of managers over you. Everybody is president , vice presidents and managers.. too less people who really work.. so of course work pressure... That's what managers are for right? Make tech slave labor work. or how else managers will get big bonuses?

Their new policy is to lure tech guys from other countries or other states to leave their good jobs dreaming big bonuses and peaceful life , come to this remote location of Cary...then make them work like slaves. Hire one senior tech guy and then hire four beginners so that this experienced guy will actually teach the beginners everything and even DO their job... as they are "no-vice".. so make sure you are not that "experienced guy"

This is not a bank. It's a bank's IT development center. So basically we develop applications for bank. So it works like a IT shop with all the crap that comes with it....

Every body ready to cut your throat to get anybody out of his bonus way. Everybody looks like in pressure and panic state.
If you are looking for great work atmosphere and peaceful life where you can work and do some innovative work then DON'T come to this Cary Development Center.
Only join this center , if you just want good pay and bonuses...but you should be ready to take this much stress, panic , and ready to be micro managed by omnipresent managers.

advice: As a recommendation to senior management, more emphasis should be placed on the build-up of new talents within the organization as well as more transparency around business lines' strategies.
pros: Deutsche Bank provides excellent opportunities for professional growth based upon the opportunities presented from very early on.  Employees have the opportunity to prove themselves from very early on and take on a wide remit of work.
cons: In terms of career advancement and financial rewards for the level of work performed, this has not been entirely satisfactory.  It seems, as in most companies, the number of years of experience is given precedence over the level / complexity of work managed and projects successfully delivered.

summary: Safe haven to hide and die as a specialist
advice: Perform a thorough employee clean-up based on merit and value they deliver. Be more result-oriented rather than process-oriented.
pros:
Good compensation in comparison with other software companies
Possibility to have very little control over yourself if you play right.
Good people.
cons: Non result-oriented and highly political environment. People spend enormous amount of time on meaningless discussions. It is absolutely possible and widely encouraged to get promotions and salary increases just by feeding bulls..t to senior management. Many good specialists, who could otherwise deliver some value, figure this out and become highly paid politicians. Not to mention a wide layer of mediocre staff who just hide there doing nothing.

summary: Good for starting your career or you don't have an university title
advice: Stop hiring or promoting people without a living cert to be the boss of an MBA owner!
pros: Good private pension contributions if you are 30 yrs old or above. Good salary, considered the low complexity of work. Very friendly environment with your pairs. HR team will help you if you want to move to another team or branch.
cons: Your tasks will be very repetitive. Low training is provided because you boss most of the time doesn't know himself the bank's products and the HR don't want to pay for external training. Expect a lot of bureaucracy, which mainly doesn't come from Germany but from your line manager, who will be obsessed about control. He/she will create tasks that are not related to your work just to check on you. The Dublin site is considered bad by other branches all around the world. Hence, colleagues from other branches can treat you very badly. The offices are based in the Eastpoint business park which is impossible to reach. The food from the canteen is low quality and the selection is poor.

advice: If you really want to have a reputation as being family friendly, this attitude / approach should be distributed from the top down.
pros: It seems pretty difficult to differentiate most of the larger investment banks from each other, but I believe Deutsche Bank is well respected on the Street.  Salaries are competitive.
cons: Similar to all banks, but also depending on what group you work in, a 40-hour work week is unrealistic.  You get paid well, but you're expected to work long hours to finish the job.  You get 5 weeks of vacation time / personal days, but I don't know anyone who would actually be bold enough to use all the allotted vacation time--face time is much more important.  Similarly, even though the company offers flex time and working from home arrangements, I'm not sure I would be willing to pursue those options for fear of jeopardizing the quality of my bonus.  Lastly, the cubicles are uncomfortably tiny (they are so short they only come up to your neck), so there's not much privacy.

advice: Your people can only perform well if they have the necessary training, time in position and clear expectations. It's not all about social networking. Some people just want to do their job and get ahead by hard work instead of playing politics all the time.
pros: Huge amount of diversity and great acceptance of others. They have great benefits and the salary is at least on par if not better in most cases. Free coffee.
cons: It's an investment bank and it's all about the money. Can be very stressful. Training is usually lacking or non existent. Expectations can be unreasonable by management but there is always someone willing to point the finger in times of trouble.

summary: Challenging projects and interesting technology slowed by bureaucracy and politics.
advice:
Further reduce bonus pay tied to "getting it out" by the end of the year. Focus instead on defect rates and production lifecycles as these are more critical and will tie management's decisions to proper SDLC.
Be more stable at the top. We've seen so many heads come and go it is dizzying.
pros:
Great team atmosphere and focus on worklife balance.
Serious focus on agile and doing projects right.
Lots of OSS in use.
Challenging projects with notable impacts.
cons:
Antiquated technology (i.e. Win XP, IE)
Bureaucracy and resources are the hardest part of any IT project.
Politics of higher ups often subverts otherwise logical implementations, dilating project rollouts.

advice: Help the bank reward employees earlier than is policy. Promote worthy candidates earlier. Position and pay on more than just years of experience.
pros: Base salary can be low but bonus can be really good.  The bank owns large systems and provides copious opportunities to learn and grow. The types of problems a big bank faces are numerous and always challenging.
cons: Poor hiring practices. Deadlines are everywhere due to regulations. London calls all the shots.  If you're not from London, growth potential is limited. US offices are shadowed greatly by the larger hub offices. Employees don't stay long.

advice: You have to buy quality otherwise you should be prepared that it will only attract fresh graduates or low skilled workforce from emerging countries who will leave as soon as a better offer comes. Sustainibility in the risk area is key and this concept does not exist at DB.
pros: Scope of covered areas, really the top of the profession. Insight to the full operation of a universal bank. Some very well educated and respectful colleagues with the necessary drive.
cons:
- Salary way below the sectoral standard in the light of the experience needed for the job
- Life-Work balance non existant
- Annoyingly unserious career plans and compensation packages
- Many mistakes and delays due to bureaucracy

advice: You have to figure out a better way to motivate and keep employees, almost all of my previous colleagues who were decent programmers left for better salaries or opportunities
pros: Initial salary was competitive, colleagues were not the typical neckbearded programmers, there were some opportunities to work with some newer technologies, development work was decent
cons: A bit of chaos in the development area, colleagues were not so well prepared technically, salary increases don't keep up with the market, rigid corporate rules - you don't have admin rights on your machine as a developer, they promise you'll work both frontend and backend, but for me it was mostly frontend and I really didn't appreciate that

advice: They just need to manage the bad press about the bank and to continue to keep the communication lines open between management and employees so they can mitigate its negative effect on employee morale.
pros: Performing your role felt like you always need to be on your toes so you always strive to be at your best. You also work with some of the best people in the industry who inspires you. Definitely a good place for people looking for personal and professional growth
cons: The work can be stressful and sometimes require long hours. May not be for people who think that work-life balance can only be achieved in an 8-hour job.

advice: Get rid of performance curve where you need to set low marks to people who doesn't deserve it.
pros: Very good compensation. Young and professional people, ability to grow. Complex and challenging projects. The best company I ever worked for. Employee can get almost any training or conference. Your skills and attitude will be noticed. Your concerns will be heard. Of course it depends on your manager, but I never met a terrible one. If you smart you can always come to an agreement. You can change roles and projects easily.
cons: Terrible burocracy monster. Access to prod servers are managed by vendors, who are actually dumbs.  Not good life-work balance.

advice: Clean house. Bring in management with investment banking experience.  Give the engineer, who wishes to be a individual contributor, a career path.
pros: There are many offices globally. This opens up a vast amount relocation possibilities.
cons: This location is unproductive due to massive amounts of redtape and ineffective management. It is not a good place for an engineer accustomed to producing results. If I were a new-hire (and I'm not), I would not want this to be my first job experience. The center resembles what you might find in a call center in India, both in terms of office layout and in ethnic headcount.

advice: Graduate program too long, evaluation needs to be 360 degrees like other banks in order to make managers accountable for themselves
pros: Deutsche Bank has one of the largest graduate programs amongst all the investment banks, rotations allow you to try a few different areas before you settle on your desk
cons: Some of the managers who take on graduates just do it for lip service, it's sometimes difficult to land rotation that has good work, so even though the general idea of the rotation is to help you gain knowledge and good overview of several different areas, you rarely get that unless you end with a good manager

summary: Don't come here now, you will probably get let go in 6 months.
advice: None that would make a difference.
pros: Not much beyond the usual, people are generally ok to work with.
cons:
-They cut rollover vaca days (use them or lose them) 
-Takes 5 years to be fully vested 
-Comp tends to be on the low end and no salary transparency (person next to you with same title probably getting paid more than you) 
-Bonuses are a joke (the attitude from managers is be grateful you have a job) 
-Senior management leaving in droves, causing major disruptions
-Massive restructuring, morale is terrible as many colleagues are losing their jobs in the next few months
-Half the stuff that you will work on will never get implemented or used because there are no resources. 
Pretty much every one is looking for a job elsewhere.

advice:
Put more qualified people at the top.
Give time to actually execute a long term vision.
Stop the turnover.
pros:
Stable employment (or has been, with new management coming in, cuts are expected)
Extra week of vacation
Good work life / work from home policies (and in practice)
cons:
Frequent (every 1-2 years) turn over in management and corresponding change in priorities, direction
People in the senior positions often are not qualified but try to make a big splash with big promises.
Supremely hard to delivery anything strategic or anything of value.
Really, really outdated technology and a spaghetti web of technology piecemeal-ed from different "strategic" efforts which fall out of favor before they are finished.. every time.

advice: Step-up of self enclosed world and focus on your people who actually do the work, not those who play kiss up and jockey for face time and give empty results with smiles.
pros:
-Great people to work with within some teams.
- Visual surrounds pleasant to eyes.
-Amazing benefit packages.
cons: 1. Management worried more about self not development of employees 2. Pay raises? Joke. 3. To many people preferring FaceTime in office politics instead of making output product better. 4. IT structure is archaic.  5. No clear objectives. 6. No one in management wants to take a lead for change, comfortable in staying in same place, hinders growth.

advice: Enter the 21st century and give flexibility to your employees. Also, do not demand or put employees in a situation where they constantly have to work 2 hours overtime.
pros:
+ Very competitive salary
+ Very good colleagues, brilliant people
cons:
- Many security trainings
- MANY security trainings
- Insane pressure
- Rigid company structure, organisational nightmare
- As a software developer; prepare to have 0 control, no admin right, have your activities monitored and no access to modern development tools unless you go through a tedious process of applying within the company
- Work-from-home only after having worked at the company for 3 months, and then only for max 1 day per week
- Very tough internal pressure to deliver, say goodbye to work-life balance

summary: A place with no ethical values and zero culture
advice: Start caring about teams. implement a culture .
pros: Good work life balance and nothing else
cons:
Back office for London, no real leadership required in Dublin, just follow whatever they ask to do from London.
The worse part is that there's no people culture: zero. The main motive is that everybody thinks for themselves with very little care for the team.
While I was there I witnessed several abused from directors towards other staff members, some quite serious, but, although complains were raised, nothing really happened.
The level of politics, especially from those in UK, is simply unsustainable and wears off after a few months. People tend to run away within 10/18 months.
The level of technology in use is very conservative, even if Dublin is supposed to be a center of excellence. The pace of technology adoption is embarrassingly slow.
