cons: Terrible burocracy monster. Access to prod servers are managed by vendors, who are actually dumbs.  Not good life-work balance.

summary: Relatively strong equity research platform. Pay could be better, but good stability and work/life balance
advice: Needs to do a better job of incentivizing employees
pros:
Work/life balance, face time is not big here
2-week mandatory time off for equity research folks is awesome
Good stability...layoff and mass cuts in the US less likely despite European troubles
Very good global network/resources
Mgmt is trying to bring more structure and resources
cons:
Pay is good when you first get here, but average to below average
Needs to do a better job of incentivizing employees
Needs more team events
No real sense of culture, siloed work environment
No good sense of what is going on in the business globally...lack of cohesion
Too many internal systems and they are old

summary: Overall Positive but Opportunities of Growth are Limited.
advice: Pay attention to the needs of your people.  Quite a bit of good talent moves on when they see no potential of growth.  The political climate of turning the other cheek needs to change as well.
pros: A global company with an international reach.
cons: Hectic work schedules, to much politics, very few opportunities for growth.  Growth is much easier out of the London or German Offices.  Any other office would be considered a satellite office with very few opportunities to grow.

advice:
Don't just say you are open to ideas. Actually listen and implement ideas 
Retain and encourage good ideas by giving less powers to VP and above
pros:
Deutsche bank is actually DBOI in Pune which is technology operations indeed

Some pros:
Great renumeration
Great transport facility
Great infrastructure
Good opportunity to learn about banking
cons:
VP dominance
Lack of strategic direction
Lack of Agile adoption or reluctance to change
Mostly maintenance projects
Expensive canteen
Low salary hikes
No onsite travel opportunity
No 4 wheeler parking for below AVP

advice: None to my direct management as they are doing well. Continue to streamline processes and operations. New CEO now will be interesting to see what he does.
pros: Smart, friendly and collaborative colleagues in my area, Fantastic manager that really looks out for his employees while providing solid direction and guidance. Good work/life balance. Many active employee network groups that hold fun events.
cons: Very large and inefficient in general. It Takes too many different groups and way too much time to get things done. Very open seating arrangement.

advice: While merit based reviews are a good start, don't adjust the bar when it is convenient.  Management should value their infrastructure support and development group as much as they do their investment group.  Arbitrary forced ranking of performance should never occur, though it is a common occurrence.
pros:
Lots of mobility opportunities
Hi intellect for most employees
Good compensation
cons:
Lots of talk about change, but nothing really changes
Ask for your lifetime salary requirements upfront since your base is not likely to go up EVER
Internal processes can be maddening

summary: Great work life balance, little rewards
advice: There needs to be a clearer way to evaluate and reward staff running projects under Vice President level. If this cannot change, there should provisions to allow for Vice Presidents to be placed in countries like Tokyo without having to be a manager.
pros: Great work life balance that allows for shifted work hours (within core hours) and working from home when needed. This caters for families with small children.
cons: No individual performance evaluation for staff below Vice President. This means that no matter how many projects we complete, we are not rewarded for our work.

summary: Great place to start your career as an engineer.
pros: Very smart people to work with, interesting projects (at least if you're an engineer) and a nice office space. It's a great place if you're a junior engineer and want to start you career. You'll learn all the essentials that help you to deliver large-scale and complex IT solutions. Very cool (local) senior management.
cons: No career opportunities for senior engineers. You either become a manager or have look for opportunities outside of the company. Definitely too much bureaucracy and a lot of cost-cutting and travel freezes over the last years.

advice: Stay the course for at least 18 months with a given technology program and management team so that something tangible can be delivered
pros: Diversity of work force; stimulating to work in such a complex matrix of multiple cultures.  People in the trenches are very down to earth and try to deliver value despite the convoluted processes needed to get things done in IT
cons: Constant re-orgs means re-branded objectives.  You end up wasting energy every time you have to start over under a new manager.  Now all jobs moving to NC and FL

advice: Make some bold decisions and move to new trading technology.  You can't really compete if you don't have the goods.
pros:
Benefits are good.  Coming from Morgan Stanley, that's a big deal.
There is a lot of responsibility placed on IT folks.  Competent people can have a big impact.
cons:
Trading systems are not world class; not even close.  Well, equities at least,  FX is top-notch.
Work in NY, senior mgt is in Europe and they try to apply "well it worked in London" theory to any new initiative or org change.  Local mgt is good, off shore mgt rots.

advice: I have no advice for you because you don't deserve any. At certain level you bring in talent for their new ideas and to help move your business forward onto excellence. When you start from Day 1 to tell us what to do, how to do it and then enforce micro-management level of control you already lost before you hired such talent.
pros:
- Salary, 
- Offices, 
- Response to and workforce organization during Covid19.
cons:

- Unrealistic targets with unrealistic deadlines 
- No real respect 
- No real trust
- Permanent control 
- No involvement just orders (agreed responsibilities are not reflected in my activity) 
- No communication No feedback
- You don't really care who I am and what motivates me 
- No work-life balance (no respect for private life hours)

summary: Challenging, rewarding, and a strong culture.
advice: A wise man once told me to be like an ape, never let go of a branch behind you before you have a firm grasp on the branch in front of you, and never leap for the branch you think will be strong, always leap for the branch you know is strong.
pros: Employee development is at the center of their game.
cons: The company is going through several regional and international changes that can make job certainty and or long term planning difficult for an employee's career.

advice: The company is too top heavy with management and big thinkers.  They need more doers to actually meet their goals and get things accomplished.
pros: The pay was good and the benefits were really nice compared to US based companies. They understand what a good work life balance is supposed to be.
cons:
It was difficult to make progress on any major projects due to the layers of bureaucracy. Some benefits were removed in the last couple of years that really disrupted moral.
The company is too top heavy with management and big thinkers. They need more doers to actually meet their goals and get things accomplished.

summary: Management are very Political and do NOT know how to Resolve Org Problems
advice: Some should be in UNDERCOVER BOSS to learn the "Real" things happening that middle management are hiding to protect their own jobs!
pros:
Well established global investment bank - largest bank in Germany
Highly talented people
Very lean organization
Employees are paid well and have good benefits
cons:
Sr Management do not know what the root of the issues - failing regulatory requirements several times in the past 5 years.
Making changes left and right like throwing darts in the dark. 
Making quarterly layoffs in the US, and not in Germany.
Very rigid organizational structure

summary: Great for Just Collecting a Paycheck
advice: Embrace new technology, and processes. Be more clear about bonus, raises, mid and year end reviews. Actually have meetings with employees. Build employees up and encourage/reward them to learn new technologies and stay current with the industry.
pros:
-Dev work was initially interesting
-Relaxed culture
-Lot of vacation and paid volunteer time
-Free coffee
cons:
-Work quickly becomes stale and repetitive
-Uses very old technology and is terrified/unable to even think about upgrading to current languages or frameworks
-Can go many days with very little or no actual dev work
-Many many many unnecessary meetings all the time
-Irrelevant required training
-Career growth is a joke here

advice: Don't worry...be happy :)
pros: They are hiring a lot of people in the North Carolina location. There are many opportunities to stand out because a lot of duplication and ineffeciency to stamp out. A slower pace compared to the tech industry and you are given time to learn on the job and slowly integrate into the culture. The people are very friendly and nice for most part, in a way find it refreshing compared to working at a tech company with less than adjusted geniuses.
cons: Mediocre talent, usual bureaucracy of a large institution, not a very nimble org.

summary: Opportunity for growth for people that work for it
advice: Challenge all employees, from interns to veterans, to stay sharp and innovative in order to keep the working environment engaging
pros: Motivated individuals will find plenty of opportunities for professional and personal growth if they seek it.  This is a company that gives back as much as you put in.  Internal transfer is strongly encouraged for individuals that want broad experience across the bank.
cons: As with many large corporations, there are individuals that are not career oriented and put in as little as possible to get by the day.  Sometimes DB confuses experience with expertise.

advice: - Promote employees who have done good work.
pros:
- Good name for resume
- Small team environment allows for more opportunity to be exposed to a greater variety of work.
- Great benefit package.
cons:
- Unwillingness to share information between teams and resulting in duplicate work to be done again and again.
- Very few women amongst the senior management.
- Management pays more attention to the total number of hours spent in the office than to worker efficiency.
- Promotion process lacks transparency.
- Inter-team cooperation is almost non-existent.
- Work environment is too political
- Excessive bureaucracy
- Senior management tends to be unreasonable and inflexible.

summary: A wonderful place to work overall
pros: Workplace is full of intelligent and dedicated colleagues. Great benefits and opportunities for international business travel and long term assignments. Excellent resume builder.
cons: The Jacksonville site is a cost saving operations center, so there is not as much room for front office or upper managment growth. Management can be short sighted at times. Internal promotions do not always carry a competitive salary increase.

summary: Great plac eto get your career going
advice: Open up to the way modern companies like Google treat their employees. Good health / financial benefits is not all we need. Provide spaces to take naps, give free healthy lunches, start a gym in the office, etc. There are many things you could improve on in this regard.
pros:
- Nice Co-workers
- Nice salads in the cafeteria
- They recognize and support talented people
- Quite diverse in the lower ranks
cons:
- Lack of diversity as you move up
- A lot of administrative overhead in getting things done
- Difficult on-boarding process

summary: One of the worst companies i ever worked for.
advice: Stay here, and don't let the local managers leave. We wouldn't want them going to other companies that are still ok and where we could find a more appropriate working environment.
pros:
Deduction of transportation costs.
Bookster account
cons:
Worst Management i ever encountered
Lazy and incompetent people are promoted, while the working and capable people are ignored and in some cases encouraged to leave the company.
Bad infrastracture, and a lot of bureaucracy. If you want to get things done, Deutsche Bank is not for you, however if you want to waste time, then here is the perfect place.

pros: Salary and benefits are good.
cons: This is a terrible place for technology workers. Aside from the fact that IT employees get penalized for all the ethical and financial screw ups of some greedy traders, this place does not provide the simplest environment for IT staff (including developers ..etc) to be successful. Everything is locked down, and the simplest tasks can take weeks if not months to happen. From career perspective, there are very limited promotions in the RTP office in North Carolina, and the site is not growing anymore.  All power is given to the UK and German offices, with remote offices acting only as implementation force, no more.

summary: Good in general but also depends on the project
advice: Promote only the skilled people, increase the number of work from home days once the pandemic is over.

advice: Wise up. There is a lot of IT talent in Jacksonville, but mediocre pay will only retain mediocre talent. You get what you pay for.

advice: Take a more active role in making sure your teams career goals are inline with their expecations.

summary: A company with lots of opportunities, yet a hot mess to work at
advice:
Provide more structural stability for employees. Limit outside hiring. Develop your existing staff; equip them with skills that will increase their marketability, as opposed to trying to trap them at DB with internal trainings and development programs that are overly limited. The staff will appreciate it and this will likely increase your retention ratio. In addition, it may help you trust them more, a trait which is necessary for proper delegation.

You need a flatter organizational structure, so that senior management can be appraised of what is going on without generating a need for bureaucratic paperwork in the form of excessive report writing, presentations and calls.

Take a close look at your back-office, specifically HR and Technology, and ensure that the right responsibilities are assigned in the right places, and (very important) that said responsibilities are aligned with the right incentives.
pros:
A world-class brand. Some great people. Truly a global bank offering lots of opportunity to work in various continents. Deutsche has beautiful buildings and good looking staff. Everyone is well dressed and professional. It offers world-class finance and banking operations. Opportunity to have exposure to people from all over the world.

Deutsche bank has a great social responsibility initiatives and is a leader in green energy buildings.
cons:
Technology is a hot mess, having grown through numerous acquisitions. Systems are outdated and dysfunctional. As a user, basic day to day tasks such as email, calendar, expenses and time off are a hassle to complete. As someone with administrative responsibilities, it is an extremely difficult environment to get anything done.

The management structure is a mess, with dotted lines all over the place. All decisions have to be approved by numerous people. It's clear that senior management distrusts lower level management to make appropriate decisions. The issue is made worse by the frequency with which new management is hired from the outside, who lack the necessary background / knowledge to make the appropriate decisions. The result is a complete inability to get anything done.

The place is a revolving door, at least in the regions.

summary: boosted my career for another job

They signed a support contract with HP and farmed my job to them. When I left the job HP took their contribution to my 401k back even though I was fully vested. Will never work for DB no matter how much they offer.

cons: The company is going through several regional and international changes that can make job certainty and or long term planning difficult for an employee's career.

summary: Fantastic during the glory days of big finance, but faltering now.

Promotion is very hard unless you are in the US or UK. There is a lot of cronyism.

summary: DB is a very messy bank everywhere you go.
advice:
some  senior managers are completely incompetent.  there's lots of politics within the IT groups.  If you think that it's not there because you don't see it, you can assure yourself that it's very much there.  you can also assure yourself that there's lots of back stabbers and mostly everyone is out there for themselves.  

the promotion process mainly involves something called a 'PMO,' which is a very one sided assessment of you by your manager.  if you have a bad manager, then tough luck.  DB does not practice the 360 review where subordinates get to review their managers.
pros: it's got a good brand name that's recognized on wall street.  Lots of interaction with people in the London office since that's their largest operation site.  lots of europeans all over the bank.  intra sites are functional and communicative.  lots of career development classes within the bank to enhance knowledge, but the classes are sometimes not very helpful.   the location is very convenient on wall st by subway transit.  For IT, there's the internal IT mobility program that's encouraged for you to move from one technology group to another.  However you still must be careful.  though it is encouraged by upper mgmt, some middle managers are still very petty about letting people leave their team.
cons:
the place is a mess everywhere you go within the bank.  I made a lateral move within the bank between 2 IT groups and things in both groups was very disorganized.  On a technical level, the bank does not have it's act together in certain IT groups.  Also from talking to people in the bank, it seems like it's messy on the business side as well.

HR at DB is pure evil.  I was sexually harassed by one of my managers and HR, not only did not help me, but also made life absolutely miserable.  At the end they denied all that's happened as if I made the entire thing up.

pros: They lure candidates in with good pay and benefits
cons: Where to begin, you could quite seriously write a dissertation on the poor career quality at this place. I have been in the Jacksonville office for 4 years and have seen countless scenarios of amazing performers being turned down for the ONCE A YEAR promotion process (no you cannot be promoted outside of this annual process) to Associate/AVP etc due to politics and department caps, yet absolute garbage employees being hired for Associate/AVP externally. Your entire job here is soul sucking because you spend all day every day fixing "breaks" between systems that the company is too cheap to properly implement. There is no IT here, only clerks in India with a poorly written manual and a manager demanding they close out the work ticket. Constant reorgs trying to figure out how to fix the myriad of issues yet they only serve to give certain people promotions while the others suffer and are left confused as to who they report to. At the end of the day you just have MORE bosses. Toxic work environment where the managers won't even talk to you or acknowledge your existence unless you quit, then they get upset because once again they have to go through the painful round of hiring a candidate which due to company bureaucracy takes between 3-4 months. If you are applying here don't give notice until just before your start date or you could go without a paycheck for months. A lot of people just quit the department to go to a competitor in town BEFORE bonuses were even paid out, that speaks for the desperation to leave and the sub par quality of bonuses. There is zero recognition for hard/above and beyond work because either your manager will take credit or simply no one cares. Once again only those favorites will get a promotion. Complete mismatch between companies stated values and actual quality of work. The department also makes the foolish mistake of only having one person trained on a unique role so that if you decide to move internally you will be stuck training your replacement for months on end, or if you quit they beg you to train your external replacement, who won't start for months.....Maybe other departments are okay to work for but certainly not product control or whatever they decided to name themselves today. If you are a manager elsewhere looking to hire a DB employee don't look down on the fact that someone here hasn't been promoted, chances are they deserved to be many times over, DB just doesn't promote promotions.... You can't even begin to explain how poor the work environment is here, you just have to witness it. Or maybe ask around.....

summary: No Leadership, No Training, No Help
pros: Job is obtainable at a decent salary even if you aren't qualified.
cons:
Many of us were lied to about what the job was when we were hired. The original job posting was for an Automation Engineer. They put us in IT Support. This caused so many people to quit that all the teams are short staffed and overworked. Now that the old site manager is gone and a new one is hiring with honest postings, no one actually wants the job. Probably why they lied in the first place.
Management is a joke, there's no plan, no training, no one helps each other, especially between regions. It's basically the uppers complaining about things until someone hopefully fixes it. They roll over when other teams push back, which means there's no consistency in how to operate, and no documentation to refer to how it's actually supposed to run.
Everyone is so swamped with work that there's no time to do the 'Automation' job that we were supposedly being hired to do. It's just user support issues. They took away the level 1 support so now both jobs fall on the production teams. Tasks that should be handled by the devs are also on the production team, again because the leadership just rolls over and doesn't stand up for their team.
On the occasion someone manages to get on a call with the uppers to raise concerns. Their solution is to stop having those calls with the teams. Mention this to the site managers and they laugh and do nothing about it. And they wonder out loud (again complaining instead of planning) why everyone is quitting.
No one is willing to help each other. There's no training. There's nothing to learn. The things you waste your afternoon talking about that's supposed to be 'training' never get used.
There's no documentation, not even for the users, who come to you constantly for advice on how to use a program you didn't make. You get yelled at for not resolving issues that you can't fix. You get yelled at for doing something that you thought was policy because someone complained so that's not policy anymore. You're constantly on the hook for another teams work that you're waiting on, and there's no accountability if they don't fix the issue because again, leadership just rolls over.
The people you work with a nice enough, because we're all in it together, but I don't know a single person there that's happy to work at Deutsche Bank.

One major concern is the negative impact of the leadership, specifically the CEO and COO. It appears that their decision-making has contributed to the overall instability and low morale that has emerged within the current workforce.

Furthermore, the changes seem to be driven by a desire for short-term gains (profit). This approach has eroded the employee trust that Nationwide once stood out for. It's disheartening to witness a financial institution, which should prioritise stability and reliability, succumb to a pattern of constant transformation that disrupts the customer experience.

While I appreciate an organisation's need to adapt to the evolving financial landscape, the frequency and seemingly abrupt nature of Nationwide's changes leave much to be desired. summary: New leadership seem determined to undo progress
advice:
Please be honest with your employees. People can see through the mindless bleating about 'water cooler chats' - why are you actually mandating people back to offices - is it because all the cool kids (ie the big banks) are doing it?

Stop making people redundant and trying to replace their roles with offshore resource. You cannot replace people with 15+ years of experience at Nationwide with underpaid foreign labour and expect the same quality and pace of output.

Please stop pretending that you want people to 'say it straight'; are you sure it shouldn't be 'say exactly what I want to hear or say nothing'?

The path you are on is leading your best employees to quit in droves, leaving behind a demotivated workforce that have neither the time nor inclination to work as hard on delivery as we had previously. Members will leave for competitors if we continue to pretend to be a bank - they want a mutual, we should be focusing on what makes us different rather than trying to be TSB or NatWest 2.0
pros:
Pension is fantastic - employer contributes 17% if you do 7%.

Some of the engineering teams have really good 'micro-cultures' separate to those of the wider business but it's entirely dependent on tech and delivery leads.

Employees in engineering are generally pleasant to work with, solution-focused, very bright and determined to deliver real benefits to the society.

Option to do compressed hours means you can work a 4-day week if you're willing to make up the time Mon-Thurs.
cons:
The new leadership team, headed up by Debbie and Suresh, seem determined to undo the good work of the previous CEO, Joe Garner. Since her arrival, the main 'achievements' of the new CEO are
- reversing the 'remote first' policy. This has proven especially controversial as many people were hired on the understanding they would not need to regularly commute to Swindon, London or Northampton and are now being told if they can't, there's no prospect of future promotions. Speaking from an engineering / tech perspective, it's also led to many of us with childcare responsibilities seriously considering if it makes financial sense to continue working.
- rebranding the society to look suspiciously like NatWest, a direct competitor. This work included blowing millions of members' money on a snazzy TV ad but surely this money could've been better spent? We've also lost the words 'building society' from our logo and branding, which cynically makes me think Debbie is determined to turn Nationwide into just another bank, but with worse pay.
- ramping up use of offshore contractors, some of whom are decent at their jobs, but many of whom aren't. At the same time, there have been multiple rounds of redundancies and restructures which have been incredibly disruptive, even to those not impacted directly. The irony of forcing UK workers back into the office whilst also increasing use of colleagues based in India, who will literally never travel to Swindon or London, has not been lost on me or my team.
- removal of the NGSU (colleague union) online forum. This was previously a safe space for colleagues to be able to discuss the direction and future of Nationwide. I've also noticed comments on internal news stories being turned off and other examples of 'policing' - despite 'say it straight' supposedly being one of our new company values.

Management is by fear, all senior managers have very slopey  shoulders and don't want to be seen taking any accountability in case something goes wrong. I heard a rumour that the head of my practice had admitted he walked around with a resignation letter in his jacket. So he could have it to hand in a seconds notice. From talking to other people around the business, no one was happy. I hope that there is, and someone leaves a positive review. I just haven't meant them there.

advice:
Stop hiring external management consultants when you already have overqualified staff who know what needs to be done. The money that could be saved would more that fund my suggestions below.

Accelerate upward progression into decision making and empowered roles, for rising stars within their disciplines who will drive innovation inside nationwide, that already happened within our competitors years ago. Just because someone has been employed by Nationwide for 25+ years, does not mean they are better for a specific role that someone who has only been for 2 years; actually quite the opposite can be argued for an organisation that needs to learn from the external marketplace.

Step up and drive the organisational processes to where they should already be. Move focus away from "delivery" and "projects" and long term financial plans and approval boards, to a truly fixed-funded model (like all other companies), who operate with a customer centric product mindset - hire product managers who are actually product managers, with market experience and suitable qualifications. 

Retrain existing delivery managers (professionally) as Scrum Masters and ban the use of the term Delivery or reference to fixed plans and timelines. 

Widen the salary banding for all roles, such that the best candidates can be secured in a competitive market. This has been a significant challenge in the engineering business where specific skills are in short supply and our engineering managers are not empowered to offer what other companies already offer.

Create clear paths for career progression (AS A PRIORITY), salary increases at least on par with our competitors and incentives to keep people in roles and to prevent attrition. With these things in place there would be no attraction to leaving Nationwide.
pros:
The business is a Mutuality - which means the whole mentality around operating is focused on the members, including the employees. 

The is the exact antithesis of most corporations with a purer capitalist mentality. The base salaries are market rate for non-technical roles, nothing to get overly excited about but not bad, but other benefits such as 30 days holiday, 8x life assurance as standard and 16% employer pension contribution when you put in 7% makes for a very comfortable employment. 

The profit sharing process is unlike anything I have experienced before where everyone either gets "the bonus" of everyone doesn't. It is in no way linked to individual performance, but there is also no incentive to perform better to increase said bonus.

Nationwide also have a work from anywhere policy, so no pressure to commute to an office if you don't want to.

I'm sure everyone in permanent roles feels incredibly secure as no one ever seems to get made redundant, maybe even when they really should be... 

It would be incredibly comfy to just sit in this role until 60 then retire on the phat pension.

Complete flexibility and no micromanagement over stepping out, hours worked etc. Completely operating on trust (based on your line manager I suppose).
cons: The organisation is very slow, old fashioned, lacks agility, a lot of "dinosaurs" in the decision making roles and it's very hard for younger innovators to get up into those roles. Sadly it seems we will have to wait for retirements to arrive... Lots of bureaucratic hoops to jump through and unnecessary approvals that other FS companies did away with years ago. A lot of focus on "delivery" and projects which inhibits organisational transformation - no one who is empowered to do so, seems keen to make the tough calls on opimtising the organisation and how it operates.
